Exceptions, Try-methods and filters

`TryParse` for expected failures, `throw` expressions for guards, `when` filters to catch only what you handle.

using System.Globalization;

static int ParsePort(string text) =>
    int.TryParse(text, NumberStyles.None, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, out var n) && n is > 0 and < 65536
        ? n
        : throw new FormatException($"not a port: {text}");

foreach (var input in new[] { "8080", "http", "70000" })
{
    try
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"port {ParsePort(input)}");
    }
    catch (FormatException e) when (e.Message.StartsWith("not a port", StringComparison.Ordinal))
    {
        Console.WriteLine(e.Message);
    }
}

Value vs reference, and `with`

A struct copies on assignment, a class aliases; `with` makes a shallow non-destructive copy of a record.

var p1 = new PointStruct { X = 1 };
var p2 = p1;                                   // copied
p2.X = 99;
var b1 = new Box { X = 1 };
var b2 = b1;                                   // the same object
b2.X = 99;
var r1 = new Settings("dark", ["x"]);
var r2 = r1 with { Theme = "light" };
Console.WriteLine($"{p1.X} {b1.X} {r1 == (r1 with { })} {ReferenceEquals(r1.Tags, r2.Tags)} {r2.Theme}");

class Box { public int X; }

Shared State — lock, Interlocked, SemaphoreSlim, Channels

Keeping threads and tasks from racing on shared data — none of it checked by the compiler.

Swift isolation → C#

Swift proves data-race freedom at compile time; C# leaves it to these tools and to discipline.

SwiftC#Difference
actorstate owned by one consumer of a Channel<T>no reentrancy unless you write it
actor-isolated mutationlock (sync code), SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync (async code)lock cannot contain an await
Sendable—no compiler check: immutable records and ImmutableArray by convention
@MainActorthe UI thread's SynchronizationContext / Dispatchera runtime mechanism
atomic countersInterlocked—

lock and Interlocked

100,000 increments from the thread pool. A plain `count++` would lose updates; both of these do not.

var gate = new Lock();
var guarded = 0;
var atomic = 0;
Parallel.For(0, 100_000, _ =>
{
    lock (gate) { guarded++; }
    Interlocked.Increment(ref atomic);
});
Console.WriteLine($"guarded={guarded} atomic={atomic}");
Result
guarded=100000 atomic=100000

An async mutex with SemaphoreSlim

A read-modify-write that spans an `await` needs an async-aware lock.

var gate = new SemaphoreSlim(1, 1);
var balance = 0;

async Task Deposit(int amount)
{
    await gate.WaitAsync();
    try
    {
        var read = balance;
        await Task.Yield();                    // an await inside the critical section
        balance = read + amount;
    }
    finally
    {
        gate.Release();
    }
}

await Task.WhenAll(Enumerable.Range(0, 100).Select(_ => Deposit(10)));
Console.WriteLine(balance);
Result
1000

One owner behind a Channel

Producers write messages; a single consumer owns the state — the actor shape, without a compiler check.

using System.Threading.Channels;

var inbox = Channel.CreateUnbounded<int>();
var total = 0;
var owner = Task.Run(async () =>
{
    await foreach (var amount in inbox.Reader.ReadAllAsync())
        total += amount;                       // only the owner touches total
});

await Task.WhenAll(Enumerable.Range(0, 100).Select(_ => inbox.Writer.WriteAsync(10).AsTask()));
inbox.Writer.Complete();
await owner;
Console.WriteLine(total);

1000

Rules

Without a compiler check, the design has to make races impossible.

  • Prefer immutable messages: record types with init properties, ImmutableArray<T>.
  • ConcurrentDictionary for a shared cache; GetOrAdd may run the factory more than once.
  • lock (this) or lock (typeof(X)): anyone can take the same lock. Lock a private object (or a Lock).
  • volatile makes writes visible, not compound updates atomic: x++ still races.

Writing atomically

Write a temporary sibling, `Flush(flushToDisk: true)`, then move it over the target in one rename.

static void WriteAtomically(string path, string text)
{
    var temp = Path.Combine(Path.GetDirectoryName(path)!, $".{Path.GetFileName(path)}.{Guid.NewGuid():N}.tmp");
    using (var stream = new FileStream(temp, FileMode.CreateNew, FileAccess.Write))
    using (var writer = new StreamWriter(stream))
    {
        writer.Write(text);
        writer.Flush();
        stream.Flush(flushToDisk: true);       // on the device before the move publishes it
    }
    File.Move(temp, path, overwrite: true);    // a rename within one volume
}

var dir = Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory("atomic-");
var settings = Path.Combine(dir.FullName, "settings.json");
WriteAtomically(settings, """{"theme":"dark"}""");
WriteAtomically(settings, """{"theme":"light"}""");
Console.WriteLine(File.ReadAllText(settings));
dir.Delete(recursive: true);
Result
{"theme":"light"}

Where things belong

Ask the runtime for the folder; a hard-coded path breaks on the next OS, user or install location.

PurposeAccessorNotes
Scratch for one operationPath.GetTempPath(), Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory()shared with every process and purged by the OS: delete what you create
App data the user never browses (caches, databases, logs)Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.LocalApplicationData) + your app's folder%LOCALAPPDATA% on Windows, ~/Library/Application Support on macOS, ~/.local/share on Linux
Settings that roam with a Windows domain userEnvironment.SpecialFolder.ApplicationData%APPDATA% on Windows, ~/.config on Linux; the same folder as above on macOS
Files the user created and expects to findEnvironment.SpecialFolder.MyDocumentswrite there only when the user asks (a save dialog), never silently
Data shared by every user of the machineEnvironment.SpecialFolder.CommonApplicationDataC:\ProgramData on Windows; writing usually needs elevated rights
Files shipped with the appAppContext.BaseDirectoryread-only once installed; not Environment.CurrentDirectory, which is wherever the app was launched from
A .NET MAUI app (Android, iOS, Mac Catalyst, Windows)FileSystem.AppDataDirectory, FileSystem.CacheDirectory, FileSystem.OpenAppPackageFileAsyncAppDataDirectory is private and backed up (Android Auto Backup, iCloud); CacheDirectory is not, and the OS may clear it; bundled assets open as streams, not paths

Sources: Environment.SpecialFolder — .NET API · File system helpers — .NET MAUI

Path.Combine, Path.Join, and untrusted names

Build paths with `Path` APIs, never `+`; `Combine` restarts at a rooted segment, `Join` does not, and neither stops `..` — resolve and check (lexically; links need one more check).

static string Show(string path) => path.Replace('\\', '/');   // print the same on Windows

// Combine restarts at a rooted segment; Join only concatenates. Neither normalizes "..".
Console.WriteLine($"Combine: {Show(Path.Combine("uploads", "2026", "invoice.pdf"))}");
Console.WriteLine($"Combine(\"uploads\", \"/etc/passwd\"): {Show(Path.Combine("uploads", "/etc/passwd"))}");
Console.WriteLine($"Join(\"uploads\", \"/etc/passwd\"):    {Show(Path.Join("uploads", "/etc/passwd"))}");

var export = Path.Join("exports", "orders.2026-11.csv");
Console.WriteLine($"{Path.GetFileName(export)} | {Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(export)}"
                  + $" | {Path.GetExtension(export)} | {Show(Path.ChangeExtension(export, ".json"))}");

// An uploaded file name is untrusted: join, resolve, then prove the result is still under the root.
var root = Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory("uploads-");
try
{
    foreach (var name in new[] { "invoice.pdf", "../../.ssh/id_rsa", "/etc/passwd", "q4/../summary.csv", "" })
    {
        var path = ResolveUnder(root.FullName, name);
        var shown = path is null ? "rejected" : Show(Path.GetRelativePath(root.FullName, path));
        Console.WriteLine($"{$"\"{name}\"",-20} -> {shown}");
    }
}
finally { root.Delete(recursive: true); }

// A lexical check only: if entries can be symbolic links (an extracted archive), also check
// new FileInfo(full).ResolveLinkTarget(returnFinalTarget: true), or refuse FileAttributes.ReparsePoint.
static string? ResolveUnder(string root, string untrustedName)
{
    var fullRoot = Path.TrimEndingDirectorySeparator(Path.GetFullPath(root)) + Path.DirectorySeparatorChar;
    var full = Path.GetFullPath(Path.Join(fullRoot, untrustedName));   // collapses ".." segments
    if (full.Length <= fullRoot.Length) return null;                   // "" or "." is the root itself
    var comparison = OperatingSystem.IsWindows()                       // Windows paths are case-insensitive
        ? StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase
        : StringComparison.Ordinal;
    return full.StartsWith(fullRoot, comparison) ? full : null;
}
Result

Join("uploads", "/etc/passwd"):    uploads/etc/passwd
orders.2026-11.csv | orders.2026-11 | .csv | exports/orders.2026-11.json
"invoice.pdf"        -> invoice.pdf
"../../.ssh/id_rsa"  -> rejected
"/etc/passwd"        -> etc/passwd

Real durability: Flush(true) and File.Replace

When "the power went out" has to be survivable (a ledger, a journal): flush to the device, then swap in the new file — a rename on Linux and macOS, not atomic on Windows — keeping a backup to restore at start-up.

using System.Text;

// The order ledger must survive a power cut: bytes on the device first, then swap the new file in.
var dir = Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory("ledger-");
try
{
    var ledger = Path.Join(dir.FullName, "ledger.json");
    SaveDurably(ledger, """{"orders":1}""");
    SaveDurably(ledger, """{"orders":2}""");
    Console.WriteLine($"current {File.ReadAllText(ledger)}, backup {File.ReadAllText(ledger + ".bak")}");
    var files = Directory.GetFiles(dir.FullName).Select(Path.GetFileName).Order();
    Console.WriteLine($"files: {string.Join(", ", files)}");
}
finally { dir.Delete(recursive: true); }

static void SaveDurably(string path, string json)
{
    var temp = path + ".tmp";                            // a sibling: same volume, so the swap is a rename
    using (var stream = new FileStream(temp, FileMode.Create, FileAccess.Write, FileShare.None))
    {
        stream.Write(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(json));
        stream.Flush(flushToDisk: true);                 // fsync / FlushFileBuffers: past the OS cache
    }
    try
    {
        // Linux/macOS: rename(2), atomic. Windows: ReplaceFileW (per the runtime source) is NOT atomic — it
        // can leave only path.bak, and it fails while a reader holds path without FileShare.Delete.
        File.Replace(temp, path, path + ".bak");
    }
    catch (FileNotFoundException) when (!File.Exists(path))   // the first save: nothing to replace yet
    {
        File.Move(temp, path);
    }
    finally
    {
        File.Delete(temp);                               // gone on success; never left behind on failure
    }
}
// On start-up: if ledger.json is missing but ledger.json.bak exists, restore the backup.
// Windows readers: open with FileShare.ReadWrite | FileShare.Delete, or the save fails while they read.
// Flush(true) is F_FULLFSYNC on macOS (per the runtime source). The BCL cannot fsync a directory, so on
// Linux and macOS the rename itself may not be durable yet: where that matters, use SQLite.

Streaming a large write

Export millions of rows in constant memory: one buffered `StreamWriter`, `await using` so the last flush is awaited, a temporary file published by a move.

using System.Globalization;
using System.Text;

// Export 200,000 order rows to CSV without holding them: one buffered writer, a temporary file, one move.
var dir = Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory("export-");
try
{
    var target = Path.Join(dir.FullName, "orders.csv");
    var temp = target + ".partial";
    var options = new FileStreamOptions
    {
        Mode = FileMode.CreateNew,
        Access = FileAccess.Write,
        Options = FileOptions.Asynchronous,
        BufferSize = 0,                                  // StreamWriter already buffers; skip a second copy
        PreallocationSize = 8 << 20,                     // a hint: reserve ~8 MB up front, fewer extents
    };
    var utf8 = new UTF8Encoding(encoderShouldEmitUTF8Identifier: false);   // Encoding.UTF8 would write a BOM
    await using (var writer = new StreamWriter(temp, utf8, options))
    {
        writer.NewLine = "\n";                           // not Environment.NewLine: same bytes on every OS
        await writer.WriteLineAsync("id,customer,total");
        foreach (var row in Orders(200_000))
            await writer.WriteLineAsync(row);            // buffered: a syscall per buffer, not per row
    }                                                    // await using: the final flush is awaited too
    File.Move(temp, target);

    var lines = 0;
    await foreach (var _ in File.ReadLinesAsync(target)) lines++;
    var size = new FileInfo(target).Length;
    Console.WriteLine(string.Create(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, $"{lines:N0} lines, {size:N0} bytes"));
}
finally { dir.Delete(recursive: true); }

static IEnumerable<string> Orders(int count)
{
    for (var i = 1; i <= count; i++)
        yield return string.Create(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, $"{i},customer-{i % 997},{i % 500 + 0.99m}");
}

200,001 lines, 5,222,805 bytes

Algorithm — external merge sort

Sort a file larger than RAM: sorted runs that fit in memory, then a k-way merge through a `PriorityQueue` holding one line per run.

// Sort an order-id file too big for memory: sorted runs of 5,000 lines, then a k-way merge.
// O(n log n) overall; the merge is O(n log k) with O(k) memory. In production, size runs by bytes.
var dir = Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory("sort-");
try
{
    var input = Path.Join(dir.FullName, "orders.txt");
    var random = new Random(5);
    File.WriteAllLines(input, Enumerable.Range(0, 20_000).Select(_ => $"ord-{random.Next(1_000_000):D6}"));

    var runs = new List<string>();
    foreach (var chunk in File.ReadLines(input).Chunk(5_000))   // lazy: one chunk in memory at a time
    {
        Array.Sort(chunk, StringComparer.Ordinal);       // ordinal: fast, and the same on every machine
        runs.Add(Path.Join(dir.FullName, $"run-{runs.Count}.txt"));
        File.WriteAllLines(runs[^1], chunk);
    }

    var output = Path.Join(dir.FullName, "orders.sorted.txt");
    MergeRuns(runs, output);
    runs.ForEach(File.Delete);
    var sorted = File.ReadAllLines(output);
    var inOrder = sorted.SequenceEqual(sorted.Order(StringComparer.Ordinal));
    Console.WriteLine($"{runs.Count} runs, {sorted.Length} lines, in order: {inOrder}, from {sorted[0]}");
}
finally { dir.Delete(recursive: true); }

static void MergeRuns(List<string> runs, string output)
{
    var readers = runs.Select(r => new StreamReader(r)).ToList();
    try
    {
        var heads = new PriorityQueue<int, string>(StringComparer.Ordinal);   // run index, by current line
        for (var i = 0; i < readers.Count; i++)
            if (readers[i].ReadLine() is { } first) heads.Enqueue(i, first);
        using var writer = new StreamWriter(output);
        while (heads.TryDequeue(out var run, out var smallest))      // always the global minimum
        {
            writer.WriteLine(smallest);
            if (readers[run].ReadLine() is { } next) heads.Enqueue(run, next);   // refill from that run
        }
    }
    finally { readers.ForEach(r => r.Dispose()); }
}
Result
4 runs, 20000 lines, in order: True, from ord-000014

Algorithm — an offset index for random access

Build the index once in one sequential pass, then read any line with one positional `RandomAccess.Read` — a log viewer that jumps to line 50,001.

using System.Text;

// Jump to any line of a large log in one read: index the byte offset of every line start once.
var dir = Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory("index-");
try
{
    var log = Path.Join(dir.FullName, "access.log");
    var lines = Enumerable.Range(0, 100_000)
        .Select(i => $"{i} GET /orders/{i * 7 % 1000} {(i % 50 == 0 ? 500 : 200)}\n");
    File.WriteAllText(log, string.Concat(lines));

    var offsets = BuildIndex(log);                       // 8 bytes per line; save it beside the file
    using var handle = File.OpenHandle(log);             // RandomAccess: positional reads, no shared cursor
    foreach (var n in new[] { 0, 50_001, 99_999 })
        Console.WriteLine($"line {n}: {ReadLine(handle, offsets, n)}");
}
finally { dir.Delete(recursive: true); }

static List<long> BuildIndex(string path)
{
    var offsets = new List<long> { 0 };
    using var stream = new FileStream(path, FileMode.Open, FileAccess.Read, FileShare.Read, 1 << 16,
                                      FileOptions.SequentialScan);
    var buffer = new byte[1 << 16];
    long position = 0;
    int read;
    while ((read = stream.Read(buffer)) > 0)
    {
        for (var i = 0; i < read; i++)
            if (buffer[i] == (byte)'\n') offsets.Add(position + i + 1);
        position += read;
    }
    if (offsets[^1] == stream.Length) offsets.RemoveAt(offsets.Count - 1);   // a final newline starts nothing
    return offsets;
}

static string ReadLine(Microsoft.Win32.SafeHandles.SafeFileHandle handle, List<long> offsets, int n)
{
    var end = n + 1 < offsets.Count ? offsets[n + 1] : RandomAccess.GetLength(handle);
    var bytes = new byte[end - offsets[n]];
    var read = RandomAccess.Read(handle, bytes, fileOffset: offsets[n]);   // fewer if the file shrank since
    return Encoding.UTF8.GetString(bytes, 0, read).TrimEnd('\r', '\n');
}
// Fixed-width records need no index: offset = n * recordSize, and a sorted file can be binary searched.
Result
line 0: 0 GET /orders/0 500
line 50001: 50001 GET /orders/7 200
line 99999: 99999 GET /orders/993 200

Algorithm — tail -n

The last lines of a huge log, reading fixed blocks backwards from the end — the same lines as `File.ReadAllLines(path).TakeLast(n)` on short, empty, blank-line and CRLF files.

using System.Text;

// tail -n: the last lines of a huge log, reading 4 KB blocks backwards from the end — never the whole file.
var dir = Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory("tail-");
try
{
    var log = Path.Join(dir.FullName, "sync.log");
    var lines = Enumerable.Range(1, 50_000).Select(i => $"sync batch {i % 1_000}: ok\n");
    File.WriteAllText(log, string.Concat(lines));
    Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" | ", Tail(log, 3)));

    var crlf = Path.Join(dir.FullName, "short.txt");     // fewer lines than asked, a blank one, CRLF ends
    File.WriteAllText(crlf, "first\r\n\r\nlast\r\n");
    Console.WriteLine($"[{string.Join("|", Tail(crlf, 10))}] same as ReadAllLines: "
                      + $"{Tail(crlf, 10).SequenceEqual(File.ReadAllLines(crlf).TakeLast(10))}");

    var empty = Path.Join(dir.FullName, "empty.txt");
    File.WriteAllText(empty, "");
    Console.WriteLine($"empty file: {Tail(empty, 3).Length} lines");
}
finally { dir.Delete(recursive: true); }

static string[] Tail(string path, int count)
{
    if (count <= 0) return [];
    using var handle = File.OpenHandle(path);
    var start = RandomAccess.GetLength(handle);
    var blocks = new List<byte[]>();
    var newlines = 0;
    while (start > 0 && newlines <= count)               // count + 1 newlines: the last line ends with one
    {
        var block = new byte[Math.Min(4_096, start)];
        start -= block.Length;
        RandomAccess.Read(handle, block, start);
        newlines += block.Count(b => b == (byte)'\n');
        blocks.Insert(0, block);
    }
    var text = Encoding.UTF8.GetString([.. blocks.SelectMany(b => b)]);
    if (text.Length == 0) return [];
    if (text.EndsWith('\n')) text = text[..^1];          // the last line's terminator, not an empty line
    return [.. text.Split('\n').TakeLast(count).Select(line => line.TrimEnd('\r'))];
}
Result
sync batch 998: ok | sync batch 999: ok | sync batch 0: ok
[first||last] same as ReadAllLines: True
empty file: 0 lines

Algorithm — distinct lines and a checksum

Count distinct lines with 8 bytes of hash each instead of the line (memory still grows with distinct lines), and SHA-256 a file of any size without loading it.

using System.Security.Cryptography;
using System.Text;

var dir = Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory("tools-");
try
{
    var log = Path.Join(dir.FullName, "sync.log");
    var lines = Enumerable.Range(1, 50_000).Select(i => $"sync batch {i % 1_000}: ok\n");
    File.WriteAllText(log, string.Concat(lines));

    // Distinct lines, keeping 8 bytes of SHA-256 per distinct line instead of the line itself: memory still
    // grows with distinct lines, and a 64-bit collision would merge two lines — fine for statistics only.
    var seen = new HashSet<ulong>();
    foreach (var line in File.ReadLines(log))
        seen.Add(BitConverter.ToUInt64(SHA256.HashData(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(line))));
    Console.WriteLine($"{seen.Count} distinct lines");

    // Checksum a file of any size: HashDataAsync reads the stream in chunks.
    await using var stream = File.OpenRead(log);
    var digest = await SHA256.HashDataAsync(stream);
    Console.WriteLine($"sha256 {Convert.ToHexString(digest).ToLowerInvariant()[..16]}...");
}
finally { dir.Delete(recursive: true); }

sha256 29010b25d5492e76...

Attributes and permissions

`FileInfo` for size, times and the read-only flag; `UnixFileMode` to create a secret owner-only — on Windows those APIs throw, and a file under the user's profile is already private to them (encrypt it with DPAPI `ProtectedData`, Windows only, from the `System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData` package).

// Metadata through FileInfo, and an API token file only its owner can read (Linux and macOS).
var dir = Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory("attrs-");
var report = new FileInfo(Path.Join(dir.FullName, "report.csv"));
try
{
    File.WriteAllText(report.FullName, "id,total\n1,9.99\n");
    report.LastWriteTimeUtc = new DateTime(2026, 11, 1, 8, 30, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc);   // the source's time
    report.IsReadOnly = true;
    report.Refresh();                                    // FileInfo caches: re-read after a change
    Console.WriteLine($"{report.Name}: {report.Length} bytes, modified {report.LastWriteTimeUtc:O}, "
                      + $"read-only {report.IsReadOnly}");

    var tokenPath = Path.Join(dir.FullName, "api-token");
    if (!OperatingSystem.IsWindows())
    {
        // Created owner-only (still filtered by the umask): a chmod after creating would leave a moment
        // when others could open it.
        var options = new FileStreamOptions
        {
            Mode = FileMode.CreateNew,
            Access = FileAccess.Write,
            UnixCreateMode = UnixFileMode.UserRead | UnixFileMode.UserWrite,   // 0600
        };
        using (var writer = new StreamWriter(tokenPath, options)) writer.Write("tok_test_123");
        Console.WriteLine($"token: {Describe(File.GetUnixFileMode(tokenPath))}");
        File.SetUnixFileMode(tokenPath, UnixFileMode.UserRead);              // read-only once written
        Console.WriteLine($"after chmod: {Describe(File.GetUnixFileMode(tokenPath))}");
    }
}
finally
{
    if (File.Exists(report.FullName)) report.IsReadOnly = false;   // Windows cannot delete a read-only file
    dir.Delete(recursive: true);
}

static string Describe(UnixFileMode mode) => $"{mode} (0{Convert.ToString((int)mode, 8)})";
Result

token: UserWrite, UserRead (0600)
after chmod: UserRead (0400)

File sharing and locking

`FileShare` says what others may do while you hold the file; on Linux and macOS it is an advisory `flock` that only other lockers honour (a no-op where `flock` is missing or `DOTNET_SYSTEM_IO_DISABLEFILELOCKING` is set), and `FileStream.Lock` (byte ranges) is unsupported on macOS.

// Only one sync job may run at a time, even across processes: hold a lock file opened with FileShare.None.
var dir = Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory("sync-");
try
{
    var lockPath = Path.Join(dir.FullName, "sync.lock");
    using (var first = TryAcquire(lockPath))
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"first job got the lock: {first is not null}");
        using var second = TryAcquire(lockPath);
        Console.WriteLine($"second job got the lock: {second is not null}");
    }
    Console.WriteLine($"lock file removed on close: {!File.Exists(lockPath)}");

    // Readers can follow a log while one writer appends, if each side allows what the other does.
    var log = Path.Join(dir.FullName, "events.log");
    var appending = new FileStream(log, FileMode.Append, FileAccess.Write, FileShare.Read);
    using var writer = new StreamWriter(appending) { AutoFlush = true };
    writer.Write("started\n");
    var following = new FileStream(log, FileMode.Open, FileAccess.Read, FileShare.ReadWrite);
    using var reader = new StreamReader(following);
    Console.WriteLine($"tail -f sees: {reader.ReadLine()}");
}
finally { dir.Delete(recursive: true); }

static FileStream? TryAcquire(string path)
{
    try
    {
        // Keep exactly these options: on Linux/macOS .NET re-checks that the locked file is still the one at
        // the path only for OpenOrCreate + FileShare.None + DeleteOnClose (per the runtime source).
        return new FileStream(path, FileMode.OpenOrCreate, FileAccess.ReadWrite, FileShare.None,
                              bufferSize: 1, FileOptions.DeleteOnClose);
    }
    catch (IOException)                                  // a sharing violation: someone holds it
    {
        return null;
    }
}
Result
first job got the lock: True
second job got the lock: False
lock file removed on close: True
tail -f sees: started

Files are blocking work: async APIs, never .Result

A disk can stall for seconds; keep it off the UI thread of a MAUI, WPF or WinUI app with the `*Async` APIs and `FileOptions.Asynchronous`, awaited all the way up.

Blocks the caller
var dir = Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory("settings-");
try
{
    var path = Path.Join(dir.FullName, "settings.json");
    File.WriteAllText(path, """{"theme":"dark"}""");

    // On a UI thread (MAUI, WPF, WinUI) this freezes the window for the whole read,
    // and .Result deadlocks when the awaited code needs that same thread back.
    string LoadSettings() => File.ReadAllTextAsync(path).Result;

    var settings = LoadSettings();
    Console.WriteLine($"{settings.Length} chars: {settings}");
}
finally { dir.Delete(recursive: true); }
Async all the way
var dir = Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory("settings-");
try
{
    var path = Path.Join(dir.FullName, "settings.json");
    await File.WriteAllTextAsync(path, """{"theme":"dark"}""");

    // Async all the way: FileOptions.Asynchronous asks for real overlapped I/O (it matters on Windows),
    // and the UI thread is free while the disk works. Cancellable when the page closes.
    async Task<string> LoadSettingsAsync(CancellationToken token)
    {
        await using var stream = new FileStream(path, FileMode.Open, FileAccess.Read, FileShare.Read,
                                                bufferSize: 4_096, FileOptions.Asynchronous);
        using var reader = new StreamReader(stream);
        return await reader.ReadToEndAsync(token);
    }

    var settings = await LoadSettingsAsync(CancellationToken.None);
    Console.WriteLine($"{settings.Length} chars: {settings}");
}
finally { dir.Delete(recursive: true); }
Result
16 chars: {"theme":"dark"}

System.IO.Pipelines in brief

For parsers over large files or sockets: `PipeReader` hands you pooled buffers and keeps a partial record for the next read, so nothing is copied into strings.

using System.Buffers;
using System.IO.Pipelines;

// Count error lines in a large log without allocating a string per line: PipeReader + SequenceReader.
var dir = Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory("pipes-");
try
{
    var log = Path.Join(dir.FullName, "app.log");
    var lines = Enumerable.Range(0, 100_000).Select(i => $"{(i % 40 == 0 ? "ERROR" : "INFO")} request {i}\n");
    await File.WriteAllTextAsync(log, string.Concat(lines));

    var reader = PipeReader.Create(File.OpenRead(log), new StreamPipeReaderOptions(bufferSize: 1 << 16));
    long total = 0, errors = 0;
    try
    {
        while (true)
        {
            var result = await reader.ReadAsync();
            var consumed = CountLines(result.Buffer, ref total, ref errors);
            reader.AdvanceTo(consumed, examined: result.Buffer.End);   // keep the partial last line for later
            if (result.IsCompleted) break;               // (a last line without '\n' stays in Buffer)
        }
    }
    finally { await reader.CompleteAsync(); }            // also disposes the FileStream
    Console.WriteLine($"{total} lines, {errors} errors");
}
finally { dir.Delete(recursive: true); }

// SequenceReader is a ref struct: it lives in a synchronous helper, not across an await.
static SequencePosition CountLines(ReadOnlySequence<byte> buffer, ref long total, ref long errors)
{
    var reader = new SequenceReader<byte>(buffer);
    while (reader.TryReadTo(out ReadOnlySequence<byte> line, (byte)'\n'))   // a line may span two segments
    {
        total++;
        if (new SequenceReader<byte>(line).IsNext("ERROR"u8)) errors++;
    }
    return reader.Position;
}
Result
100000 lines, 2500 errors

Error handling by exception

Try the operation and catch the specific exception — a check first (`File.Exists`) is stale by the time you act on it.

SituationYou catchNotes
File missingFileNotFoundExceptionderives from IOException, so catch it first; FileName says which file
A folder in the path missingDirectoryNotFoundExceptionalso an IOException; Directory.CreateDirectory is idempotent — call it before writing
No permission, or a read-only fileUnauthorizedAccessExceptionnot an IOException: a catch (IOException) alone misses it
Open elsewhere (sharing violation)IOExceptionon Windows HResult is 0x80070020; retry with backoff, then name the file in the error
Already exists (FileMode.CreateNew, File.Move without overwrite)IOExceptionon Windows HResult & 0xFFFF is 80 or 183
Disk fullIOExceptionon Windows 0x80070070; often thrown by Flush or Dispose, not by Write
Path too longPathTooLongExceptionan IOException too
Any of the above, genericallycatch (IOException e)on Linux and macOS the HResult of a plain IOException is not a Windows code: decide by type and operation, not by number

Sources: Handling I/O errors in .NET

Testing file code in a temp directory

A directory per test from `Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory`, deleted in `Dispose` whatever happens — in xUnit, the test class's constructor and `Dispose` — around code that takes its root as a parameter.

// Each test gets its own directory, removed whatever happens: tests can run in parallel and leave nothing.
SaveReplacesTheFileAndLeavesNoTemporaries();
Console.WriteLine("PASS save replaces the file and leaves no temporaries");
// The failure paths, in a directory of their own: see the next card.

static void SaveReplacesTheFileAndLeavesNoTemporaries()
{
    using var dir = new TempDirectory();             // xUnit: create in the constructor, delete in Dispose
    var store = new SettingsStore(dir.Root);
    store.Save("""{"theme":"dark"}""");
    store.Save("""{"theme":"light"}""");
    Expect(Directory.GetFiles(dir.Root).Select(Path.GetFileName).SequenceEqual(["settings.json"]));
    Expect(store.Load() == """{"theme":"light"}""");
}

static void Expect(bool condition)
{
    if (!condition) throw new InvalidOperationException("expectation failed");
}

sealed class TempDirectory : IDisposable
{
    public string Root { get; } = Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory("test-").FullName;
    public void Dispose() => Directory.Delete(Root, recursive: true);
}

// The code under test takes its root directory instead of a hard-coded or ambient path.
sealed class SettingsStore(string root)
{
    private readonly string _path = Path.Join(root, "settings.json");

    public string Load() => File.ReadAllText(_path);

    public void Save(string json)                        // flush and durability: see real-durability
    {
        var temp = $"{_path}.{Guid.NewGuid():N}.tmp";    // unique: two writers never share a temp file
        File.WriteAllText(temp, json);
        File.Move(temp, _path, overwrite: true);
    }
}
Result
PASS save replaces the file and leaves no temporaries

Testing the failure path of file code

A throwaway directory makes the error cases cheap to test too — here, loading before any save must throw `FileNotFoundException`, the case a `File.Exists` shortcut would hide.

// Failure paths are cheap to test in a throwaway directory: nothing to mock, nothing left behind.
LoadBeforeAnySaveThrowsFileNotFound();
Console.WriteLine("PASS load before any save throws FileNotFoundException");

static void LoadBeforeAnySaveThrowsFileNotFound()
{
    using var dir = new TempDirectory();
    ExpectThrows<FileNotFoundException>(() => new SettingsStore(dir.Root).Load());
}

static void ExpectThrows<T>(Action act) where T : Exception   // xUnit: Assert.Throws<T>(act)
{
    try
    {
        act();
    }
    catch (T)
    {
        return;
    }
    throw new InvalidOperationException($"expected {typeof(T).Name}");
}

sealed class TempDirectory : IDisposable
{
    public string Root { get; } = Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory("test-").FullName;
    public void Dispose() => Directory.Delete(Root, recursive: true);
}

{
    private readonly string _path = Path.Join(root, "settings.json");

    {
        var temp = $"{_path}.{Guid.NewGuid():N}.tmp";    // unique: two writers never share a temp file

Rules that prevent data loss

.NET adds a few platform differences.

  • Dispose every stream (using / await using) — Dispose flushes; a missed one loses the tail.
  • Replace a file with a temporary sibling + move; never truncate the original first.
  • File.Replace(temp, path, backup) also keeps a backup of the old file and the target's metadata; it needs both files on the same volume.
  • Path.GetTempFileName() creates a file in the shared temp folder — do not use it as a sibling for an atomic move to another volume.
  • Paths: Path.Combine and Path.GetRelativePath, never string concatenation with \.

MVVM State — INotifyPropertyChanged & Observable Collections

The change notifications XAML bindings listen to, written by hand and with the MVVM Toolkit's source generators.

  • dotnet

Sources: How to implement property change notification — WPF · Introduction to the MVVM Toolkit — .NET Community Toolkit

SwiftUI → .NET MVVM

The view model is the observable object; the XAML binding is the view's subscription.

SwiftUI.NET MVVM
@Observable / ObservableObjectINotifyPropertyChanged (or the Toolkit's ObservableObject)
@Published propertya property that raises PropertyChanged
a button actionICommand (the Toolkit's [RelayCommand])
ForEach over an arrayObservableCollection<T> raising CollectionChanged

INotifyPropertyChanged by hand

Raise the event for the property and for anything derived from it; skip equal values.

using System.ComponentModel;
using System.Runtime.CompilerServices;

var vm = new CounterViewModel();
vm.PropertyChanged += (_, e) => Console.WriteLine($"{e.PropertyName} changed");   // what a binding listens to
vm.Increment();
vm.Count = 1;                                  // the same value: no notification
Console.WriteLine(vm.Label);

class CounterViewModel : INotifyPropertyChanged
{
    public event PropertyChangedEventHandler? PropertyChanged;
    private int count;

    public int Count
    {
        get => count;
        set
        {
            if (count == value) return;
            count = value;
            OnPropertyChanged();
            OnPropertyChanged(nameof(Label));
        }
    }

    public string Label => $"Clicked {Count} times";
    public void Increment() => Count++;

    private void OnPropertyChanged([CallerMemberName] string? name = null) =>
        PropertyChanged?.Invoke(this, new PropertyChangedEventArgs(name));
}
Result
Count changed
Label changed
Clicked 1 times

using CommunityToolkit.Mvvm.ComponentModel;

public partial class CounterViewModel : ObservableObject
{

Rules

Most binding bugs are one of these.

  • Raising PropertyChanged off the UI thread in WPF or WinUI — marshal to the dispatcher first.
  • Replacing an ObservableCollection instance without raising PropertyChanged for it: the bound list keeps the old one.
  • Derived properties raise their own notification when a source changes (NotifyPropertyChangedFor).
  • View models stay UI-free, so they run and are tested in a plain console or test project — as above.

Rx.NET — Core

IObservable → operators → IDisposable. Cold until subscribed, push-only, and an error ends the stream — in a shop app's searches, carts and order feeds.

  • dotnet
  • System.Reactive
  • csharp >=12
  • dotnet >=8
  • system-reactive >=6.0
  • .NET (System.Reactive)

Sources: Reactive Extensions for .NET — dotnet/reactive · Introduction to Rx.NET · Introduction to Rx.NET — Key types

Mental model and operators: Combine → Rx.NET

Rx.NET is the same push model with LINQ names; the grammar is `OnNext* (OnError | OnCompleted)?` and nothing after the terminal call.

CombineRx.NETDifference
Publisher<Output, Failure>IObservable<T>no typed failure: any Exception arrives through OnError
SubscriberIObserver<T>: OnNext, OnError, OnCompletedusually a lambda: Subscribe(onNext, onError, onCompleted)
AnyCancellable, Set<AnyCancellable>IDisposable, CompositeDisposablelosing the reference does not cancel: call Dispose()
Just, Empty, FailObservable.Return, Empty, Throw—
Deferred { Future { … } }Observable.FromAsync(ct => …)lazy, once per subscriber, the token cancels on Dispose()
PassthroughSubject, CurrentValueSubjectSubject<T>, BehaviorSubject<T>ReplaySubject<T> replays the last N
map, filter, scan, removeDuplicatesSelect, Where, Scan, DistinctUntilChangedDistinct remembers every value ever seen
flatMap, switchToLatestSelectMany, Select(…).Switch()Select(…).Concat() runs one inner at a time
combineLatest, zip, mergeCombineLatest, Zip, Mergeplus WithLatestFrom (sample without triggering)
catch, retry, replaceErrorCatch, Retry(n), Catch(Observable.Return(x))Retry(3) is three attempts in total
debounce, throttleThrottle, SampleRx.NET's Throttle is a debounce
receive(on:), subscribe(on:)ObserveOn, SubscribeOnpass a SynchronizationContext for the UI thread
share(), multicastPublish().RefCount(), Publish() + Connect()Publish().RefCount() gives a subscriber nothing after completion; Replay(1).RefCount() replays
publisher.valuesawait observable (its last value), ToTask()IAsyncEnumerable<T> needs System.Interactive.Async (7.x) or a Channel<T>
Demand (backpressure)nonea fast source floods a slow observer: sample, buffer or use a Channel<T>

Cold sources: Return, Range, Create, FromAsync

A cold observable is a recipe: nothing runs until a subscription, and every subscriber gets its own run.

using System.Reactive.Linq;
using System.Reactive.Threading.Tasks;

var calls = 0;
var latestOrder = Observable.FromAsync(async ct =>
{
    calls++;                                     // runs per subscription, not at creation
    await Task.Delay(10, ct);
    return $"order #{1040 + calls}";
});
Console.WriteLine($"calls before subscribing: {calls}");
Console.WriteLine(await latestOrder);           // awaiting subscribes and yields the last value
Console.WriteLine(await latestOrder);

var statuses = Observable.Create<string>(observer =>
{
    observer.OnNext("placed");
    observer.OnNext("packed");
    observer.OnCompleted();
    return () => Console.WriteLine("status feed closed");   // teardown: completion or Dispose
});
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" > ", await statuses.ToList()));

var pages = Observable.Range(1, 3).Select(page => $"page {page}").Concat(Observable.Return("end"));
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", await pages.ToArray()));

// A Task is already running: ToObservable wraps it, it does not start or restart it
var warmCache = Task.FromResult("cache warmed");
Console.WriteLine(await warmCache.ToObservable());

Hot sources: events and subjects

A hot source emits whether or not anyone listens; a late subscriber sees only what a subject chooses to replay.

using System.Reactive;
using System.Reactive.Linq;
using System.Reactive.Subjects;

var tracker = new OrderTracker();
var statusChanges = Observable
    .FromEventPattern<string>(h => tracker.StatusChanged += h, h => tracker.StatusChanged -= h)
    .Select(e => e.EventArgs);
tracker.Report("shipped");                         // nobody subscribed: lost
using (statusChanges.Subscribe(s => Console.WriteLine($"event: {s}")))
    tracker.Report("delivered");                   // Dispose removed the handler again

var refreshTapped = new Subject<Unit>();             // an event stream: no memory
var cart = new CartStore();                          // state: always has a current value
var recentSearches = new ReplaySubject<string>(bufferSize: 2);

refreshTapped.OnNext(Unit.Default);                  // lost, like the event above
cart.Add();
foreach (var term in new[] { "laptop", "monitor", "keyboard" }) recentSearches.OnNext(term);

using var a = refreshTapped.Subscribe(_ => Console.WriteLine("refresh"));
using var b = cart.Count.Subscribe(n => Console.WriteLine($"badge: {n}"));
using var c = recentSearches.Subscribe(s => Console.WriteLine($"recent: {s}"));
refreshTapped.OnNext(Unit.Default);
cart.Add();

class OrderTracker
{
    public event EventHandler<string>? StatusChanged;
    public void Report(string status) => StatusChanged?.Invoke(this, status);
}

class CartStore
{
    private readonly BehaviorSubject<int> count = new(0);
    public IObservable<int> Count => count.AsObservable();   // callers cannot push into it
    public void Add() => count.OnNext(count.Value + 1);       // Value: the current state, synchronously
}

event: delivered
badge: 1
recent: monitor
recent: keyboard
refresh

SelectMany vs Switch vs Concat

Search-as-you-type is `Select(Search).Switch()`: a new query disposes the request in flight, so a slow stale answer never lands.

using System.Reactive.Linq;
using Microsoft.Reactive.Testing;

var scheduler = new TestScheduler();                 // virtual time: runs instantly
var queries = scheduler.CreateHotObservable(
    ReactiveTest.OnNext(Ms(10), "lap"),
    ReactiveTest.OnNext(Ms(100), "laptop"));

// The server is slow for the short query
IObservable<string> Search(string query) =>
    Observable.Timer(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(query == "lap" ? 250 : 50), scheduler)
              .Select(_ => query);

var runs = new (string Name, IObservable<string> Results)[]
{
    ("SelectMany", queries.SelectMany(Search)),      // every inner stays alive: a stale answer lands last
    ("Switch", queries.Select(Search).Switch()),     // a new query disposes the one in flight
    ("Concat", queries.Select(Search).Concat()),     // queued: one inner at a time, in order
};
var logs = new List<(string Name, List<string> Seen)>();
foreach (var (name, results) in runs)
{
    var seen = new List<string>();
    results.Subscribe(q => seen.Add($"{q}@{scheduler.Clock / TimeSpan.TicksPerMillisecond}ms"));
    logs.Add((name, seen));
}

scheduler.Start();
foreach (var (name, seen) in logs) Console.WriteLine($"{name,-10} {string.Join("  ", seen)}");

static long Ms(int milliseconds) => TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(milliseconds).Ticks;
Result
SelectMany laptop@150ms  lap@260ms
Switch     laptop@150ms
Concat     lap@260ms  laptop@310ms

CombineLatest vs Zip vs Merge vs WithLatestFrom, and Scan

CombineLatest for derived form state, WithLatestFrom for 'on tap, read the form', Zip to pair by position, Merge to interleave, Scan for a running total.

using System.Reactive;
using System.Reactive.Linq;
using System.Reactive.Subjects;

var email = new BehaviorSubject<string>("");
var password = new BehaviorSubject<string>("");
var signInTapped = new Subject<Unit>();

// CombineLatest: re-evaluates when ANY input changes; completes when ALL inputs have completed
email.CombineLatest(password, (e, p) => e.Contains('@') && p.Length >= 8)
     .DistinctUntilChanged()
     .Subscribe(ok => Console.WriteLine($"sign-in enabled: {ok}"));

// WithLatestFrom: only the tap triggers, typing does not; completes when the taps complete
signInTapped.WithLatestFrom(email, (_, e) => e)
            .Subscribe(e => Console.WriteLine($"signing in {e}"));

email.OnNext("ana@shop.example");                // still False: DistinctUntilChanged stays quiet
password.OnNext("correct-horse");
signInTapped.OnNext(Unit.Default);

var placed = new Subject<string>();
var receipts = new Subject<string>();
// Zip: pairs by position; once a finished input has nothing queued, the next value completes it
placed.Zip(receipts, (order, receipt) => $"{order}={receipt}")
      .Subscribe(pair => Console.WriteLine($"zip {pair}"), () => Console.WriteLine("zip completed"));
// Merge: as they arrive; completes when ALL inputs complete (an error in any input ends all of these)
placed.Merge(receipts).Subscribe(x => Console.WriteLine($"merge {x}"));
// Scan: a running fold that emits every intermediate result
placed.Scan(0, (count, _) => count + 1).Subscribe(n => Console.WriteLine($"orders today: {n}"));

placed.OnNext("order-1");
placed.OnNext("order-2");
receipts.OnNext("R-1");
placed.OnCompleted();                            // order-2 still waits for its receipt
receipts.OnNext("R-2");
receipts.OnNext("R-3");                          // no order left to pair with: Zip completes
Result
sign-in enabled: False
sign-in enabled: True
signing in ana@shop.example
merge order-1
orders today: 1
merge order-2
orders today: 2
zip order-1=R-1
merge R-1
zip order-2=R-2
merge R-2
zip completed
merge R-3

A pipeline with Retry and Catch

Retry and Catch go INSIDE the per-query observable, because an error that reaches the outer stream ends it for good.

using System.Reactive.Linq;

var api = new FlakyCatalogApi();
var results = new[] { "laptop", "broken-category" }.ToObservable()
    .Select(query => Observable
        .FromAsync(ct => api.SearchAsync(query, ct))   // each subscription is a new request
        .Retry(3)                                       // 3 attempts in total, resubscribing at once
        .Catch((HttpRequestException e) => Observable.Return($"'{query}' unavailable: {e.Message}")))
    .Concat();                                          // Switch() for live typing; Concat keeps order

// Retry has no delay: for backoff wrap the attempt in Observable.Defer with a Delay, use RetryWhen,
// or put a policy (Polly) around the Task — the timers sheet shows exponential backoff
await results.ForEachAsync(result => Console.WriteLine(result));
Console.WriteLine("stream still completed normally");

class FlakyCatalogApi
{
    private readonly Dictionary<string, int> attempts = [];

    public async Task<string> SearchAsync(string query, CancellationToken token)
    {
        await Task.Delay(5, token);
        var attempt = attempts[query] = attempts.GetValueOrDefault(query) + 1;
        Console.WriteLine($"attempt {attempt}: {query}");
        if (query.StartsWith("broken") || attempt < 3) throw new HttpRequestException("503");
        return $"3 results for {query}";
    }
}

attempt 2: laptop
attempt 3: laptop

stream still completed normally

Subscription lifetime and threads: Dispose, TakeUntil, ObserveOn

A screen owns a CompositeDisposable and disposes it on close; SubscribeOn moves the subscribing work, ObserveOn moves delivery.

using System.Reactive;
using System.Reactive.Concurrency;
using System.Reactive.Disposables;
using System.Reactive.Disposables.Fluent;          // DisposeWith, new in Rx 6.1
using System.Reactive.Linq;
using System.Reactive.Subjects;

var orderUpdates = new Subject<string>();
var screenClosed = new Subject<Unit>();
var subscriptions = new CompositeDisposable();

orderUpdates.Subscribe(u => Console.WriteLine($"list: {u}")).DisposeWith(subscriptions);
orderUpdates.TakeUntil(screenClosed)                 // ends itself: no handle to keep
            .Finally(() => Console.WriteLine("banner detached"))
            .Subscribe(u => Console.WriteLine($"banner: {u}"));

orderUpdates.OnNext("packed");
screenClosed.OnNext(Unit.Default);
orderUpdates.OnNext("shipped");                       // the list still listens
subscriptions.Dispose();                              // the screen closes
orderUpdates.OnNext("delivered");                     // nobody prints this

using var io = new EventLoopScheduler(start => new Thread(start) { Name = "io", IsBackground = true });
using var ui = new EventLoopScheduler(start => new Thread(start) { Name = "ui", IsBackground = true });
var load = Observable.Create<string>(observer =>
{
    Console.WriteLine($"loading on {Thread.CurrentThread.Name}");
    observer.OnNext("3 orders");
    observer.OnCompleted();
    return Disposable.Empty;
});
// In WPF, WinUI or MAUI: .ObserveOn(SynchronizationContext.Current!) captured on the UI thread
await load.SubscribeOn(io)
          .ObserveOn(ui)
          .Do(v => Console.WriteLine($"rendering '{v}' on {Thread.CurrentThread.Name}"));
Result
list: packed
banner: packed
banner detached
list: shipped
loading on io
rendering '3 orders' on ui

Sharing one subscription: Publish, RefCount, Replay

For a request that completes, Publish().RefCount() gives a later screen nothing and Replay(1).RefCount() replays the answer, but that replay buffer also survives everyone leaving, so a live feed's next subscriber first sees a stale value.

using System.Globalization;
using System.Reactive.Linq;
using System.Reactive.Subjects;
using System.Reactive.Threading.Tasks;

CultureInfo.CurrentCulture = CultureInfo.InvariantCulture;
var requests = 0;
var profile = Observable.FromAsync(async ct =>         // cold: one HTTP call per subscription
{
    requests++;
    await Task.Delay(10, ct);
    return "Ada";
});

Console.WriteLine("variant              requests  a later screen gets");
foreach (var (name, shared) in new (string, IObservable<string>)[]
{
    ("cold", profile),
    ("Publish().RefCount()", profile.Publish().RefCount()),   // shares while subscribed, keeps nothing
    ("Replay(1).RefCount()", profile.Replay(1).RefCount()),   // shares, and keeps the last value
})
{
    requests = 0;
    await Task.WhenAll(shared.ToTask(), shared.ToTask());      // header and sidebar, at the same time
    var later = await shared.FirstOrDefaultAsync() ?? "nothing (completed)";   // settings, afterwards
    Console.WriteLine($"{name,-20} {requests,8}  {later}");
}

// A live feed: the replay buffer outlives the disconnect
var socket = new Subject<decimal>();
var prices = Observable.Create<decimal>(observer =>
{
    Console.WriteLine("socket open");
    return socket.Subscribe(observer);
}).Replay(1).RefCount();
using (prices.Subscribe()) socket.OnNext(101.5m);       // a chart, then the user leaves
socket.OnNext(103m);                                    // nobody listens: missed
using (prices.Subscribe(p => Console.WriteLine($"next screen sees {p}"))) socket.OnNext(104m);
Result

cold                        3  Ada

Replay(1).RefCount()        1  Ada
socket open
next screen sees 101.5

next screen sees 104

Bridging to Task and IAsyncEnumerable

FirstAsync, LastAsync and ToTask ship in System.Reactive, but ToAsyncEnumerable does not: it is `AsyncEnumerableEx.ToAsyncEnumerable` in System.Interactive.Async 7.x (System.Linq.Async up to 6.x), so here it is written with a Channel.

using System.Reactive.Linq;
using System.Reactive.Threading.Tasks;
using System.Runtime.CompilerServices;
using System.Threading.Channels;

var statuses = new[] { "placed", "packed", "shipped" }.ToObservable();

Console.WriteLine(await statuses.FirstAsync());        // the first value, then it unsubscribes
Console.WriteLine(await statuses);                     // awaiting an observable: its LAST value
Task<string> asTask = statuses.LastAsync().ToTask();   // for APIs that want a Task
Console.WriteLine(await asTask);

await foreach (var status in ToAsyncEnumerable(statuses))
    Console.WriteLine($"pulled {status}");

// Push to pull: buffer pushed values until the consumer asks for them
static async IAsyncEnumerable<T> ToAsyncEnumerable<T>(
    IObservable<T> source, [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token = default)
{
    var buffer = Channel.CreateUnbounded<T>();         // bound it if the source can outrun the reader
    using var subscription = source.Subscribe(
        value => buffer.Writer.TryWrite(value),
        error => buffer.Writer.TryComplete(error),
        () => buffer.Writer.TryComplete());
    await foreach (var value in buffer.Reader.ReadAllAsync(token))
        yield return value;
}

shipped
shipped

Gotchas, and when not to use Rx

Most Rx bugs are lifetime or error-placement bugs.

  • Discarding the IDisposable from Subscribe on a long-lived source: the subscription (and the screen it captures) lives as long as the source.
  • Retry/Catch on the outer stream: the first failure ends search for the rest of the session. Put them inside the Select before Switch.
  • SelectMany for search-as-you-type: stale answers can overwrite fresh ones. Use Select(…).Switch().
  • task.ToObservable() when you meant laziness: the task is already running. Observable.FromAsync(ct => …) starts per subscriber and cancels on dispose.
  • Calling OnNext on a subject from several threads at once breaks the grammar; serialise with Subject.Synchronize(subject) or one producer.
  • await observable returns the last value and throws InvalidOperationException on an empty sequence; use FirstAsync() or FirstOrDefaultAsync() for the first.
  • Subscribing to a cold source twice runs it twice (two HTTP calls). Screens subscribing at the same time: Publish().RefCount(). A result later screens should reuse: Replay(1).RefCount(), or cache the Task (Lazy<Task<T>>) — Publish().RefCount() gives a late subscriber nothing once the source has completed.
  • Replay(1).RefCount() on a live feed keeps its buffer after everyone leaves: the next subscriber gets the old value first, then the source reconnects. Check freshness (Timestamp()) or build a new Replay per session.
  • One request/response: a plain Task. A pull-based sequence (pages, a file): IAsyncEnumerable<T>. One producer handing work to a consumer with backpressure: Channel<T>. Reach for Rx when you compose several push sources over time.

Timing Operators — Rx.NET vs Plain Async

Throttle (a debounce!), Sample, Delay, Timeout, Buffer, Window, Interval: what each one drops, how to write it by hand, and how TestScheduler makes every test instant.

  • dotnet
  • csharp >=12
  • dotnet >=8
  • system-reactive >=6.0
  • .NET (System.Reactive, Microsoft.Reactive.Testing)

Sources: Reactive Extensions for .NET — dotnet/reactive · Introduction to Rx.NET — Time-based sequences · Introduction to Rx.NET — Scheduling and threading (virtual time)

Operator → meaning → hand-written equivalent

Names differ across libraries: Rx.NET's `Throttle` is everyone else's debounce, and Rx.NET has no leading-edge throttle at all.

Rx.NETMeaningDrops values?Plain async equivalent
Throttle(t)emit after t of silence; keeps the last of a burst — what Combine, RxJS and Flow call debounceyes, mostcancel-and-restart: a new CancellationTokenSource and Task.Delay(t, time, token) per input
Sample(t)every t, the latest value if one arrived since the last tick (a trailing throttle, RxJS sampleTime)yesa PeriodicTimer reading the latest value
(none built in)leading throttle: the first value, then ignore for t (RxJS throttleTime, Combine throttle(latest: false))yesa last-accepted timestamp from TimeProvider.GetTimestamp()
Delay(t)shift every value laternoawait Task.Delay(t, time, token) before acting
Timeout(t)fail with TimeoutException when the next value (every gap, not just the first) takes longer than tterminatesCancelAfter(t) on a linked token, or task.WaitAsync(t, time)
Timeout(t, fallback)switch to fallback instead of failingnocatch (TimeoutException) and use the fallback
Buffer(t, n)a list per window of t or n items, whichever comes firstno (batches)a Channel<T> reader with a deadline
Window(t)like Buffer, but each batch is itself an IObservable<T>no—
Interval(t), Timer(due, period)ticks 0, 1, 2… every t (after due)n/aPeriodicTimer (does not drift)
DistinctUntilChanged()drop a value equal to the previous oneyescompare with the last value you kept
Timestamp(), TimeInterval()attach the time, or the gap since the previous valuenoTimeProvider.GetElapsedTime(start)

Throttle — search when they stop typing

The search-as-you-type pipeline: Throttle (debounce), trim, DistinctUntilChanged, a minimum length, a Catch inside each search so one failure does not end the box, then Switch so a stale answer never lands.

using System.Reactive.Linq;
using Microsoft.Reactive.Testing;

var scheduler = new TestScheduler();
var keystrokes = scheduler.CreateHotObservable(
    ReactiveTest.OnNext(Ms(0), "l"),
    ReactiveTest.OnNext(Ms(100), "la"),
    ReactiveTest.OnNext(Ms(200), "lap"),        // a pause: 300 ms of silence follow
    ReactiveTest.OnNext(Ms(700), "lapt"),
    ReactiveTest.OnNext(Ms(800), "lapto"),
    ReactiveTest.OnNext(Ms(900), "laptop"),
    ReactiveTest.OnNext(Ms(1600), "laptop "));  // a trailing space: the same query

IObservable<string> Search(string query) =>      // a 50 ms round trip; the server fails 'lap' with a 503
    Observable.Timer(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(50), scheduler)
        .Select(_ => query == "lap" ? throw new HttpRequestException("503") : $"results for '{query}'");

keystrokes
    .Throttle(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(300), scheduler)   // Rx.NET's debounce
    .Select(text => text.Trim())
    .DistinctUntilChanged()                    // "laptop " trims to "laptop": no second request
    .Where(query => query.Length >= 2)
    .Select(query => Search(query)            // Catch per query: the next keystroke still searches
        .Catch((HttpRequestException e) => Observable.Return($"'{query}' unavailable ({e.Message})")))
    .Switch()
    .Subscribe(r => Console.WriteLine($"{scheduler.Clock / TimeSpan.TicksPerMillisecond} ms: {r}"));

scheduler.Start();                               // two seconds of typing, run instantly

static long Ms(int milliseconds) => TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(milliseconds).Ticks;
Result
550 ms: 'lap' unavailable (503)
1250 ms: results for 'laptop'

One input, three decisions: Throttle vs Sample vs a leading throttle

Scroll events every 50 ms for half a second: debounce waits for the end, Sample reports the latest per tick, a leading throttle takes the first per window.

using System.Reactive.Concurrency;
using System.Reactive.Linq;
using Microsoft.Reactive.Testing;

var scheduler = new TestScheduler();
var scrolls = Enumerable.Range(0, 10).Select(i => ReactiveTest.OnNext(Ms(10 + 50 * i), (i + 1) * 100));
var scrollOffsets = scheduler.CreateHotObservable([.. scrolls, ReactiveTest.OnCompleted<int>(Ms(700))]);

var window = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(175);
Record("Throttle", scrollOffsets.Throttle(window, scheduler));              // after silence
Record("Sample", scrollOffsets.Sample(window, scheduler));                  // latest per tick
Record("ThrottleFirst", scrollOffsets.ThrottleFirst(window, scheduler));    // first per window

scheduler.AdvanceTo(Ms(1000));                   // Sample ticks forever: advance, don't Start()

void Record(string name, IObservable<int> results)
{
    var seen = new List<string>();
    results.Subscribe(
        v => seen.Add($"{v}@{scheduler.Clock / TimeSpan.TicksPerMillisecond}"),
        () => seen.Add($"done@{scheduler.Clock / TimeSpan.TicksPerMillisecond}"));   // the scroll ended
    var print = () => Console.WriteLine($"{name,-13} {string.Join(" ", seen)}");
    scheduler.Schedule(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(999), print);
}

static long Ms(int milliseconds) => TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(milliseconds).Ticks;

static class TimingOperators
{
    // Not in Rx.NET: take one value, then a silent window on the scheduler's timer (not its wall clock)
    public static IObservable<T> ThrottleFirst<T>(this IObservable<T> source, TimeSpan window,
        IScheduler scheduler) =>
        source.Publish(shared => shared
            .Take(1)
            .Concat(Observable.Empty<T>().Delay(window, scheduler))   // completes after the window
            .Repeat()                                                 // then waits for the next value
            .TakeUntil(shared.LastOrDefaultAsync()));                 // and ends when the source ends
}

Sample        400@175 700@350 1000@525 done@700
ThrottleFirst 100@10 500@210 900@410 done@700

Delay and Timeout

Delay shifts every value and drops none; Timeout gives up when a gap is too long — fail, or switch to a fallback.

using System.Reactive.Linq;
using Microsoft.Reactive.Testing;

var scheduler = new TestScheduler();
void Log(string text) => Console.WriteLine($"{scheduler.Clock / TimeSpan.TicksPerSecond}s {text}");

// Hide the "Saved" toast two seconds after it appears
Observable.Return("hide toast").Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2), scheduler).Subscribe(Log);

// A slow request: answers after 5 s
var slowProfile = Observable.Timer(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5), scheduler).Select(_ => "fresh profile");

slowProfile
    .Timeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3), scheduler)
    .Subscribe(Log, error => Log($"failed: {error.GetType().Name}"));

slowProfile
    .Timeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3), Observable.Return("cached profile"), scheduler)
    .Subscribe(Log);

slowProfile
    .Timeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10), scheduler)
    .Subscribe(Log);

scheduler.Start();
Result
2s hide toast
3s failed: TimeoutException
3s cached profile
5s fresh profile

Buffer and Window — batching by time and count

Upload analytics in batches of 3 or every 2 s, whichever comes first; count events per second with Window.

using System.Reactive.Linq;
using Microsoft.Reactive.Testing;

var scheduler = new TestScheduler();
var taps = scheduler.CreateHotObservable(
    ReactiveTest.OnNext(Ms(100), "add-to-cart"),
    ReactiveTest.OnNext(Ms(200), "view-item"),
    ReactiveTest.OnNext(Ms(300), "view-item"),   // third event: the batch is full
    ReactiveTest.OnNext(Ms(2500), "checkout"),
    ReactiveTest.OnCompleted<string>(Ms(6500)));
string At() => $"{scheduler.Clock / TimeSpan.TicksPerMillisecond} ms";

taps.Buffer(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2), 3, scheduler)
    .Where(batch => batch.Count > 0)               // a quiet window still emits an empty list
    .Subscribe(batch => Console.WriteLine($"{At()} upload [{string.Join(", ", batch)}]"));

taps.Window(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), scheduler)
    .SelectMany(second => second.Count())          // each window is an IObservable<string>
    .Where(count => count > 0)
    .Subscribe(count => Console.WriteLine($"{At()} {count} event(s) in the last second"));

scheduler.Start();

static long Ms(int milliseconds) => TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(milliseconds).Ticks;
Result
300 ms upload [add-to-cart, view-item, view-item]
1000 ms 3 event(s) in the last second
3000 ms 1 event(s) in the last second
4300 ms upload [checkout]

Interval and Timer — polling without drift

Interval schedules each tick from the start, so a 300 ms poll does not push the next one later; a delay-then-poll loop drifts by the work's cost every time.

using System.Reactive.Concurrency;
using System.Reactive.Linq;
using Microsoft.Reactive.Testing;

var scheduler = new TestScheduler();
// Asking the server for the order status takes 300 ms
IObservable<string> PollStatus() =>
    Observable.Timer(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(300), scheduler).Select(_ => "polled");

var anchored = Observable.Interval(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), scheduler)
    .Select(_ => PollStatus())
    .Concat();                                     // one poll at a time, ticks stay on the 1 s grid

var drifting = Observable.Timer(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), scheduler)
    .SelectMany(_ => PollStatus())
    .Repeat();                                     // wait 1 s, poll, wait 1 s again: + 300 ms each round

Record("Interval", anchored);
Record("delay loop", drifting);
scheduler.AdvanceTo(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(4).Ticks);

void Record(string name, IObservable<string> polls)
{
    var finishedAt = new List<string>();
    polls.Subscribe(_ => finishedAt.Add($"{scheduler.Clock / TimeSpan.TicksPerMillisecond}"));
    var print = () => Console.WriteLine($"{name,-10} {string.Join(" ", finishedAt)}");
    scheduler.Schedule(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(4), print);
}
Result
Interval   1300 2300 3300
delay loop 1300 2600 3900

Inject the scheduler — and the test is instant

Every timing operator takes an `IScheduler`: production passes the default, tests pass a TestScheduler and assert on recorded notifications.

using System.Reactive.Concurrency;
using System.Reactive.Linq;
using System.Reactive.Subjects;
using Microsoft.Reactive.Testing;

var scheduler = new TestScheduler();
var model = new SearchModel(scheduler);
scheduler.Schedule(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(250), () => model.Query.OnNext("lap"));
scheduler.Schedule(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(400), () => model.Query.OnNext("laptop"));

// created 0, subscribed 0, disposed 2 s (the default overload uses ticks 100, 200, 1000)
var observer = scheduler.Start(() => model.Suggestions, 0, 0, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2).Ticks);

var expected = new[] { ReactiveTest.OnNext(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(700).Ticks, "laptop") };
var passed = observer.Messages.SequenceEqual(expected);
Console.WriteLine(passed ? "debounced to one suggestion at 700 ms" : "FAILED");

sealed class SearchModel(IScheduler scheduler)      // production: new SearchModel(DefaultScheduler.Instance)
{
    public Subject<string> Query { get; } = new();

    public IObservable<string> Suggestions =>
        Query.Throttle(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(300), scheduler).DistinctUntilChanged();
}

The same debounce by hand: CancellationTokenSource and an injected TimeProvider

Without Rx, each keystroke cancels the pending wait and starts a new one, and the token is checked again after the request so a late answer to an old query is dropped.

var requested = new SemaphoreSlim(0);
var answers = new Dictionary<string, TaskCompletionSource<string>> { ["lap"] = new(), ["laptop"] = new() };
Task<string> SearchAsync(string query, CancellationToken token)   // a server that ignores the token
{
    Console.WriteLine($"request: {query}");
    requested.Release();
    return answers[query].Task;
}

var search = new DebouncedSearch(SearchAsync, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100), TimeProvider.System);
search.ResultsChanged += Console.WriteLine;

foreach (var text in new[] { "l", "la", "lap" }) search.QueryChanged(text);   // one burst: one request
await requested.WaitAsync();                         // 'lap' is in flight…
search.QueryChanged("laptop");                       // …when the user types again
answers["lap"].SetResult("results for 'lap'");       // the old answer arrives late: dropped
answers["laptop"].SetResult("results for 'laptop'");
await search.Pending;

sealed class DebouncedSearch(
    Func<string, CancellationToken, Task<string>> searchAsync, TimeSpan delay, TimeProvider time)
{
    private CancellationTokenSource? pending;
    public event Action<string>? ResultsChanged;
    public Task Pending { get; private set; } = Task.CompletedTask;

    public void QueryChanged(string query)          // called on the UI thread
    {
        pending?.Cancel();                            // restart the clock: the last keystroke wins
        pending = new CancellationTokenSource();      // no timer inside it, so nothing to Dispose
        Pending = SearchAfterQuietAsync(query, pending.Token);
    }

    private async Task SearchAfterQuietAsync(string query, CancellationToken token)
    {
        try
        {
            await Task.Delay(delay, time, token);     // tests pass a fake TimeProvider here
            var results = await searchAsync(query, token);
            token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();     // it answered, but a newer keystroke superseded it
            ResultsChanged?.Invoke(results);
        }
        catch (OperationCanceledException) { }      // superseded: not an error
    }
}

request: laptop
results for 'laptop'

Owning the timer subscription safely

A SerialDisposable holds at most one timer: Start twice replaces instead of doubling, Stop and Dispose end it, and nothing fires after the screen is gone.

using System.Reactive.Concurrency;
using System.Reactive.Disposables;
using System.Reactive.Linq;
using Microsoft.Reactive.Testing;

var scheduler = new TestScheduler();
var screen = new OrdersScreen(scheduler);
screen.StartAutoRefresh();
scheduler.AdvanceBy(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1.5).Ticks);
screen.StartAutoRefresh();                         // e.g. OnAppearing ran twice: still one timer
scheduler.AdvanceBy(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2).Ticks);
screen.StopAutoRefresh();
scheduler.AdvanceBy(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5).Ticks);
screen.StartAutoRefresh();
scheduler.AdvanceBy(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1).Ticks);
screen.Dispose();                                  // the user left the screen
scheduler.AdvanceBy(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5).Ticks);
Console.WriteLine($"refreshes after dispose: {screen.Refreshes}");

sealed class OrdersScreen(IScheduler scheduler) : IDisposable
{
    private readonly SerialDisposable autoRefresh = new();   // assigning disposes the previous one
    public int Refreshes { get; private set; }

    public void StartAutoRefresh() =>
        autoRefresh.Disposable = Observable.Interval(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), scheduler)
            .Subscribe(_ => Console.WriteLine($"refresh #{++Refreshes} at {scheduler.Now:s.f}s"));

    public void StopAutoRefresh() => autoRefresh.Disposable = Disposable.Empty;

    public void Dispose() => autoRefresh.Dispose();  // the timer captured `this`: release it
}

Safety checklist for timing code

Most timing bugs are naming, lifetime or real-time-in-tests bugs.

  • Reaching for Throttle to rate-limit a button: in Rx.NET it is a debounce and waits for silence. Use Sample (trailing) or a leading-edge throttle like ThrottleFirst above.
  • Pass an IScheduler to every time-based operator (Throttle, Delay, Timeout, Buffer, Interval) and inject it, so tests use a TestScheduler.
  • Test with AdvanceBy/AdvanceTo when a sequence never ends (Interval, Sample): Start() runs until nothing is scheduled, which is never.
  • Keep a timer subscription in a SerialDisposable (restartable) or CompositeDisposable (many) and dispose it when the screen goes away — the callback captures the screen.
  • Deliver results on the UI thread with ObserveOn(SynchronizationContext.Current!) after the timing operators; the timers themselves fire on the scheduler's thread.
  • Buffer(t) emits empty lists on quiet windows — filter batch.Count > 0 before uploading.
  • Timeout(t) applies to every gap between values, not to the whole sequence; for an overall deadline use Timeout(scheduler.Now + t, scheduler) (fails with TimeoutException), or TakeUntil(Observable.Timer(t, scheduler)) (completes quietly, so the caller cannot tell it gave up).
  • Hand-written debounce without cancelling the request too: a slow answer to an old query can still arrive after a newer one. Pass the same token to the call.
  • Polling with Interval(…).Select(poll).Concat() queues ticks when a poll runs longer than the period; with SelectMany polls overlap. Pick one deliberately.

Timers, Delays & Scheduled Work

Delays, PeriodicTimer, polling, timeouts, backoff, concurrency limits, debounce and throttle — cancelled with a CancellationToken and made testable with an injected TimeProvider.

Which timer — and which scheduler for work that outlives the screen

In new code: `Task.Delay` for once, `PeriodicTimer` for repeating, a dispatcher timer only for short UI work, and the OS or a job scheduler for anything that must survive the process.

A one-shot delay, cancelled correctly

`Task.Delay` holds no thread while it waits, and a cancelled token ends the wait at once with `OperationCanceledException`.

var time = TimeProvider.System;                    // tests pass a fake (see below)

// The "Saved" toast hides itself after a short delay
var saved = HideToastAfterAsync("Saved", TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(50), time, CancellationToken.None);
Console.WriteLine(await saved);

// The user leaves the screen long before the 30 s "Undo?" toast would hide
using var screen = new CancellationTokenSource();
var undo = HideToastAfterAsync("Undo?", TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30), time, screen.Token);
screen.Cancel();
Console.WriteLine(await undo);

static async Task<string> HideToastAfterAsync(
    string message, TimeSpan after, TimeProvider time, CancellationToken token)
{
    try
    {
        await Task.Delay(after, time, token);      // never Thread.Sleep: it blocks a thread for the wait
        return $"'{message}' hidden after {after.TotalMilliseconds} ms";
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException)
    {
        return $"'{message}' cancelled: the screen is gone";
    }
}

'Undo?' cancelled: the screen is gone

A repeating job: Task.Delay loop vs PeriodicTimer

Both count a reservation down and print the same thing — the difference is the schedule: the Delay loop waits after the work and drifts by its cost every tick, while PeriodicTimer keeps a fixed grid and never overlaps (the Rx timing sheet's interval-without-drift card measures the drift).

Task.Delay loop
using var leaving = new CancellationTokenSource();
await CountdownAsync(3, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(20), leaving.Token);

static async Task CountdownAsync(int from, TimeSpan every, CancellationToken token)
{
    for (var remaining = from; ; remaining--)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(remaining > 0 ? $"reservation expires in {remaining}" : "expired");
        if (remaining == 0) return;
        // The wait starts only after the work: interval + work time, every tick
        await Task.Delay(every, token);
    }
}
PeriodicTimer
using var leaving = new CancellationTokenSource();
await CountdownAsync(3, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(20), leaving.Token);

static async Task CountdownAsync(int from, TimeSpan every, CancellationToken token)
{
    using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(every);  // ticks on a fixed grid from its creation
    var remaining = from;
    Console.WriteLine($"reservation expires in {remaining}");
    // One tick at a time: a slow iteration delays the next, it never runs beside it
    while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(token))
    {
        remaining--;
        Console.WriteLine(remaining > 0 ? $"reservation expires in {remaining}" : "expired");
        if (remaining == 0) return;
    }
}

reservation expires in 3
reservation expires in 2
reservation expires in 1
expired

Polling until a condition, with a timeout

CancelAfter on a token linked to the screen cancels the work itself; WaitAsync only stops waiting for a call that ignores tokens.

var every = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(20);
var exports = new ExportApi(readyOnCheck: 3);

using var screen = new CancellationTokenSource();                  // cancelled if the user leaves
using var deadline = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(screen.Token);
deadline.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));                     // whichever comes first
Console.WriteLine(await PollUntilReadyAsync(exports, every, deadline.Token));

using var tight = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(30));   // CancelAfter, built in
try { await PollUntilReadyAsync(new ExportApi(readyOnCheck: 1000), every, tight.Token); }
catch (OperationCanceledException) { Console.WriteLine("gave up: the export took too long"); }

try { await exports.LegacyArchiveAsync().WaitAsync(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(30)); }
catch (TimeoutException) { Console.WriteLine("archive timed out (and keeps running: it takes no token)"); }

static async Task<string> PollUntilReadyAsync(ExportApi api, TimeSpan every, CancellationToken token)
{
    using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(every);
    while (true)
    {
        if (await api.CheckAsync(token) is { } url) return $"ready: {url}";
        await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(token);               // throws when the token is cancelled
    }
}

sealed class ExportApi(int readyOnCheck)
{
    private int checks;
    public Task<string?> CheckAsync(CancellationToken token) =>
        Task.FromResult(++checks >= readyOnCheck ? $"/exports/orders.csv (check {checks})" : null);
    public Task LegacyArchiveAsync() => Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10));
}

Retry with exponential backoff and jitter

Retry only what is transient (408, 429, 500, 502–504, or no response at all), double the wait each time with jitter, and give up after a fixed number of attempts.

using System.Net;

var server = new ScriptedHandler(HttpStatusCode.ServiceUnavailable, HttpStatusCode.TooManyRequests,
    HttpStatusCode.OK);
using var http = new HttpClient(server) { BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.shop.example/") };

var orders = await RetryAsync(token => http.GetStringAsync("orders", token),
    maxAttempts: 4, baseDelay: TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(10), TimeProvider.System, CancellationToken.None);
Console.WriteLine(orders);

static async Task<T> RetryAsync<T>(Func<CancellationToken, Task<T>> operation, int maxAttempts,
    TimeSpan baseDelay, TimeProvider time, CancellationToken token)
{
    for (var attempt = 1; ; attempt++)
    {
        try
        {
            return await operation(token);
        }
        catch (HttpRequestException e) when (attempt < maxAttempts && IsTransient(e.StatusCode))
        {
            // 10, 20, 40 ms… each ±20 %, so a thousand clients do not retry in lockstep
            var delay = baseDelay * Math.Pow(2, attempt - 1) * (0.8 + 0.4 * Random.Shared.NextDouble());
            Console.WriteLine($"attempt {attempt} got {(int?)e.StatusCode}: backing off");
            await Task.Delay(delay, time, token);
        }
    }
}

// 501 or 505 never succeed on a retry; null means no response arrived at all
static bool IsTransient(HttpStatusCode? status) => status is null
    or HttpStatusCode.RequestTimeout or HttpStatusCode.TooManyRequests or HttpStatusCode.InternalServerError
    or HttpStatusCode.BadGateway or HttpStatusCode.ServiceUnavailable or HttpStatusCode.GatewayTimeout;

sealed class ScriptedHandler(params HttpStatusCode[] replies) : HttpMessageHandler
{
    private int calls;
    protected override Task<HttpResponseMessage> SendAsync(HttpRequestMessage request, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var body = new StringContent("[1041, 1042]");
        return Task.FromResult(new HttpResponseMessage(replies[calls++]) { Content = body });
    }
}
