N jobs — one at a time, or at most two in flight

Uploading six photos: serially, with Parallel.ForEachAsync's degree of parallelism, or with a SemaphoreSlim around any shape of work (all at once with `Task.WhenAll` is on the async sheet).

var photos = Enumerable.Range(1, 6).Select(i => $"photo-{i}.jpg").ToArray();
var uploader = new Uploader();

foreach (var photo in photos) await uploader.UploadAsync(photo, CancellationToken.None);
Console.WriteLine($"serial            peak {uploader.TakePeak()} in flight");

// On the first failure it stops taking new photos and cancels the token it passes to the others
var options = new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 2 };
await Parallel.ForEachAsync(photos, options, uploader.UploadAsync);
Console.WriteLine($"ForEachAsync(2)   peak {uploader.TakePeak()} in flight");

// The same limit for any shape of work; after a failure the rest still run unless you pass a token
using var gate = new SemaphoreSlim(2);
await Task.WhenAll(photos.Select(async photo =>
{
    await gate.WaitAsync();
    try { await uploader.UploadAsync(photo, CancellationToken.None); }
    finally { gate.Release(); }
}));
Console.WriteLine($"SemaphoreSlim(2)  peak {uploader.TakePeak()} in flight");

sealed class Uploader
{
    private readonly object gate = new();
    private int inFlight, peak;

    public async ValueTask UploadAsync(string photo, CancellationToken token)
    {
        lock (gate) peak = Math.Max(peak, ++inFlight);
        await Task.Delay(20, token);                       // stand-in for the upload
        lock (gate) inFlight--;
    }

    public int TakePeak()
    {
        lock (gate)
        {
            var result = peak;
            peak = 0;
            return result;
        }
    }
}

ForEachAsync(2)   peak 2 in flight
SemaphoreSlim(2)  peak 2 in flight

Debounce without Rx: one ITimer re-armed per keystroke

Every keystroke pushes a single one-shot ITimer back with Change, and closing the editor flushes the pending edit instead of dropping it.

var firstSave = new SemaphoreSlim(0);
var quiet = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(50);
var debouncer = new DraftDebouncer(quiet, TimeProvider.System, text =>
{
    Console.WriteLine($"save '{text}'");                 // hand it to the saver (next card)
    firstSave.Release();
});

foreach (var text in new[] { "H", "He", "Hello" }) debouncer.TextChanged(text);   // one burst, one save
await firstSave.WaitAsync();
debouncer.TextChanged("Hello, world");
debouncer.Dispose();                                     // closed inside the quiet period: flushed, not lost

sealed class DraftDebouncer(TimeSpan quiet, TimeProvider time, Action<string> onQuiet) : IDisposable
{
    private ITimer? timer;
    private string? pending;                             // the newest edit not handed over yet

    public void TextChanged(string text)                // called on the UI thread
    {
        Volatile.Write(ref pending, text);
        var once = Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan;             // no period: one shot, re-armed per keystroke
        timer ??= time.CreateTimer(state => Flush(), null, once, once);   // fires on the thread pool
        timer.Change(quiet, once);                       // every keystroke pushes the save back
    }

    public void Dispose()
    {
        timer?.Dispose();
        Flush();
    }

    private void Flush()                                 // the timer and Dispose can race: Exchange picks one
    {
        if (Interlocked.Exchange(ref pending, null) is { } text) onQuiet(text);
    }
}

save 'Hello, world'

An autosave that never loses or reorders a draft

Saves run one at a time so an older draft never lands last, and a failed save puts its draft back so the next tick or the close flush retries it.

var attempts = 0;
async Task UploadDraftAsync(string text)                 // 150 ms; the first attempt fails
{
    Console.WriteLine($"uploading '{text}'");
    await Task.Delay(150);
    if (++attempts == 1) throw new HttpRequestException("network down");
    Console.WriteLine($"stored '{text}'");
}

var saver = new DraftSaver(UploadDraftAsync);
saver.Changed("Hello");
var debounced = saver.SaveLatestAsync();                 // the debounce fired: the upload starts…
var onClose = saver.SaveLatestAsync();                   // …and the user closes while it runs: this waits
await Task.WhenAll(debounced, onClose);

sealed class DraftSaver(Func<string, Task> save)
{
    private readonly SemaphoreSlim oneAtATime = new(1, 1);
    private string? unsaved;                             // the newest edit not saved yet

    public void Changed(string text) => Volatile.Write(ref unsaved, text);

    public async Task SaveLatestAsync()
    {
        await oneAtATime.WaitAsync();                    // one save at a time: an older one never lands last
        try
        {
            if (Interlocked.Exchange(ref unsaved, null) is not { } draft) return;
            try
            {
                await save(draft);
            }
            catch (Exception e)                          // put it back, unless a newer edit arrived meanwhile
            {
                Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref unsaved, draft, null);
                Console.WriteLine($"autosave failed: {e.Message}");
            }
        }
        finally
        {
            oneAtATime.Release();
        }
    }
}
Result
uploading 'Hello'
autosave failed: network down
uploading 'Hello'
stored 'Hello'

A leading-edge throttle: pull-to-refresh at most every two seconds

The first call in a window runs and the rest are dropped, measured with the monotonic `GetTimestamp` of an injected TimeProvider so a tiny fake clock tests it.

using System.Globalization;

CultureInfo.CurrentCulture = CultureInfo.InvariantCulture;
var clock = new ManualClock();
var refresh = new RefreshThrottle(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2), clock);

foreach (var second in new[] { 0.0, 0.5, 1.9, 2.0, 3.0, 4.5 })   // when the user pulls to refresh
{
    clock.Seconds = second;
    Console.WriteLine($"{second:0.0} s: {(refresh.TryEnter() ? "refresh" : "skipped")}");
}

sealed class RefreshThrottle(TimeSpan window, TimeProvider time)
{
    private long? lastAccepted;

    public bool TryEnter()                                    // UI thread only; lock it otherwise
    {
        var now = time.GetTimestamp();                        // monotonic, unlike DateTime.Now
        if (lastAccepted is { } last && time.GetElapsedTime(last, now) < window) return false;
        lastAccepted = now;
        return true;
    }
}

sealed class ManualClock : TimeProvider                       // only the timestamp is faked here
{
    public double Seconds { get; set; }
    public override long GetTimestamp() => (long)(Seconds * TimestampFrequency);
    public override long TimestampFrequency => TimeSpan.TicksPerSecond;
}
Result
0.0 s: refresh
0.5 s: skipped
1.9 s: skipped
2.0 s: refresh
3.0 s: skipped
4.5 s: refresh

Inject TimeProvider — fifteen minutes of timer in no time

Every timer API here takes a TimeProvider, so a test passes a fake that fires timers only when told — this one fakes the clock and one timer slot on one thread but leaves `GetTimestamp` (and so `GetElapsedTime`) on the real clock, and `FakeTimeProvider` (Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing) is the general version.

var time = new ManualTimeProvider();
using var everyFiveMinutes = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), time);   // takes the fake

time.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(15));       // three ticks fall due; PeriodicTimer keeps one; ':' is quoted
Console.WriteLine($"ticked {await everyFiveMinutes.WaitForNextTickAsync()} at {time.GetUtcNow():HH':'mm}");

sealed class ManualTimeProvider : TimeProvider, ITimer      // one timer slot, one thread: a test fake
{
    private DateTimeOffset now = new(2026, 11, 16, 9, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero), next = DateTimeOffset.MaxValue;
    private TimeSpan period;
    private Action? tick;                                    // null once disposed

    public override DateTimeOffset GetUtcNow() => now;

    public override ITimer CreateTimer(TimerCallback callback, object? state, TimeSpan due, TimeSpan period)
    {
        tick = () => callback(state);
        Change(due, period);
        return this;                                         // the fake is its own (only) timer
    }

    public void Advance(TimeSpan by)                         // fire the timer each time it falls due
    {
        var end = now + by;
        while (tick is not null && next <= end)
        {
            now = next;
            next = period > TimeSpan.Zero ? next + period : DateTimeOffset.MaxValue;
            tick();
        }
        now = end;
    }

    public bool Change(TimeSpan due, TimeSpan newPeriod)
    {
        next = due == Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan ? DateTimeOffset.MaxValue : now + due;
        period = newPeriod;
        return tick is not null;                             // false once disposed, like a real timer
    }

    public void Dispose() => tick = null;

    public ValueTask DisposeAsync()
    {
        Dispose();
        return ValueTask.CompletedTask;
    }
}
Result
ticked True at 09:15

Recurring work that outlives a screen — BackgroundService

A hosted service runs for the life of the process, not of a page, and the host cancels `stoppingToken` on shutdown — so that is the only cancellation allowed to end the loop.

// OrderSyncWorker.cs
using Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;

public interface IOrderSync
{
    Task PushPendingOrdersAsync(CancellationToken token);
}

public sealed class OrderSyncWorker(IOrderSync sync, TimeProvider time, ILogger<OrderSyncWorker> logger)
    : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        await Task.Yield();                             // hand back at once: start-up never waits on a sync
        using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), time);
        do
        {
            try
            {
                await sync.PushPendingOrdersAsync(stoppingToken);
            }
            catch (Exception e) when (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
            {
                // Anything but shutdown is logged, including an HttpClient timeout (a TaskCanceledException);
                // an exception that escapes ExecuteAsync stops the whole host (the default since .NET 6)
                logger.LogError(e, "Order sync failed; trying again on the next tick");
            }
        }
        while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken));
    }
}

// Program.cs
var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddSingleton(TimeProvider.System);     // tests register a fake instead
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IOrderSync, OrderSync>();
builder.Services.AddHostedService<OrderSyncWorker>();
await builder.Build().RunAsync();
Result

Pushes pending orders at start-up and every five minutes until the process stops; a failed push, an HttpClient timeout included, is logged and retried on the next tick, and Ctrl+C or SIGTERM stops it cleanly.

Setup

  2. Two files: OrderSyncWorker.cs (replacing the template's Worker.cs) and Program.cs, plus your own OrderSync : IOrderSync; then dotnet run --project OrderSync

Excerpt, not compiled or run here: it needs a .NET Worker Service project (Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting), with your own OrderSync class.

Pitfalls

Timer bugs are lifetime and thread bugs far more often than timing bugs.

  • async void timer callbacks (timer.Elapsed += async (_, _) => …): exceptions crash the process and ticks overlap. Use a PeriodicTimer loop you await.
  • A System.Threading.Timer that nothing references can be garbage-collected and silently stop. Keep it in a field and dispose it.
  • The opposite leak: a timer callback that captures a view model keeps the closed screen alive. Dispose the timer (or cancel the loop) when the screen goes away.
  • Touching UI from a thread-pool timer callback: WPF and WinUI throw, and Android and iOS views under MAUI fail too. Use the dispatcher timer, or marshal with Dispatcher.Dispatch (MAUI), DispatcherQueue.TryEnqueue (WinUI) or Dispatcher.InvokeAsync (WPF).
  • DateTime.Now differences for elapsed time: the wall clock jumps (NTP, daylight saving). Use TimeProvider.GetTimestamp() with GetElapsedTime, or a Stopwatch.
  • Real sleeps in tests: inject TimeProvider everywhere (Task.Delay, PeriodicTimer, CancellationTokenSource, WaitAsync all accept one).
  • Honour Retry-After on 429/503, cap the backoff, and in production prefer a policy library (Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience, Polly) over a hand-rolled loop.
  • Pass the token to the work, not only to the wait: CancelAfter stops the request; WaitAsync merely abandons it.
  • PeriodicTimer allows one waiter at a time, and its Period can be changed while it runs (.NET 8+) — handy for backing a poll off.

Modularization — Projects, Assemblies & NuGet

Class-library projects and ProjectReference, `internal`, InternalsVisibleTo and `file` types, contracts projects and the composition root, Directory.Build.props and central package management, packaging for NuGet, architecture tests, trimming and AOT.

  • dotnet
  • csharp >=12
  • dotnet >=8
  • .NET SDK (MSBuild, NuGet); the same projects back .NET MAUI, WPF, WinUI, Blazor and ASP.NET Core apps

Sources: MSBuild reference for .NET SDK projects · Central Package Management — NuGet · Customize your build by folder — MSBuild · Friend assemblies — .NET

The units of modularity in .NET

The project — one assembly — is the unit the compiler enforces; everything smaller is convention, everything larger is distribution.

UnitBoundary it gives youReach for it when
feature folder + namespacenone enforced — only naminga small app or service; start here
file type (C# 11)visible only inside one source filea helper that must not leak even inside its assembly, such as a generator's output
project (.csproj → one .dll)internal is invisible outside it; references are explicit and acyclica feature, a layer or an adapter that deserves its own public surface
solution (.sln / .slnx)none — a list of projects to build and open togetherone repository's apps, libraries and tests
NuGet packageversioned with SemVer; consumers upgrade on their own schedulecode shared across repositories or teams

Why modularize at all

Have concrete reasons ready; "cleanliness" is not one.

  • Enforced boundaries — internal and the reference graph make a forbidden dependency a compile error instead of a review comment.
  • Incremental builds — MSBuild rebuilds only projects whose inputs changed, and a project whose public API did not change does not force its dependents to recompile (reference assemblies).
  • Parallel teams and ownership — a project per feature gives each team a surface to own, review and version.
  • Reuse across apps — the same Shop.Checkout library serves the MAUI app, the WPF back-office and the ASP.NET Core API.
  • Faster, focused tests — a test project references one library and its fakes, not the whole app.
  • The cost is real — every project adds build-graph overhead, restore time and a .csproj to maintain; the answer is a few meaningful projects, not one per folder.

A solution of class libraries with ProjectReference

Each feature is a class library with an explicit reference list; the app project is the only one that references everything.

Shop.sln
Directory.Build.props                 ← shared build settings (see the Directory.Build.props card)
Directory.Packages.props              ← one version per NuGet package
src/
  Shop.App/                           ← MAUI, WPF or ASP.NET Core: the composition root
  Shop.Checkout/                      ← a feature: public surface + internals
  Shop.Payments.Abstractions/         ← contracts only: interfaces and records
  Shop.Payments.Card/                 ← an adapter implementing the contracts
tests/
  Shop.Checkout.Tests/

<!-- src/Shop.Checkout/Shop.Checkout.csproj -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net9.0</TargetFramework>
    <RootNamespace>Shop.Checkout</RootNamespace>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- depends on the contract, never on Shop.Payments.Card -->
    <ProjectReference Include="..\Shop.Payments.Abstractions\Shop.Payments.Abstractions.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- generates [assembly: InternalsVisibleTo("Shop.Checkout.Tests")] -->
    <InternalsVisibleTo Include="Shop.Checkout.Tests" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
Result

dotnet build Shop.sln builds the projects in dependency order; a ProjectReference that would close a cycle fails the build.

Setup
  1. .NET 8 SDK or later
  2. dotnet new sln -n Shop, dotnet new classlib -o src/Shop.Checkout, dotnet sln add src/Shop.Checkout
  3. dotnet add src/Shop.Checkout reference src/Shop.Payments.Abstractions

Excerpt, not compiled or run here: it needs a multi-project .NET solution.

`internal` and `file` types: the enforcement mechanism

A project exposes a small `public` surface; `internal` hides the rest from other projects, and `file` hides a helper from the rest of its own project.

using Shop.Orders;

var checkout = OrdersModule.CreateCheckout();          // the public surface
Console.WriteLine(checkout.Place("ada"));
Console.WriteLine(checkout.Place("grace"));
// From another project:  new OrderNumbers()  → error CS0122: inaccessible due to its protection level
// From another file:     OrderNumberFormat   → error CS0103: the name does not exist in the current context

namespace Shop.Orders
{
    public interface ICheckout
    {
        string Place(string customer);
    }

    public static class OrdersModule
    {
        public static ICheckout CreateCheckout() => new Checkout(new OrderNumbers());
    }

    internal sealed class Checkout(OrderNumbers numbers) : ICheckout
    {
        public string Place(string customer) => $"{numbers.Next()} placed for {customer}";
    }

    internal sealed class OrderNumbers                 // tests reach it through InternalsVisibleTo
    {
        private int last;
        public string Next() => OrderNumberFormat.Format(++last);
    }

    file static class OrderNumberFormat                // only this file can name it
    {
        public static string Format(int sequence) => $"A-{sequence:0000}";
    }
}
Result
A-0001 placed for ada
A-0002 placed for grace
Setup
  1. .NET 8 SDK or later
  2. dotnet new console -o Demo, replace Demo/Program.cs with the example, then dotnet run --project Demo
  3. In a real solution the Shop.Orders namespace is its own class-library project

A contracts project and the composition root

Features depend on an abstractions project, adapters implement it, and each project offers one `Add…` extension so the app's composition root wires modules without knowing their internals.

using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Shop.Checkout;
using Shop.Payments.Card;

// Shop.App — the only project that references every module
var services = new ServiceCollection().AddCheckout().AddCardPayments();
using var provider = services.BuildServiceProvider(new ServiceProviderOptions { ValidateOnBuild = true });
Console.WriteLine(provider.GetRequiredService<ICheckout>().Pay("A-1"));

namespace Shop.Payments.Abstractions                    // references nothing
{
    public interface IPaymentGateway { string Charge(string orderId); }
}

namespace Shop.Checkout                                 // references Abstractions only
{
    using Shop.Payments.Abstractions;

    public interface ICheckout { string Pay(string orderId); }

    internal sealed class Checkout(IPaymentGateway gateway) : ICheckout
    {
        public string Pay(string orderId) => $"{orderId} paid: {gateway.Charge(orderId)}";
    }

    public static class CheckoutModule
    {
        public static IServiceCollection AddCheckout(this IServiceCollection services) =>
            services.AddTransient<ICheckout, Checkout>();
    }
}

namespace Shop.Payments.Card                            // references Abstractions only
{
    using Shop.Payments.Abstractions;

    internal sealed class CardGateway : IPaymentGateway
    {
        public string Charge(string orderId) => $"card charged for {orderId}";
    }

    public static class CardPaymentsModule
    {
        public static IServiceCollection AddCardPayments(this IServiceCollection services) =>
            services.AddSingleton<IPaymentGateway, CardGateway>();
    }
}
Result
A-1 paid: card charged for A-1

Directory.Build.props: shared settings, and a test-project override

Settings every project shares live in one root `Directory.Build.props`; a nested one for `tests/` imports it and relaxes only what tests need, such as CA1707 for underscore test names.

<!-- Directory.Build.props at the root — imported into every project in this folder and below -->
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <AnalysisLevel>latest-recommended</AnalysisLevel>
    <EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>true</EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>
    <!-- Each project sees only its direct references. The cost: a project must then also reference every
         project whose types it uses, including types in a referenced project's public API (else CS0012). -->
    <DisableTransitiveProjectReferences>true</DisableTransitiveProjectReferences>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>

<!-- tests/Directory.Build.props — only the nearest file is imported, so pull in the root one first -->
<Project>
  <Import Project="../Directory.Build.props" />                 <!-- relative to this file -->
  <PropertyGroup>
    <IsPackable>false</IsPackable>
    <!-- Test names like Rejects_an_expired_order read as sentences; CA1707 forbids underscores -->
    <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);CA1707</NoWarn>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
Result

The whole solution builds with latest-recommended analyzers as errors, and the tests build too — without the tests/ file, Rejects_an_expired_order fails with error CA1707: Remove the underscores from member name.

Setup

Central package management and PrivateAssets

One `Directory.Packages.props` holds every package version, test packages included, and projects list package names only; build-time packages are marked `PrivateAssets="all"`.

<!-- Directory.Packages.props — one version of each package for the whole repository -->
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>true</ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>
    <CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled>true</CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Abstractions" Version="9.0.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Roslynator.Analyzers" Version="4.12.9" />
    <!-- every package a test project references needs its version here too -->
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk" Version="17.12.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="xunit" Version="2.9.2" />
    <PackageVersion Include="xunit.runner.visualstudio" Version="2.8.2" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>

<!-- src/Shop.Checkout/Shop.Checkout.csproj — names only; VersionOverride="…" is the escape hatch -->
<ItemGroup>
  <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Abstractions" />
  <!-- an analyzer runs at build time only: PrivateAssets="all" keeps it out of consumers and the .nupkg -->
  <PackageReference Include="Roslynator.Analyzers" PrivateAssets="all" />
</ItemGroup>
Result

Every project restores the same versions; a Version attribute left on a PackageReference fails restore with NU1008, and Shop.Checkout.nuspec lists Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Abstractions but not the analyzer.

Packaging a library as NuGet: versions, multi-targeting, AOT

Pack a library when another repository needs it: SemVer the public API, multi-target the frameworks your consumers run, validate against the last release, and declare it trim- and AOT-safe.

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFrameworks>netstandard2.0;net8.0;net9.0</TargetFrameworks>
    <!-- netstandard2.0 would default to C# 7.3; records, init and required also need polyfills there -->
    <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>
    <PackageId>Shop.Money</PackageId>
    <Version>2.1.0</Version>                          <!-- MAJOR breaks, MINOR adds, PATCH fixes -->
    <Description>Money and currency types shared by the shop's apps and services.</Description>
    <PackageLicenseExpression>MIT</PackageLicenseExpression>
    <PackageReadmeFile>README.md</PackageReadmeFile>
    <GenerateDocumentationFile>true</GenerateDocumentationFile>
    <IncludeSymbols>true</IncludeSymbols>
    <SymbolPackageFormat>snupkg</SymbolPackageFormat>
    <!-- fails the pack if 2.1.0 breaks the public API of 2.0.0 -->
    <EnablePackageValidation>true</EnablePackageValidation>
    <PackageValidationBaselineVersion>2.0.0</PackageValidationBaselineVersion>
    <!-- turns on the trim, single-file and AOT analyzers; they need net8.0 or later -->
    <IsAotCompatible Condition="$([MSBuild]::IsTargetFrameworkCompatible('$(TargetFramework)', 'net8.0'))"
        >true</IsAotCompatible>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <None Include="README.md" Pack="true" PackagePath="\" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>

// Money.cs — every API exists on every target; the span overload is added where the framework has Span
using System;                                     // explicit: the project may not enable ImplicitUsings
using System.Globalization;

namespace Shop.Money;

/// <summary>Formats amounts held as whole cents.</summary>
public static class MoneyFormat
{
    /// <summary>Formats <paramref name="cents"/> as an amount such as <c>42.50</c>.</summary>
    public static string FormatCents(long cents) =>
        (cents / 100m).ToString("0.00", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);

#if NET8_0_OR_GREATER
    /// <summary>Formats into <paramref name="destination"/> without allocating a string.</summary>
    public static bool TryFormatCents(long cents, Span<char> destination, out int written) =>
        (cents / 100m).TryFormat(destination, out written, "0.00", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
#endif
}
Result

dotnet pack produces one package with a lib/ folder per target framework; consumers on .NET 8+ also get the span-based overload and an AOT-analysed build, everyone else the netstandard2.0 build, and package validation fails the pack if an API disappears between versions or targets.

Architecture tests: a red test when a dependency points outward

When layers share one assembly nothing stops `Domain` from using `Infrastructure`; NetArchTest reads the IL, so even a `new` inside a method body fails the test (reflection over signatures cannot see method bodies).

using NetArchTest.Rules;
using Xunit;

namespace Shop.ArchitectureTests;

public class LayeringTests
{
    // NetArchTest reads the compiled IL (with Mono.Cecil): it sees `new` and calls inside method bodies,
    // generic arguments and base types, which reflection over signatures misses.
    private static readonly Types ShopTypes = Types.InAssembly(typeof(Shop.Domain.Order).Assembly);

    [Fact]
    public void Domain_does_not_depend_on_infrastructure()
    {
        var result = ShopTypes
            .That().ResideInNamespace("Shop.Domain")
            .ShouldNot().HaveDependencyOn("Shop.Infrastructure")
            .GetResult();

        Assert.True(result.IsSuccessful, $"Domain types using Infrastructure: {Names(result)}");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Infrastructure_types_are_sealed()
    {
        var result = ShopTypes
            .That().ResideInNamespace("Shop.Infrastructure")
            .Should().BeSealed()
            .GetResult();

        Assert.True(result.IsSuccessful, $"Not sealed: {Names(result)}");
    }

    private static string Names(TestResult result) => string.Join(", ", result.FailingTypeNames ?? []);
}
Result

With PricingService.PriceOf doing new Shop.Infrastructure.SqlPriceTable(), the first test fails with Domain types using Infrastructure: Shop.Domain.PricingService; injecting an IPriceTable port makes both pass.

  2. dotnet new xunit -o Shop.ArchitectureTests, then dotnet add Shop.ArchitectureTests package NetArchTest.Rules and a reference to the project under test
  3. Add the file and run dotnet test Shop.ArchitectureTests

Choosing a strategy

Start with folders in one project; promote a folder to a project when one of these reasons appears, and to a package only when another repository needs it.

SituationStrategyWhy
one small app or service, one teamfeature folders in one projectno build-graph cost; vertical slices still read cleanly
a boundary keeps being crossed in reviewpromote the feature to a project; make its internals internalthe compiler enforces what reviews could not
two apps (MAUI and WPF, or app and API) share logica shared class library per feature, referenced by bothone implementation, two hosts
a feature needs a vendor SDK (payments, maps)an *.Abstractions project plus one adapter projectthe SDK stays out of every other project and every test
layers in one assemblyarchitecture tests in CI (NetArchTest, ArchUnitNET)cheaper than projects, still a red build on violation; separate projects remain the stronger guarantee
code shared across repositoriesa NuGet package with SemVer and package validationconsumers upgrade deliberately
a trimmed or Native AOT appIsAotCompatible on every library it referencesreflection and dynamic loading surface as build warnings, not run-time crashes

Pitfalls

Most module graphs fail in one of these ways.

  • Cycles — MSBuild refuses a ProjectReference cycle, so teams "fix" it by merging projects or adding a Common; extract the shared contract into an *.Abstractions project instead.
  • The god Common / Shared / Utils project — everything references it, so every change rebuilds everything; split it by what it is about (Shop.Money, Shop.Time).
  • Too many tiny projects — a project per folder slows restore, build and the IDE; a project has to earn its place with a boundary, a reuse or a team.
  • InternalsVisibleTo to production assemblies — it is for test projects; a second consumer of internals means they are really a public API.
  • Transitive leakage — without DisableTransitiveProjectReferences, the app can use Domain types through Infrastructure without ever referencing Domain; the graph you see is not the one you get.
  • Reflection-driven modules under trimming or AOT — Assembly.Load plugins and assembly scanning for DI registration break; prefer explicit Add…Module() extension methods.
  • Dependencies point one way — app → features → abstractions → nothing; adapters point at abstractions; tests point at what they test.

SwiftUI → .NET MAUI XAML

MAUI pages are long-lived objects that bindings keep up to date, so nothing rebuilds a `body`.

SwiftUI.NET MAUI XAML

A ContentPage with compiled bindings

Set `x:DataType` where the `BindingContext` is set, so every `{Binding}` below it is checked at build time and generated without reflection.

<ContentPage xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/dotnet/2021/maui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2009/xaml"
             xmlns:vm="clr-namespace:Shop.ViewModels"
             x:Class="Shop.Views.OrdersPage"
             x:DataType="vm:OrdersViewModel"
             Title="Orders">
    <Grid RowDefinitions="Auto,Auto,*" RowSpacing="8" Padding="16">
        <SearchBar Text="{Binding Query}" Placeholder="Search by customer" />
        <Label Grid.Row="1" Text="{Binding Orders.Count, StringFormat='{0} orders'}" />
        <ActivityIndicator Grid.Row="2" IsRunning="{Binding IsLoading}" IsVisible="{Binding IsLoading}" />
        <!-- Grid.Row="2" also holds the CollectionView from the next card -->
    </Grid>
</ContentPage>

// OrdersPage.xaml.cs
public partial class OrdersPage : ContentPage
{
    private readonly OrdersViewModel viewModel;

    public OrdersPage(OrdersViewModel viewModel)
    {
        InitializeComponent();
        BindingContext = this.viewModel = viewModel;
    }

    protected override async void OnAppearing()
    {
        base.OnAppearing();
        await viewModel.LoadAsync();      // runs on every appearance, so LoadAsync skips work it already did
    }
}

<!-- Shop.csproj: a misspelled path is only warning XC0045, so make it fail the build;
     the second line compiles Source bindings too, which clears XC0025 -->
<PropertyGroup>
    <WarningsAsErrors>$(WarningsAsErrors);XC0022;XC0023;XC0025;XC0045</WarningsAsErrors>
    <MauiEnableXamlCBindingWithSourceCompilation>true</MauiEnableXamlCBindingWithSourceCompilation>
</PropertyGroup>
Result

The page shows a search bar, an order count that updates as the view model changes, and a spinner while loading; with the WarningsAsErrors line, a misspelled binding path such as {Binding Querry} fails the build (XC0045) instead of leaving a blank label.

Setup
  1. The .NET 9 SDK with the MAUI workload: dotnet workload install maui, then dotnet new maui -o Shop
  2. Save as Views/OrdersPage.xaml with its code-behind Views/OrdersPage.xaml.cs, and add the WarningsAsErrors line to Shop.csproj
  3. Register both in MauiProgram.cs — builder.Services.AddTransient<OrdersPage>() and AddTransient<OrdersViewModel>() — so Shell builds the page through dependency injection

Layouts and sizing

A `Grid` sizes rows and columns as `Auto`, `*` (a share of what is left) or fixed, the stacks place children in a line with `Spacing`, and `FlexLayout` wraps.

<VerticalStackLayout Spacing="12" Padding="16">
    <!-- the name takes the room left after the total; the date spans both columns -->
    <Grid ColumnDefinitions="*,Auto" RowDefinitions="Auto,Auto" ColumnSpacing="12">
        <Label Text="{Binding Customer}" FontSize="20" LineBreakMode="TailTruncation" />
        <Label Grid.Column="1" Text="{Binding Total, StringFormat='{0:C}'}" FontAttributes="Bold" />
        <Label Grid.Row="1" Grid.ColumnSpan="2"
               Text="{Binding PlacedOn, StringFormat='Placed {0:d MMM yyyy}'}" />
    </Grid>

    <HorizontalStackLayout Spacing="6">
        <Image Source="truck.png" WidthRequest="20" HeightRequest="20" />
        <Label Text="{Binding ShippingStatus}" VerticalOptions="Center" />
    </HorizontalStackLayout>

    <!-- Border replaces Frame, which is obsolete in MAUI 9 -->
    <Border Stroke="LightGray" StrokeShape="RoundRectangle 8" Padding="12">
        <Label Text="{Binding Notes}" />
    </Border>

    <!-- tags flow onto the next line when the row is full -->
    <FlexLayout Wrap="Wrap" BindableLayout.ItemsSource="{Binding Tags}">
        <BindableLayout.ItemTemplate>
            <DataTemplate x:DataType="x:String">
                <Border Margin="0,0,6,6" Padding="8,2" StrokeShape="RoundRectangle 10">
                    <Label Text="{Binding .}" FontSize="12" />
                </Border>
            </DataTemplate>
        </BindableLayout.ItemTemplate>
    </FlexLayout>
</VerticalStackLayout>
Result

The customer name is truncated before it can push the total off screen, the notes get a rounded border and the tags wrap onto as many lines as they need; HorizontalOptions defaults to Fill, and Frame and the *AndExpand options are obsolete, a CS0618 warning in C# but silent in XAML.

Setup
  1. A .NET MAUI app project (dotnet new maui -o Shop)
  2. Use inside the Content of an order detail ContentPage whose x:DataType is the order

CollectionView with a DataTemplate and selection

Every `DataTemplate` declares its own `x:DataType`, and a command on the view model is reached through `RelativeSource AncestorType`.

<CollectionView Grid.Row="2"
                ItemsSource="{Binding Orders}"
                SelectionMode="Single"
                SelectedItem="{Binding SelectedOrder}"
                SelectionChangedCommand="{Binding OpenSelectedCommand}"
                RemainingItemsThreshold="5"
                RemainingItemsThresholdReachedCommand="{Binding LoadMoreCommand}">
    <CollectionView.ItemsLayout>
        <LinearItemsLayout Orientation="Vertical" ItemSpacing="8" />
    </CollectionView.ItemsLayout>

    <CollectionView.EmptyView>
        <Label Text="No orders match your search." HorizontalOptions="Center" />
    </CollectionView.EmptyView>

    <CollectionView.ItemTemplate>
        <DataTemplate x:DataType="models:Order">
            <Grid ColumnDefinitions="*,Auto,Auto" ColumnSpacing="8" Padding="12">
                <Label Text="{Binding Customer}" VerticalOptions="Center" />
                <Label Grid.Column="1" VerticalOptions="Center"
                       Text="{Binding Total, StringFormat='{0:C}'}" />
                <Button Grid.Column="2" Text="Cancel"
                        Command="{Binding x:DataType='vm:OrdersViewModel',
                                          Source={RelativeSource AncestorType={x:Type vm:OrdersViewModel}},
                                          Path=CancelCommand}"
                        CommandParameter="{Binding .}" />
            </Grid>
        </DataTemplate>
    </CollectionView.ItemTemplate>
</CollectionView>
Result

Tapping a row sets SelectedOrder (TwoWay by default) and runs OpenSelectedCommand, nearing the end runs LoadMoreCommand, an empty list shows the message, and Cancel passes its row's order to the page's command; that Source binding falls back to reflection (warning XC0025) unless the project sets MauiEnableXamlCBindingWithSourceCompilation to true, as the previous card's project file does.

  3. Register both in MauiProgram.cs — builder.Services.AddTransient<OrdersPage>() and AddTransient<OrdersViewModel>() — so Shell builds the page through dependency injection

Binding modes, formatting and converters

Choose the cheapest mode that works, and keep a converter a thin `IValueConverter` that calls plain logic, as the next card shows.

<ContentPage.Resources>
    <conv:OrderStatusToColorConverter x:Key="StatusColor" />
</ContentPage.Resources>

<!-- OneWay (the default for most properties): view model → view -->
<Label Text="{Binding Status}" TextColor="{Binding Status, Converter={StaticResource StatusColor}}" />

<!-- TwoWay is the default for Entry.Text, SearchBar.Text and Slider.Value -->
<Entry Text="{Binding DeliveryNote}" Placeholder="Note for the courier" />

<!-- OneTime: read once, no change subscription; the cheapest binding -->
<Label Text="{Binding Id, Mode=OneTime, StringFormat='Order #{0}'}" />

<!-- TargetNullValue when the value is null, FallbackValue when the path cannot be resolved -->
<Label Text="{Binding TrackingCode, TargetNullValue='Not shipped yet', FallbackValue='—'}" />

// Converters/OrderStatusToColorConverter.cs
public class OrderStatusToColorConverter : IValueConverter
{
    public object? Convert(object? value, Type targetType, object? parameter, CultureInfo culture) =>
        value is OrderStatus status ? Color.FromArgb(StatusPalette.HexFor(status)) : Colors.Gray;

    public object? ConvertBack(object? value, Type targetType, object? parameter, CultureInfo culture) =>
        throw new NotSupportedException("Status colours are display-only.");
}
Result

The status label is coloured by state, the courier note writes back to the view model as you type, the order number never re-reads, and a missing tracking code shows "Not shipped yet".

Setup
  1. A .NET MAUI app project (dotnet new maui -o Shop)
  2. Declare xmlns:conv="clr-namespace:Shop.Converters" on the page; put the C# class in Converters/OrderStatusToColorConverter.cs

The converter's logic, run without a UI

Keep the mapping in a plain class so it can be tested without a UI, and pass "today" in instead of reading the clock inside a converter.

using System.Globalization;

var today = new DateOnly(2026, 11, 16);
var culture = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("en-US");

foreach (var status in Enum.GetValues<OrderStatus>())
    Console.WriteLine($"{status}: {StatusPalette.HexFor(status)}");

DateOnly[] placed = [today, today.AddDays(-1), today.AddDays(-3), new(2026, 9, 2), today.AddDays(2)];
foreach (var day in placed)
    Console.WriteLine(OrderText.Placed(day, today, culture));

enum OrderStatus { Pending, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled }

static class StatusPalette
{
    public static string HexFor(OrderStatus status) => status switch
    {
        OrderStatus.Pending => "#B26A00",
        OrderStatus.Shipped => "#1565C0",
        OrderStatus.Delivered => "#2E7D32",
        OrderStatus.Cancelled => "#757575",
        _ => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(status)),
    };
}

static class OrderText
{
    public static string Placed(DateOnly placed, DateOnly today, CultureInfo culture)
    {
        var days = today.DayNumber - placed.DayNumber;
        return days switch
        {
            < 0 or >= 7 => "Placed " + placed.ToString("d MMM yyyy", culture),   // future: clock skew
            0 => "Placed today",
            1 => "Placed yesterday",
            _ => $"Placed {days} days ago",
        };
    }
}
Result
Pending: #B26A00
Shipped: #1565C0
Delivered: #2E7D32
Cancelled: #757575
Placed today
Placed yesterday
Placed 3 days ago
Placed 2 Sep 2026
Placed 18 Nov 2026
Setup
  1. .NET 8 SDK or later
  2. dotnet new console -o Demo, replace Demo/Program.cs with the example, then dotnet run --project Demo (a MAUI converter calls these same methods)

Shell routes and query parameters

Visual routes live in `AppShell.xaml`, while detail pages are registered with `Routing.RegisterRoute` and reached with `GoToAsync`.

<!-- AppShell.xaml -->
<Shell xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/dotnet/2021/maui"
       xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2009/xaml"
       xmlns:views="clr-namespace:Shop.Views"
       x:Class="Shop.AppShell">
    <TabBar>
        <ShellContent Title="Orders" Route="orders" ContentTemplate="{DataTemplate views:OrdersPage}" />
        <ShellContent Title="Account" Route="account" ContentTemplate="{DataTemplate views:AccountPage}" />
    </TabBar>
</Shell>

// AppShell.xaml.cs: a detail page that is not in the tab bar
Routing.RegisterRoute("detail", typeof(OrderDetailPage));

// App.xaml.cs: MAUI 9 marks Application.MainPage obsolete; create the window instead
protected override Window CreateWindow(IActivationState? activationState) => new(new AppShell());

// OrdersViewModel: the command is declared by hand, not with [RelayCommand],
// so typed C# bindings can reach it too (see the C# UI sheet)
public IAsyncRelayCommand OpenSelectedCommand { get; }

public OrdersViewModel() => OpenSelectedCommand = new AsyncRelayCommand(OpenSelectedAsync);

private async Task OpenSelectedAsync()
{
    if (SelectedOrder is not { } order) return;
    SelectedOrder = null;                       // so the same row can be tapped again after Back
    await Shell.Current.GoToAsync("detail", new ShellNavigationQueryParameters { { "Order", order } });
}

// OrderDetailViewModel: IQueryAttributable is trim-safe; [QueryProperty] is not
public void ApplyQueryAttributes(IDictionary<string, object> query) => Order = (Order)query["Order"];

// Back: GoToAsync("..").  A string id instead: GoToAsync($"detail?id={order.Id}")
Result

Tapping an order pushes the detail page on top of the Orders tab with the order object as its single-use parameter, and .. pops back to the list, where the row can be tapped again.

Setup
  1. A .NET MAUI app project (dotnet new maui -o Shop) with the CommunityToolkit.Mvvm NuGet package
  2. Edit AppShell.xaml, AppShell.xaml.cs and App.xaml.cs; the methods go in OrdersViewModel and OrderDetailViewModel, both deriving from ObservableObject

Animations in code-behind, and cancelling them

The `ViewExtensions` animations return `Task<bool>` that is true when cancelled, so check it, and give the pause between animations its own token.

private CancellationTokenSource? bannerCts;

private async void OnPlaceOrderClicked(object? sender, EventArgs e)
{
    await viewModel.PlaceOrderAsync();
    await ShowConfirmationAsync();
}

private async Task ShowConfirmationAsync()
{
    bannerCts?.Cancel();                                   // a second order restarts the banner
    bannerCts = new CancellationTokenSource();
    var token = bannerCts.Token;

    // Lay the banner out in its final place and animate from an offset;
    // a view translated in from off screen keeps its hit area off screen
    ConfirmationBanner.Opacity = 0;
    ConfirmationBanner.TranslationY = -40;
    ConfirmationBanner.IsVisible = true;

    bool[] cancelled = await Task.WhenAll(
        ConfirmationBanner.FadeTo(1, 250, Easing.CubicOut),
        ConfirmationBanner.TranslateTo(0, 0, 250, Easing.CubicOut));
    if (cancelled.Contains(true)) return;                  // the page went away mid-animation

    try { await Task.Delay(2000, token); }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) { return; }

    if (await ConfirmationBanner.FadeTo(0, 400)) return;
    ConfirmationBanner.IsVisible = false;
}

protected override void OnDisappearing()
{
    base.OnDisappearing();
    bannerCts?.Cancel();                                    // stops the pause
    ConfirmationBanner.CancelAnimations();                  // stops a running fade
}

// MAUI 10 renames these FadeToAsync, TranslateToAsync…; the old names are [Obsolete]
Result

After the order is placed the banner fades and slides into place, stays for two seconds and fades out, and leaving the page at any point stops it without the fade-out running later.

Setup
  1. A .NET MAUI app project (dotnet new maui -o Shop)
  2. In CheckoutPage.xaml add <Border x:Name="ConfirmationBanner" IsVisible="False"> holding an "Order placed" label, and <Button Text="Place order" Clicked="OnPlaceOrderClicked" />; this code goes in CheckoutPage.xaml.cs

A reusable ContentView with a BindableProperty

A component's inputs are `BindableProperty`s that callers can bind, so react to a change in `propertyChanged` and never set the control's own `BindingContext`.

<!-- Controls/StatusBadge.xaml -->
<ContentView xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/dotnet/2021/maui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2009/xaml"
             x:Class="Shop.Controls.StatusBadge">
    <Border x:Name="Pill" StrokeThickness="0" StrokeShape="RoundRectangle 10" Padding="8,2">
        <Label x:Name="Caption" FontSize="12" TextColor="White" />
    </Border>
</ContentView>

// Controls/StatusBadge.xaml.cs
public partial class StatusBadge : ContentView
{
    public static readonly BindableProperty StatusProperty = BindableProperty.Create(
        nameof(Status), typeof(OrderStatus), typeof(StatusBadge), OrderStatus.Pending,
        propertyChanged: (bindable, _, newValue) => ((StatusBadge)bindable).Render((OrderStatus)newValue));

    public OrderStatus Status
    {
        get => (OrderStatus)GetValue(StatusProperty);
        set => SetValue(StatusProperty, value);      // no logic here: bindings call SetValue directly
    }

    public StatusBadge()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
        Render(Status);                                // the default value raises no change
    }

    private void Render(OrderStatus status)
    {
        Caption.Text = status.ToString();
        Pill.BackgroundColor = Color.FromArgb(StatusPalette.HexFor(status));
    }
}
Result

Each row shows a coloured pill that updates when that order's Status changes, while the row's own binding context, the order, keeps flowing into the control untouched.

Setup
  1. A .NET MAUI app project (dotnet new maui -o Shop)
  2. Add a .NET MAUI ContentView named Controls/StatusBadge.xaml; StatusPalette is the class from the converter-logic card
  3. Use it inside a template: <controls:StatusBadge Status="{Binding Status}" />

Performance rules

Measure and arrange passes cost the most, then reflection bindings.

  • Put x:DataType on every page and every DataTemplate: compiled bindings are typically 8–20× quicker, and full trimming and NativeAOT require them.
  • Use CollectionView for lists: ListView and the cells are deprecated in MAUI 10, and MAUI 9 adds faster opt-in CollectionViewHandler2 handlers on iOS and Mac Catalyst (the default in MAUI 10).
  • Flatten layouts: one Grid instead of nested stacks, and no layout around a single child, because every level of nesting adds layout calculations.
  • Prefer fixed or * rows and columns to Auto where you can: the Grid docs note that each auto-sized row or column makes the layout engine do extra calculations.
  • Ship images near the size they are displayed at, so the platform doesn't decode a large bitmap for a small slot.
  • Use OneTime (or plain assignment) for values that never change, such as Button.Text = "Accept": every binding costs a subscription.
  • A CollectionView inside a VerticalStackLayout or ScrollView gets infinite height, renders every row, and incremental loading can loop.
  • x:DataType="x:Object" to silence XC0022 turns compiled bindings off for that whole subtree; fix the type instead.
  • Replacing ItemsSource with a new list on each refresh rebuilds every row and resets the scroll position; update the ObservableCollection in place.
  • Treat the binding warnings as errors in CI: <WarningsAsErrors>$(WarningsAsErrors);XC0022;XC0023;XC0025;XC0045</WarningsAsErrors>.

Sources: Improve app performance — .NET MAUI · Grid — .NET MAUI (sizing rows and columns)

XAML → C#

XAML is an object initialiser with a compiler on top, so every element and attribute has a C# equivalent.

XAMLC#
<Label Text="Orders" FontSize="20" />new Label { Text = "Orders", FontSize = 20 }
x:Name="Banner"a field holding the instance
InitializeComponent()nothing: the constructor builds the tree and assigns Content
Grid.Row="1" (attached property)Grid.SetRow(view, 1), or grid.Add(view, column: 0, row: 1)
RowDefinitions="Auto,*"grid.RowDefinitions = [new RowDefinition(GridLength.Auto), new RowDefinition(GridLength.Star)]; the RowDefinitions = { … } form compiles only inside new Grid { … }
Text="{Binding Customer}" + x:DataTypelabel.SetBinding(Label.TextProperty, static (Order o) => o.Customer) (MAUI 9; not for members another source generator writes)
Clicked="OnSave"button.Clicked += OnSave;
Command="{Binding SaveCommand}"button.SetBinding(Button.CommandProperty, static (OrdersViewModel vm) => vm.SaveCommand) with SaveCommand declared by hand (a [RelayCommand] one gives BSG0006: bind it with new Binding("SaveCommand"))
<DataTemplate>…</DataTemplate>new DataTemplate(() => new OrderRow()); the factory runs once per realized row
{StaticResource Accent}(Color)Application.Current!.Resources["Accent"] reads app-level resources only; {StaticResource} searches the element's ancestors first
<Style TargetType="Label">new Style(typeof(Label)) { Setters = { new Setter { Property = Label.FontSizeProperty, Value = 14 } } }

The orders page in C#

This is the screen the XAML sheet builds, with the same bindings written as typed lambdas and no XAML file.

public class OrdersPage : ContentPage
{
    public OrdersPage(OrdersViewModel viewModel)
    {
        Title = "Orders";
        BindingContext = viewModel;

        var search = new SearchBar { Placeholder = "Search by customer" };
        search.SetBinding(SearchBar.TextProperty, static (OrdersViewModel vm) => vm.Query);  // TwoWay

        var list = new CollectionView
        {
            SelectionMode = SelectionMode.Single,
            EmptyView = "No orders match your search.",
            ItemTemplate = new DataTemplate(() => new OrderRow()),
        };
        list.SetBinding(ItemsView.ItemsSourceProperty, static (OrdersViewModel vm) => vm.Orders);
        list.SetBinding(SelectableItemsView.SelectedItemProperty,
            static (OrdersViewModel vm) => vm.SelectedOrder);
        list.SetBinding(SelectableItemsView.SelectionChangedCommandProperty,
            static (OrdersViewModel vm) => vm.OpenSelectedCommand);

        var grid = new Grid { Padding = 16, RowSpacing = 8 };
        grid.RowDefinitions = [new RowDefinition(GridLength.Auto), new RowDefinition(GridLength.Star)];
        grid.Add(search);
        grid.Add(list, column: 0, row: 1);
        Content = grid;
    }
}

class OrderRow : Grid                                   // the row template, built once per realized row
{
    public OrderRow()
    {
        Padding = 12;
        ColumnDefinitions = [new ColumnDefinition(GridLength.Star), new ColumnDefinition(GridLength.Auto)];

        var customer = new Label();
        customer.SetBinding(Label.TextProperty, static (Order o) => o.Customer);
        this.Add(customer);

        var total = new Label();
        total.SetBinding(Label.TextProperty, static (Order o) => o.Total, stringFormat: "{0:C}");
        this.Add(total, column: 1);
    }
}
Result

The same page as the XAML version: a search bar over a selectable, virtualized list of customers and totals, bound to the same OrdersViewModel.

Setup

  2. Save as Views/OrdersPage.cs; register OrdersPage and OrdersViewModel in MauiProgram.cs with builder.Services.AddTransient<…>()
  3. OrdersViewModel declares Query, SelectedOrder and OpenSelectedCommand by hand, not with MVVM Toolkit generators (see the next card)

String-path binding versus a typed lambda

In MAUI 9, `SetBinding` takes a `Func` that the compiler checks and a source generator turns into binding code with no reflection, which is also what trimming and NativeAOT need.

String path (reflection)
// Resolved by name at run time: a typo is a silent blank label,
// and full trimming / NativeAOT can remove the property it reads
customer.SetBinding(Label.TextProperty, new Binding(nameof(Order.Customer)));
total.SetBinding(Label.TextProperty, new Binding("Total", stringFormat: "{0:C}"));
note.SetBinding(Entry.TextProperty, new Binding("DeliveryNote", BindingMode.TwoWay));

// A binding to the view model from inside a row
var ancestor = new RelativeBindingSource(RelativeBindingSourceMode.FindAncestorBindingContext,
                                         typeof(OrdersViewModel));
cancel.SetBinding(Button.CommandProperty, new Binding("CancelCommand", source: ancestor));

// Only this column could also bind a command that [RelayCommand] generates
// (the string is resolved at run time, after every generator has run)
Typed lambda (MAUI 9)
// Only simple member access: no method calls or string interpolation
customer.SetBinding(Label.TextProperty, static (Order o) => o.Customer);
total.SetBinding(Label.TextProperty, static (Order o) => o.Total, stringFormat: "{0:C}");
note.SetBinding(Entry.TextProperty, static (OrderDraft d) => d.DeliveryNote, mode: BindingMode.TwoWay);

// A Binding object, for a MultiBinding, a Style setter or a source of your own.
// CancelCommand is declared by hand: a lambda can't see members another source
// generator writes ([ObservableProperty], [RelayCommand]) and fails with BSG0006
var ancestor = new RelativeBindingSource(RelativeBindingSourceMode.FindAncestorBindingContext,
                                         typeof(OrdersViewModel));
var commandBinding = Binding.Create(static (OrdersViewModel vm) => vm.CancelCommand, source: ancestor);
cancel.SetBinding(Button.CommandProperty, commandBinding);

// XAML x:DataType bindings and Markup's .Bind() do see generated members
Result

Both columns display the same values, but on the typed side a renamed property is a compile error and the binding code is generated at build time.

Setup
  1. A .NET MAUI 9 app project (dotnet new maui -o Shop); the lines run in a page's constructor that has created customer, total, note and cancel
  2. OrdersViewModel declares public IRelayCommand<Order> CancelCommand { get; } by hand and assigns it in its constructor, because a typed lambda can't see what [RelayCommand] generates (BSG0006)

The fluent style — CommunityToolkit.Maui.Markup

Markup builds the same tree with extension methods, where `Bind` takes a getter (plus a setter for `TwoWay`) and `Row`/`Column` replace the attached-property calls.

using CommunityToolkit.Maui.Markup;
using static CommunityToolkit.Maui.Markup.GridRowsColumns;

public class OrdersPage : ContentPage
{
    public OrdersPage(OrdersViewModel viewModel)
    {
        BindingContext = viewModel;

        Content = new Grid
        {
            RowDefinitions = Rows.Define(Auto, Star),
            Padding = 16,
            Children =
            {
                new SearchBar { Placeholder = "Search by customer" }
                    .Bind(SearchBar.TextProperty,
                          getter: static (OrdersViewModel vm) => vm.Query,
                          setter: static (OrdersViewModel vm, string? text) => vm.Query = text ?? "")
                    .Row(0),

                new CollectionView { ItemTemplate = new DataTemplate(() => new OrderRow()) }
                    .Bind(ItemsView.ItemsSourceProperty, getter: static (OrdersViewModel vm) => vm.Orders)
                    .Row(1),
            },
        };
    }
}

class OrderRow : Grid
{
    public OrderRow()
    {
        ColumnDefinitions = Columns.Define(Star, Auto);
        Padding = 12;

        Children.Add(new Label()
            .Bind(Label.TextProperty, getter: static (Order o) => o.Customer)
            .Column(0));

        Children.Add(new Label()
            .Font(bold: true)
            .Bind(Label.TextProperty, getter: static (Order o) => o.Total, stringFormat: "{0:C}")
            .Column(1));
    }
}
Result

The search and list part of the orders screen, each control one chained expression close to the shape of the XAML; selection binds the same way with .Bind(SelectableItemsView.SelectedItemProperty, getter: …, setter: …).

  2. Call builder.UseMauiCommunityToolkitMarkup() in MauiProgram.cs

Keeping the screen in sync by hand

Without bindings every handler that changes the data must also repaint what depends on it, so funnel all of it through one `Render()` method (the bound version is the page-in-code card).

public class OrdersByHandPage : ContentPage
{
    private readonly List<Order> all;
    private readonly SearchBar search = new() { Placeholder = "Search by customer" };
    private readonly Label count = new();
    private readonly CollectionView list = new()
    {
        SelectionMode = SelectionMode.Single,
        ItemTemplate = new DataTemplate(() => new OrderRow()),
    };

    public OrdersByHandPage(IEnumerable<Order> orders)
    {
        all = [.. orders];
        var cancel = new Button { Text = "Cancel selected order" };

        search.TextChanged += (_, _) => Render();
        cancel.Clicked += (_, _) =>
        {
            if (list.SelectedItem is not Order order) return;
            all.Remove(order);
            Render();                          // forget this and the list and the count go stale
        };

        var header = new VerticalStackLayout { Spacing = 8, Children = { search, count, cancel } };
        var grid = new Grid { Padding = 16, RowSpacing = 8 };
        grid.RowDefinitions = [new RowDefinition(GridLength.Auto), new RowDefinition(GridLength.Star)];
        grid.Add(header);
        grid.Add(list, column: 0, row: 1);
        Content = grid;

        Render();
    }

    // The one method that turns the data into screen state
    private void Render()
    {
        var query = search.Text ?? "";
        var visible = all.Where(o => o.Customer.Contains(query, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)).ToList();
        count.Text = $"{visible.Count} orders";
        list.ItemsSource = visible;            // a new list: the CollectionView rebuilds every row
    }
}
Result

Typing filters the list and updates the count, and cancelling removes the order from both, because each handler ends in Render(); every new feature has to remember that call.

Setup
  1. The .NET 9 SDK with the MAUI workload: dotnet workload install maui, then dotnet new maui -o Shop
  2. Save as Views/OrdersPage.cs; register OrdersPage and OrdersViewModel in MauiProgram.cs with builder.Services.AddTransient<…>()
  3. OrdersViewModel declares Query, SelectedOrder and OpenSelectedCommand by hand, not with MVVM Toolkit generators (see the next card)

An event handler versus a command

A `Clicked` handler runs on every tap, but an `AsyncRelayCommand` reports `CanExecute` false while it runs, so the bound button disables itself and a double tap places one order.

using CommunityToolkit.Mvvm.Input;

// Event style: button.Clicked += async (_, _) => await api.PlaceAsync();
var eventApi = new CountingOrderApi();
async Task OnPlaceOrderClicked() => await eventApi.PlaceAsync();
await Task.WhenAll(OnPlaceOrderClicked(), OnPlaceOrderClicked());     // a double tap
Console.WriteLine($"event handler, double tap: {eventApi.Placed} placed");

// Command style: Button.Command asks CanExecute before every tap;
// the command raises CanExecuteChanged as it starts and as it ends
var commandApi = new CountingOrderApi();
var placeOrder = new AsyncRelayCommand(commandApi.PlaceAsync);

var firstTap = placeOrder.ExecuteAsync(null);
Console.WriteLine($"  button enabled while placing: {placeOrder.CanExecute(null)}");
if (placeOrder.CanExecute(null))
    await placeOrder.ExecuteAsync(null);                           // the second tap is refused
await firstTap;
Console.WriteLine($"  button enabled afterwards: {placeOrder.CanExecute(null)}");
Console.WriteLine($"command, double tap: {commandApi.Placed} placed");

class CountingOrderApi
{
    private int placed;
    public int Placed => placed;

    public async Task PlaceAsync()
    {
        await Task.Delay(50);                     // the network call
        Interlocked.Increment(ref placed);
    }
}
Result
event handler, double tap: 2 placed
  button enabled while placing: False
  button enabled afterwards: True
command, double tap: 1 placed
Setup
  1. .NET 8 SDK or later
  2. dotnet new console -o Demo, dotnet add Demo package CommunityToolkit.Mvvm, replace Demo/Program.cs with the example, then dotnet run --project Demo

Keeping a list in sync in place

Clearing and re-adding raises `Reset`, which rebuilds every row and loses the scroll position, while applying the new snapshot as removes, inserts, moves and replaces touches only the rows that changed.

using System.Collections.ObjectModel;

Order[] initial = [new(1, "Ada", "Pending"), new(2, "Grace", "Pending"), new(3, "Linus", "Shipped")];
Order[] latest = [new(1, "Ada", "Pending"), new(2, "Grace", "Shipped"), new(4, "Ken", "Pending")];

var rebuilt = Watch(new ObservableCollection<Order>(initial), out var rebuiltEvents);
rebuilt.Clear();
foreach (var order in latest) rebuilt.Add(order);
Console.WriteLine($"clear and re-add: {string.Join(", ", rebuiltEvents)}");

var synced = Watch(new ObservableCollection<Order>(initial), out var syncedEvents);
Sync(synced, latest);
Console.WriteLine($"sync in place:    {string.Join(", ", syncedEvents)}");
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" | ", synced.Select(o => $"{o.Id} {o.Customer} {o.Status}")));

static ObservableCollection<Order> Watch(ObservableCollection<Order> list, out List<string> events)
{
    var log = events = [];
    list.CollectionChanged += (_, e) => log.Add(e.Action.ToString());
    return list;
}

static void Sync(ObservableCollection<Order> shown, IReadOnlyList<Order> latest)
{
    var ids = latest.Select(o => o.Id).ToHashSet();
    for (var i = shown.Count - 1; i >= 0; i--)
        if (!ids.Contains(shown[i].Id)) shown.RemoveAt(i);

    for (var i = 0; i < latest.Count; i++)
    {
        var at = IndexOfId(shown, latest[i].Id, from: i);     // rows before i are already in place
        if (at < 0) shown.Insert(i, latest[i]);
        else if (at != i) shown.Move(at, i);

        if (shown[i] != latest[i]) shown[i] = latest[i];       // records compare by value
    }
}

static int IndexOfId(IList<Order> list, int id, int from)
{
    for (var j = from; j < list.Count; j++)
        if (list[j].Id == id) return j;
    return -1;
}

record Order(int Id, string Customer, string Status);
Result
clear and re-add: Reset, Add, Add, Add
sync in place:    Remove, Replace, Add
1 Ada Pending | 2 Grace Shipped | 4 Ken Pending
Setup
  1. .NET 8 SDK or later
  2. dotnet new console -o Demo, replace Demo/Program.cs with the example, then dotnet run --project Demo (a bound CollectionView, ListBox or ListView reacts to exactly these events)

A WPF Window in code-behind, and the Dispatcher

WPF controls and the collections bound to them belong to the thread that created them, so a socket callback or a timer reaches them through `Dispatcher.InvokeAsync`.

using System.Windows;
using System.Windows.Controls;
using System.Windows.Data;

public class OrdersWindow : Window
{
    private readonly OrdersViewModel viewModel;

    public OrdersWindow(OrdersViewModel viewModel)
    {
        this.viewModel = viewModel;
        Title = "Orders";
        Width = 480;
        Height = 640;
        DataContext = viewModel;

        var search = new TextBox { Margin = new Thickness(0, 0, 0, 8) };
        var query = new Binding(nameof(OrdersViewModel.Query))
        {
            UpdateSourceTrigger = UpdateSourceTrigger.PropertyChanged,    // TextBox defaults to LostFocus
        };
        search.SetBinding(TextBox.TextProperty, query);
        DockPanel.SetDock(search, Dock.Top);

        var list = new ListBox { DisplayMemberPath = nameof(Order.Customer) };   // virtualizes by default
        list.SetBinding(ItemsControl.ItemsSourceProperty, new Binding(nameof(OrdersViewModel.Orders)));
        list.MouseDoubleClick += (_, _) =>
        {
            if (list.SelectedItem is Order order) OpenDetail(order);
        };

        var dock = new DockPanel { Margin = new Thickness(16) };      // the last child fills the rest
        dock.Children.Add(search);
        dock.Children.Add(list);
        Content = dock;
        Loaded += async (_, _) => await viewModel.LoadAsync();
    }

    private void OpenDetail(Order order) => new OrderDetailWindow(order) { Owner = this }.ShowDialog();

    // Called by the push-notification client on a background thread; InvokeAsync queues
    // the work and returns, where Invoke would block (and deadlock if the UI waits on the client)
    public void OnOrderPushed(Order order) => Dispatcher.InvokeAsync(() => viewModel.Orders.Add(order));
}
Result

A window with a live-filtering search box over the orders list, where double-clicking an order opens its detail as a modal dialog and pushed orders appear without a cross-thread exception.

Setup
  1. Windows with the .NET 9 SDK: dotnet new wpf -o ShopDesk
  2. Save as OrdersWindow.cs; show it from App.OnStartup with new OrdersWindow(viewModel).Show()

A WinUI Page in code-behind, and DispatcherQueue.TryEnqueue

WinUI cannot build a `DataTemplate` from a lambda (it needs `XamlReader.Load`), so a code-only list uses `DisplayMemberPath`, and background work reaches the UI through `DispatcherQueue`.

using Microsoft.UI.Xaml;
using Microsoft.UI.Xaml.Controls;
using Microsoft.UI.Xaml.Data;
using Microsoft.UI.Xaml.Navigation;

public sealed class OrdersPage : Page
{
    private readonly TextBlock status = new() { Opacity = 0.7 };

    public OrdersPage()
    {
        var search = new TextBox { PlaceholderText = "Search by customer" };
        search.SetBinding(TextBox.TextProperty, new Binding
        {
            Path = new PropertyPath(nameof(OrdersViewModel.Query)),
            Mode = BindingMode.TwoWay,                    // WinUI {Binding} defaults to OneWay
            UpdateSourceTrigger = UpdateSourceTrigger.PropertyChanged,
        });

        var list = new ListView { DisplayMemberPath = nameof(Order.Customer), IsItemClickEnabled = true };
        var orders = new Binding { Path = new PropertyPath(nameof(OrdersViewModel.Orders)) };
        list.SetBinding(ItemsControl.ItemsSourceProperty, orders);
        list.ItemClick += (_, e) => Frame.Navigate(typeof(OrderDetailPage), e.ClickedItem);

        var root = new Grid { Padding = new Thickness(16), RowSpacing = 8 };
        foreach (var unit in new[] { GridUnitType.Auto, GridUnitType.Star, GridUnitType.Auto })
            root.RowDefinitions.Add(new RowDefinition { Height = new GridLength(1, unit) });
        Grid.SetRow(list, 1);
        Grid.SetRow(status, 2);
        root.Children.Add(search);
        root.Children.Add(list);
        root.Children.Add(status);
        Content = root;
    }

    protected override void OnNavigatedTo(NavigationEventArgs e) => DataContext = e.Parameter;

    // Called when a background sync finishes (a thread-pool thread)
    public void OnSyncFinished(int count) =>
        DispatcherQueue.TryEnqueue(() => status.Text = $"{count} orders synced");
}
Result

The same list screen in a WinUI page, where the search box filters as you type, clicking an order navigates the frame to its detail, and the status line updates safely from the sync thread.

Handlers and custom controls, in brief

A handler maps a cross-platform control onto a native view: append to a mapper to tweak every instance, or write a handler for a control of your own.

// Tweak an existing control everywhere, no subclass of the handler needed (MauiProgram.cs)
Microsoft.Maui.Handlers.EntryHandler.Mapper.AppendToMapping("NoUnderline", (handler, view) =>
{
    if (view is not SearchField) return;                  // scope it to your own Entry subclass
#if ANDROID
    handler.PlatformView.BackgroundTintList =
        Android.Content.Res.ColorStateList.ValueOf(Android.Graphics.Color.Transparent);
#elif IOS || MACCATALYST
    handler.PlatformView.BorderStyle = UIKit.UITextBorderStyle.None;
#endif
});

// A control of your own: a View with bindable properties…
public class Barcode : View
{
    public static readonly BindableProperty ValueProperty =
        BindableProperty.Create(nameof(Value), typeof(string), typeof(Barcode), string.Empty);

    public string Value
    {
        get => (string)GetValue(ValueProperty);
        set => SetValue(ValueProperty, value);
    }
}

// …and a handler: each Platforms/<os>/BarcodeHandler.cs declares
// `partial class BarcodeHandler : ViewHandler<Barcode, NativeBarcodeView>`, CreatePlatformView and MapValue
public partial class BarcodeHandler
{
    public static IPropertyMapper<Barcode, BarcodeHandler> PropertyMapper =
        new PropertyMapper<Barcode, BarcodeHandler>(ViewHandler.ViewMapper)
        {
            [nameof(Barcode.Value)] = MapValue,
        };

    public BarcodeHandler() : base(PropertyMapper) { }
}

// MauiProgram.cs
builder.ConfigureMauiHandlers(handlers => handlers.AddHandler(typeof(Barcode), typeof(BarcodeHandler)));
Result

Every SearchField drops the platform underline, and <local:Barcode Value="{Binding TrackingCode}" /> renders through the native view each platform's handler creates.

Traps

UI built in code gets no help from the XAML compiler, so these slip through.

  • Leaked subscriptions: service.OrdersChanged += OnOrdersChanged in a page constructor keeps the page alive as long as the service, so subscribe in OnAppearing and unsubscribe in OnDisappearing (or Unloaded).
  • Bindings on a plain class: a property without INotifyPropertyChanged is read once and later changes never reach the screen; a List<T> behaves the same way, so use ObservableCollection<T>.
  • Touching UI off the UI thread after ConfigureAwait(false) or on a timer callback: marshal with MainThread.BeginInvokeOnMainThread (MAUI), Dispatcher.InvokeAsync (WPF) or DispatcherQueue.TryEnqueue (WinUI).
  • Assigning ItemsSource = newList on every refresh raises a Reset that rebuilds every row; keep one collection and sync it in place.
  • Mixing bindings and direct assignment: label.Text = "…" on a bound property replaces a OneWay binding.
  • Typed SetBinding lambdas on MVVM Toolkit members: [ObservableProperty] and [RelayCommand] output is invisible to the binding generator (BSG0006), so declare those members by hand or use a string path.
  • Typed bindings (SetBinding with a static lambda) give C# the build-time checks XAML gets from x:DataType, for every member the C# compiler can see without another generator.
  • Build one small class per row (OrderRow) and pass a factory to DataTemplate, so the list creates rows only as they scroll into view.
  • Keep constructors to building the tree: data loaded there arrives before the page is on screen and can't be retried, so load in OnAppearing, Loaded or OnNavigatedTo.

All three are XAML over C#, but the namespaces, binding engines and threading APIs differ, so code moves between them more easily than markup does.

A WPF Window with layout panels

A `DockPanel` pins children to its edges in order and gives the last child the rest, while a `Grid` shares space with `*` columns and a `GridSplitter`.

<Window x:Class="ShopDesk.MainWindow"
        xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
        xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
        Title="Orders" Width="900" Height="560">
    <DockPanel Margin="12">
        <StackPanel DockPanel.Dock="Top" Orientation="Horizontal" Margin="0,0,0,8">
            <TextBox Width="260" Text="{Binding Query, UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged}" />
            <Button Content="Refresh" Margin="8,0,0,0" Command="{Binding RefreshCommand}" />
        </StackPanel>

        <TextBlock DockPanel.Dock="Bottom" Margin="0,8,0,0" Text="{Binding Summary}" />

        <!-- the last child fills what is left -->
        <Grid>
            <Grid.ColumnDefinitions>
                <ColumnDefinition Width="2*" MinWidth="220" />
                <ColumnDefinition Width="Auto" />
                <ColumnDefinition Width="3*" />
            </Grid.ColumnDefinitions>

            <ListBox ItemsSource="{Binding Orders}" SelectedItem="{Binding SelectedOrder}" />
            <GridSplitter Grid.Column="1" Width="5" HorizontalAlignment="Stretch" />

            <!-- shows the selected Order through its implicit DataTemplate (the lists card) -->
            <ContentControl Grid.Column="2" Margin="12,0,0,0" Content="{Binding SelectedOrder}" />
        </Grid>
    </DockPanel>
</Window>
Result

A toolbar across the top, a status line at the bottom and a resizable list and detail split in the middle, where the search box filters on every keystroke because TextBox.Text otherwise updates its source only on lost focus.

{Binding} versus {x:Bind}

`{x:Bind}` is generated code checked at build time and rooted at the page's code-behind, and its default mode is `OneTime`, so anything that changes needs `Mode=OneWay`.

WPF {Binding}
<!-- Resolved at run time against DataContext; a typo only logs to the Output window -->
<StackPanel>
    <TextBlock Text="{Binding SelectedOrder.Customer}" />
    <TextBlock Text="{Binding SelectedOrder.Total, StringFormat={}{0:C}}" />

    <!-- TextBox.Text is TwoWay by default in WPF -->
    <TextBox Text="{Binding DeliveryNote, UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged}" />

    <Button Content="Ship"
            Command="{Binding ShipCommand}"
            CommandParameter="{Binding SelectedOrder}"
            Visibility="{Binding CanShip, Converter={StaticResource BoolToVisibility}}" />
</StackPanel>
WinUI {x:Bind}
<!-- Compiled against the page class: a typo is a build error -->
<StackPanel Spacing="4">
    <TextBlock Text="{x:Bind ViewModel.SelectedOrder.Customer, Mode=OneWay}" />

    <!-- a function binding instead of a converter -->
    <TextBlock Text="{x:Bind local:Format.Money(ViewModel.SelectedOrder.Total), Mode=OneWay}" />

    <TextBox Text="{x:Bind ViewModel.DeliveryNote, Mode=TwoWay, UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged}" />

    <!-- bool to Visibility converts implicitly -->
    <Button Content="Ship"
            Command="{x:Bind ViewModel.ShipCommand}"
            CommandParameter="{x:Bind ViewModel.SelectedOrder, Mode=OneWay}"
            Visibility="{x:Bind ViewModel.CanShip, Mode=OneWay}" />
</StackPanel>
Result

Both show the selected order's customer and total, edit the delivery note and show Ship only when shipping is allowed; without Mode=OneWay the {x:Bind} version would keep showing whatever was there when the page loaded, usually nothing.

Lists, DataTemplates and virtualization

`ListBox`, `ListView` and WinUI's `ListView` virtualize by creating containers only for visible rows, a bare `ItemsControl` does not, and WinUI's `x:Phase` defers costly parts of a row during fast scrolling.

<!-- WPF: an implicit template (DataType, no x:Key) applies wherever an Order is shown -->
<Window.Resources>
    <DataTemplate DataType="{x:Type models:Order}">
        <Grid Margin="4">
            <Grid.ColumnDefinitions>
                <ColumnDefinition Width="*" />
                <ColumnDefinition Width="Auto" />
            </Grid.ColumnDefinitions>
            <TextBlock Text="{Binding Customer}" />
            <TextBlock Grid.Column="1" Text="{Binding Total, StringFormat={}{0:C}}" />
        </Grid>
    </DataTemplate>
</Window.Resources>

<ListBox ItemsSource="{Binding Orders}"
         VirtualizingPanel.VirtualizationMode="Recycling"
         VirtualizingPanel.ScrollUnit="Pixel" />

<!-- WinUI: a template needs x:DataType for x:Bind; OneTime is enough for the source
     because the ObservableCollection itself raises CollectionChanged -->
<ListView ItemsSource="{x:Bind ViewModel.Orders}" SelectionMode="None"
          IsItemClickEnabled="True" ItemClick="OnOrderClicked">
    <ListView.ItemTemplate>
        <DataTemplate x:DataType="models:Order">
            <StackPanel Padding="8" Spacing="2">
                <TextBlock Text="{x:Bind Customer}" Style="{StaticResource BodyStrongTextBlockStyle}" />
                <TextBlock Text="{x:Bind Notes}" x:Phase="1" Opacity="0.7" />
            </StackPanel>
        </DataTemplate>
    </ListView.ItemTemplate>
</ListView>
Result

Both lists stay smooth with tens of thousands of orders because only visible rows get containers; the WPF list scrolls by pixel and recycles containers, and the WinUI list fills in the notes line just after the name.

  2. WinUI part: a WinUI 3 page with xmlns:models="using:Shop.Models", a ViewModel property, and an OnOrderClicked(object sender, ItemClickEventArgs e) handler
