Commands with a parameter and CanExecute

A button bound to a command asks `CanExecute(parameter)` before enabling itself and calls `Execute(parameter)` on click, and since WinUI and MAUI have no `CommandManager` the view model announces changes with `NotifyCanExecuteChanged()`.

using System.Windows.Input;
using CommunityToolkit.Mvvm.Input;

Order[] orders = [new(1, "Ada", "Pending"), new(2, "Grace", "Shipped")];
var vm = new OrdersViewModel();
ICommand ship = vm.ShipCommand;                    // all a Button sees

foreach (var order in orders)                      // what each row's button does
{
    Console.WriteLine($"#{order.Id} Ship enabled: {ship.CanExecute(order)}");
    if (ship.CanExecute(order)) ship.Execute(order);
}
Console.WriteLine($"shipped: {string.Join(", ", vm.Shipped)}");

ship.CanExecuteChanged += (_, _) => Console.WriteLine("buttons re-query CanExecute");
vm.ShippingPaused = true;                           // e.g. the warehouse closed
Console.WriteLine($"#1 Ship enabled now: {ship.CanExecute(orders[0])}");

class OrdersViewModel
{
    private bool shippingPaused;
    public List<int> Shipped { get; } = [];
    public RelayCommand<Order> ShipCommand { get; }

    public OrdersViewModel() => ShipCommand = new RelayCommand<Order>(
        execute: order => Shipped.Add(order!.Id),
        canExecute: order => !shippingPaused && order?.Status == "Pending");

    public bool ShippingPaused
    {
        get => shippingPaused;
        set { shippingPaused = value; ShipCommand.NotifyCanExecuteChanged(); }
    }
}

record Order(int Id, string Customer, string Status);
Result
#1 Ship enabled: True
#2 Ship enabled: False
shipped: 1
buttons re-query CanExecute
#1 Ship enabled now: False
Setup
  1. .NET 8 SDK or later
  2. dotnet new console -o Demo, dotnet add Demo package CommunityToolkit.Mvvm, replace Demo/Program.cs with the example, then dotnet run --project Demo
  3. In XAML: <Button Content="Ship" Command="{Binding DataContext.ShipCommand, RelativeSource={RelativeSource AncestorType=ListBox}}" CommandParameter="{Binding}" /> inside the row template

Ran with .NET SDK 9.0.304 (net9.0, C# 13), CommunityToolkit.Mvvm 8.4.2 on 2026-11-16: the output matched the result shown.

Dependency properties on a templated control

A templated control's inputs are dependency properties so they can be bound, styled and animated, and the change callback, not the CLR setter, is where the control reacts.

using Microsoft.UI.Xaml;
using Microsoft.UI.Xaml.Controls;

public sealed class StatusBadge : Control
{
    public static readonly DependencyProperty StatusProperty = DependencyProperty.Register(
        nameof(Status), typeof(string), typeof(StatusBadge),
        new PropertyMetadata("Pending", OnStatusChanged));

    public string Status
    {
        get => (string)GetValue(StatusProperty);
        set => SetValue(StatusProperty, value);    // no logic here: bindings call SetValue directly
    }

    public StatusBadge() => DefaultStyleKey = typeof(StatusBadge);

    protected override void OnApplyTemplate()
    {
        base.OnApplyTemplate();
        GoToStatus(Status);                        // the template's states exist only now
    }

    private static void OnStatusChanged(DependencyObject d, DependencyPropertyChangedEventArgs e) =>
        ((StatusBadge)d).GoToStatus((string)e.NewValue);

    private void GoToStatus(string status) =>
        VisualStateManager.GoToState(this, status, useTransitions: true);
}
Result

<local:StatusBadge Status="{x:Bind Order.Status, Mode=OneWay}" /> switches visual state whenever the order's status changes.

Setup
  1. A WinUI 3 app (Windows App SDK); add StatusBadge.cs, and the badge's template in Themes/Generic.xaml (the visual-states card)
  2. WPF has the same shape in System.Windows; use FrameworkPropertyMetadata for flags such as AffectsRender or BindsTwoWayByDefault

An attached property that adds behaviour

An attached property lets any element carry a value it doesn't define, and its change callback can attach behaviour, here selecting a text box's text on focus.

using Microsoft.UI.Xaml;
using Microsoft.UI.Xaml.Controls;

public static class Input
{
    public static readonly DependencyProperty SelectAllOnFocusProperty =
        DependencyProperty.RegisterAttached(
            "SelectAllOnFocus", typeof(bool), typeof(Input), new PropertyMetadata(false, OnChanged));

    public static bool GetSelectAllOnFocus(DependencyObject element) =>
        (bool)element.GetValue(SelectAllOnFocusProperty);

    public static void SetSelectAllOnFocus(DependencyObject element, bool value) =>
        element.SetValue(SelectAllOnFocusProperty, value);

    private static void OnChanged(DependencyObject d, DependencyPropertyChangedEventArgs e)
    {
        if (d is not TextBox box) return;

        // remove as well as add, so setting it back to False really turns it off
        if ((bool)e.NewValue) box.GotFocus += SelectAll;
        else box.GotFocus -= SelectAll;
    }

    private static void SelectAll(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e) => ((TextBox)sender).SelectAll();
}
Result

Every text box marked SelectAllOnFocus="True" selects its whole text when it gets focus, such as a quantity field the user retypes.

Setup
  1. A WinUI 3 app; add Input.cs and use it as <TextBox local:Input.SelectAllOnFocus="True" />
  2. WPF: the same code with System.Windows types; the static Get/Set pair is what XAML calls

Control templates and visual states, in brief

A `ControlTemplate` defines a control's look and `VisualStateManager` switches between named states from code or from an `AdaptiveTrigger`, where WPF uses `Trigger`s instead.

<!-- Themes/Generic.xaml: the look of StatusBadge; GoToState picks the state -->
<Style TargetType="local:StatusBadge">
    <Setter Property="Template">
        <Setter.Value>
            <ControlTemplate TargetType="local:StatusBadge">
                <Border x:Name="Pill" CornerRadius="10" Padding="8,2" Background="DimGray">
                    <VisualStateManager.VisualStateGroups>
                        <VisualStateGroup x:Name="StatusStates">
                            <VisualState x:Name="Pending" />
                            <VisualState x:Name="Shipped">
                                <VisualState.Setters>
                                    <Setter Target="Pill.Background" Value="SteelBlue" />
                                </VisualState.Setters>
                            </VisualState>
                        </VisualStateGroup>
                    </VisualStateManager.VisualStateGroups>
                    <TextBlock Text="{TemplateBinding Status}" Foreground="White" />
                </Border>
            </ControlTemplate>
        </Setter.Value>
    </Setter>
</Style>

<!-- A page that adapts: the collapsed detail pane appears once the window is wide enough -->
<VisualStateManager.VisualStateGroups>
    <VisualStateGroup>
        <VisualState x:Name="Wide">
            <VisualState.StateTriggers>
                <AdaptiveTrigger MinWindowWidth="720" />
            </VisualState.StateTriggers>
            <VisualState.Setters>
                <Setter Target="DetailPane.Visibility" Value="Visible" />
            </VisualState.Setters>
        </VisualState>
    </VisualStateGroup>
</VisualStateManager.VisualStateGroups>

<!-- WPF: VisualState holds only a Storyboard (no Setters, no StateTriggers); use
     <ControlTemplate.Triggers><Trigger Property="IsMouseOver" Value="True">…</Trigger> -->
Result

A pending badge is grey and a shipped one is blue, and widening the window past 720 pixels shows the detail pane with no code involved.

Setup
  1. A WinUI 3 app; the Style goes in Themes/Generic.xaml (a ResourceDictionary merged by default for custom controls)
  2. The adaptive part goes on the first child of a page's root, which holds an element named DetailPane with Visibility="Collapsed"

WinUI navigation — NavigationView and Frame

The window holds a `NavigationView` around a `Frame`, and `Frame.Navigate` creates each page, hands it a parameter and keeps the back stack.

<NavigationView x:Name="Nav"
                IsBackEnabled="{x:Bind ContentFrame.CanGoBack, Mode=OneWay}"
                ItemInvoked="OnItemInvoked" BackRequested="OnBackRequested">
    <NavigationView.MenuItems>
        <NavigationViewItem Content="Orders" Tag="orders" Icon="Shop" />
        <NavigationViewItem Content="Customers" Tag="customers" Icon="People" />
    </NavigationView.MenuItems>
    <Frame x:Name="ContentFrame" />
</NavigationView>

// MainWindow.xaml.cs
public MainWindow()
{
    InitializeComponent();
    ContentFrame.Navigate(typeof(OrdersPage));             // open on the first item, selected
    Nav.SelectedItem = Nav.MenuItems[0];
}

private void OnItemInvoked(NavigationView sender, NavigationViewItemInvokedEventArgs args)
{
    var page = args.IsSettingsInvoked
        ? typeof(SettingsPage)
        : args.InvokedItemContainer?.Tag switch
        {
            "customers" => typeof(CustomersPage),
            _ => typeof(OrdersPage),
        };
    if (ContentFrame.CurrentSourcePageType != page) ContentFrame.Navigate(page);
}

private void OnBackRequested(NavigationView sender, NavigationViewBackRequestedEventArgs args)
{
    if (ContentFrame.CanGoBack) ContentFrame.GoBack();
}

// OrdersPage: Frame.Navigate(typeof(OrderDetailPage), order);  OrderDetailPage receives it:
protected override void OnNavigatedTo(NavigationEventArgs e) => Order = (Order)e.Parameter;
Result

The window opens on Orders with that item selected, picking a pane item swaps the page in the frame, and opening an order pushes its detail page so the back arrow appears and walks back through the history.

Setup
  1. A WinUI 3 app; the XAML is MainWindow.xaml's content and the C# goes in MainWindow.xaml.cs
  2. OrdersPage, CustomersPage, SettingsPage and OrderDetailPage are Pages in the project

Windows and dialogs — WPF versus WinUI

In WPF any `Window` can be modal with `ShowDialog`, while WinUI awaits a `ContentDialog` that needs the page's `XamlRoot`, and only one can be open per UI thread at a time, even across windows.

WPF — ShowDialog
// ShowDialog blocks this handler until the dialog closes
private void OnCancelOrderClicked(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
{
    var answer = MessageBox.Show(this, "Cancel this order?", "Orders",
                                 MessageBoxButton.YesNo, MessageBoxImage.Question);
    if (answer != MessageBoxResult.Yes) return;

    var reason = new CancelReasonWindow
    {
        Owner = this,
        WindowStartupLocation = WindowStartupLocation.CenterOwner,
    };

    // bool?: false or null means the user dismissed it
    if (reason.ShowDialog() == true)
        viewModel.Cancel(reason.SelectedReason);
}
WinUI 3 — ContentDialog
// Awaited; without XamlRoot, ShowAsync throws
private async void OnCancelOrderClicked(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
{
    var dialog = new ContentDialog
    {
        XamlRoot = XamlRoot,
        Title = "Cancel this order?",
        Content = "The customer is refunded in full.",
        PrimaryButtonText = "Cancel order",
        CloseButtonText = "Keep it",
        DefaultButton = ContentDialogButton.Close,
    };

    if (await dialog.ShowAsync() == ContentDialogResult.Primary)
        viewModel.Cancel(CancelReason.CustomerRequest);
}

// A second top-level window instead: new OrderWindow().Activate();
Result

WPF asks yes or no, then opens a centred, owned reason window and cancels only on OK, while WinUI shows one overlay dialog with "Keep it" as the default and cancels on the primary button.

Setup
  1. WPF column: in a Window's code-behind; CancelReasonWindow sets DialogResult = true when the user confirms
  2. WinUI column: in a Page's code-behind; both are wired to Click="OnCancelOrderClicked"

Excerpt, not compiled or run here: it needs a WPF app (compiled for net9.0-windows with EnableWindowsTargeting) and a WinUI 3 app (C# compiled against Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK 1.6).

Sources: Dialog boxes overview — WPF · ContentDialog — Windows App SDK API

Pitfalls

Most of these produce no error, only a screen that is wrong or slow.

  • {x:Bind} without Mode=OneWay on anything that changes is OneTime by default and keeps the first value.
  • Changing a bound ObservableCollection from a background thread throws (NotSupportedException in WPF, a wrong-thread COM exception in WinUI); marshal first, or use BindingOperations.EnableCollectionSynchronization (WPF only).
  • WPF virtualization breaks with a plain ItemsControl, ScrollViewer.CanContentScroll="False", ListBoxItems added directly, or grouping without VirtualizingPanel.IsVirtualizingWhenGrouping (it defaults to false).
  • A list inside a StackPanel or ScrollViewer gets infinite height and realizes every row; give it a Grid row with *.
  • Logic in a dependency property's CLR setter never runs for bindings and styles, which call SetValue directly; put it in the PropertyChangedCallback.
  • The WinUI Window is not a DependencyObject, so Window.Resources and Window.DataContext don't exist; put them on the root Grid or Page.
  • WPF TextBox.Text updates its source on lost focus, so add UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged for search-as-you-type.
  • In WinUI, call Bindings.Update() after changing many OneTime values at once (for example after loading) rather than making them all OneWay.
  • Moving WPF to WinUI: Dispatcher becomes DispatcherQueue, Triggers become visual states, DockPanel becomes Grid or RelativePanel, {Binding} becomes {x:Bind}, and CommandManager is gone.

Render modes (.NET 8 and later)

The render mode decides where a component runs and whether it reacts to clicks, it is chosen per page or per component, and with none set a component is static.

ModeHow to set itWhere the code runsInteractivityReach for it when
Static SSRnothing: the defaultserver, once per request, HTML outnone: links, form posts, enhanced navigationcontent pages, SEO, simple forms
Streaming SSR@attribute [StreamRendering]server; sends a placeholder, then streams the rest as awaits finishnonea static page with a slow query
Interactive Server@rendermode InteractiveServerserver; DOM diffs and UI events travel over a SignalR circuitfull; each event is a round tripintranet apps, data next to the server, tiny download
Interactive WebAssembly@rendermode InteractiveWebAssembly (component in the .Client project).NET on WebAssembly in the browserfull, no round trips once downloadedrich client UI, offline-ish work, low server load
Interactive Auto@rendermode InteractiveAuto (component in .Client)Server on the first visit, WebAssembly once the runtime is cachedfullfast first load and client-side later
Prerenderingon by default; @rendermode @(new InteractiveServerRenderMode(prerender: false)) turns it offa static pass first, then the interactive oneOnInitializedAsync runs twiceturn it off for pages that are pointless without interactivity
Detect at run time (.NET 9)RendererInfo.Name, RendererInfo.IsInteractive, AssignedRenderModeStatic, Server, WebAssembly or WebViewIsInteractive is false while prerenderingdisable a button until the page is interactive

A routable page with a list, @key and a shareable search

`@bind:after` runs once the bound value has been written, `@key` lets the diff move rows instead of rewriting them, and after an event handler returns the component re-renders by itself.

@page "/orders"
@rendermode InteractiveServer
@inject IOrderService OrderService
@inject NavigationManager Navigation

<input placeholder="Search by customer"
       @bind="query" @bind:event="oninput" @bind:after="SearchAsync" />

@if (orders is null)
{
    <p>Loading…</p>
}
else if (orders.Count == 0)
{
    <p>No orders match "@query".</p>
}
else
{
    <ul>
        @foreach (var order in orders)
        {
            <OrderRow @key="order.Id" Order="order" />
        }
    </ul>
}

@code {
    [SupplyParameterFromQuery(Name = "q")] private string? InitialQuery { get; set; }   // /orders?q=ada
    private string query = "";
    private List<Order>? orders;

    protected override async Task OnInitializedAsync()
    {
        query = InitialQuery ?? "";
        orders = await OrderService.SearchAsync(query);
    }

    // Server: one round trip per keystroke, so real apps debounce this
    private async Task SearchAsync()
    {
        Navigation.NavigateTo(Navigation.GetUriWithQueryParameter("q", query), replace: true);
        orders = await OrderService.SearchAsync(query);
    }
}
Result

Typing filters the list on each keystroke and keeps the URL shareable (/orders?q=ada) without adding history entries, and because rows are keyed, rows that stay in the results keep their DOM elements.

  1. The .NET 9 SDK: dotnet new blazor -o Shop --interactivity Server; its Program.cs already calls AddInteractiveServerComponents() and AddInteractiveServerRenderMode(), and _Imports.razor has @using static Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Web.RenderMode
  2. Save as Components/Pages/Orders.razor; register the service in Program.cs with builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>()

Parameters, EventCallback and two-way component binding

Data flows down through `[Parameter]` and events flow up through `EventCallback`, and a bindable component pairs `Value` with `ValueChanged` without ever assigning its own parameter.

@* OrderRow.razor *@
<li>
    <a href="orders/@Order.Id">#@Order.Id · @Order.Customer</a>
    <span>@Order.Total.ToString("C")</span>
    @if (Order.Status == OrderStatus.Pending)
    {
        <button @onclick="() => OnCancel.InvokeAsync(Order)">Cancel</button>
    }
</li>

@code {
    [Parameter, EditorRequired] public Order Order { get; set; } = default!;
    [Parameter] public EventCallback<Order> OnCancel { get; set; }   // re-renders the parent when done
}

@* QuantityInput.razor, used as
   <QuantityInput @bind-Value="line.Quantity" @bind-Value:after="SaveCartAsync" /> *@
<input type="number" min="1" max="99" @bind:get="Value" @bind:set="SetAsync" />

@code {
    [Parameter] public int Value { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public EventCallback<int> ValueChanged { get; set; }

    private Task SetAsync(int value) => ValueChanged.InvokeAsync(Math.Clamp(value, 1, 99));
}
Result

Each row links to its order and only pending orders show Cancel, which calls the parent's handler; the quantity box clamps what is typed to 1–99, pushes it into line.Quantity, then saves the cart.

Composition with RenderFragment, and ErrorBoundary

Markup a caller nests inside a component arrives as a `RenderFragment` (`ChildContent`), a `RenderFragment<T>` lets the caller template each item, and `ErrorBoundary` contains a failure to its subtree.

@* Panel.razor — a wrapper *@
<section class="panel">
    <h2>@Title</h2>
    @ChildContent
</section>

@code {
    [Parameter, EditorRequired] public string Title { get; set; } = "";
    [Parameter] public RenderFragment? ChildContent { get; set; }
}

@* DataTable.razor — a templated component: the caller decides what each row shows *@
@typeparam TItem

<table>
    @foreach (var item in Items)
    {
        <tr @key="item">@RowTemplate(item)</tr>
    }
</table>

@code {
    [Parameter, EditorRequired] public IReadOnlyList<TItem> Items { get; set; } = [];
    [Parameter, EditorRequired] public RenderFragment<TItem> RowTemplate { get; set; } = default!;
}

@* Using both: if a row throws, ErrorContent replaces the boundary's content until Recover() *@
<Panel Title="Recent orders">
    <ErrorBoundary @ref="boundary">
        <ChildContent>
            <DataTable Items="recent" Context="order">
                <RowTemplate>
                    <td>#@order.Id</td>
                    <td>@order.Customer</td>
                </RowTemplate>
            </DataTable>
        </ChildContent>
        <ErrorContent>
            <button @onclick="() => boundary?.Recover()">Couldn't show the orders. Try again</button>
        </ErrorContent>
    </ErrorBoundary>
</Panel>

@code {
    private ErrorBoundary? boundary;
}
Result

A titled panel holding a table with one templated row per order; an exception thrown while rendering a row shows a Try again button inside the panel instead of taking down the whole page, and Try again re-renders the rows once the cause is gone (on an interactive page).

Lifecycle, a polling refresh and StateHasChanged

`OnInitialized` runs once per instance (twice with prerendering) and `OnParametersSet` on every parameter change, and a timer tick is not a UI event, so it re-renders through `InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged)`.

@page "/orders/{OrderId:int}"
@rendermode InteractiveServer
@implements IDisposable
@inject IOrderService OrderService
@inject ILogger<OrderDetail> Logger

<p>Order #@OrderId: @(order?.Status.ToString() ?? "loading…")</p>
<p hidden="@(!refreshFailed)">Couldn't refresh; showing the last known status.</p>

@code {
    [Parameter] public int OrderId { get; set; }
    private Order? order;
    private bool refreshFailed;
    private readonly PeriodicTimer timer = new(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));   // ticks never overlap

    protected override void OnInitialized()
    {
        if (RendererInfo.IsInteractive) _ = PollAsync();     // not in the throwaway prerender pass
    }

    protected override async Task OnParametersSetAsync() =>   // runs again for /orders/7 → /orders/8
        order = await OrderService.GetAsync(OrderId);

    private async Task PollAsync()
    {
        while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync())             // false once Dispose stops the timer
            await InvokeAsync(RefreshAsync);
    }

    // Catch here: under per-page interactivity no ErrorBoundary encloses a page; a throw ends the circuit
    private async Task RefreshAsync()
    {
        try
        {
            order = await OrderService.GetAsync(OrderId);
            refreshFailed = false;
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            Logger.LogWarning(ex, "Refreshing order {OrderId} failed", OrderId);
            refreshFailed = true;
        }
        StateHasChanged();
    }

    public void Dispose() => timer.Dispose();
}
Result

The page loads the order when it opens and whenever the route's id changes, refreshes the status every 30 seconds while the user stays, shows the last status with a "couldn't refresh" line when a poll fails (and logs it) instead of ending the circuit, and stops polling when the user leaves.

Setup
  1. A Blazor Web App project (dotnet new blazor -o Shop --interactivity Server) with IOrderService registered as in the orders-page card
  2. Save as Components/Pages/OrderDetail.razor

Cascading values and dependency injection

Root-level cascading values reach interactive components and scoped services resolve in every render mode, but static rendering and the circuit each get their own scoped instance, so per-user state must be filled inside the circuit.

// Program.cs
builder.Services.AddCascadingValue(sp => new ShopSettings { Currency = "EUR" });   // every component

// Per-user state: one instance per scope, and the static render and the circuit are two scopes
builder.Services.AddScoped<CustomerSession>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<ICustomerService, CustomerService>();

@* OrderSummary.razor *@
@inject CustomerSession Session
@inject ICustomerService Customers

<p>@Session.Customer?.Name pays in @Settings.Currency</p>

@code {
    [CascadingParameter] private ShopSettings Settings { get; set; } = default!;

    // Runs inside the circuit, so later components in it read the same session; a value set
    // during static rendering (the layout, the prerender) lives in a different instance
    protected override async Task OnInitializedAsync() =>
        Session.Customer ??= await Customers.GetCurrentAsync();
}

@* Doesn't reach an interactive page under per-page interactivity, because MainLayout renders
   statically and cascading values don't cross render-mode boundaries (fine with global
   interactivity, <Routes @rendermode="InteractiveServer" /> in App.razor):
   <CascadingValue Value="currentCustomer">@Body</CascadingValue> *@

// .NET 9: constructor injection, in OrderHistory.razor.cs
public partial class OrderHistory(IOrderService orderService)
{
    private Task<List<Order>> LoadAsync() => orderService.GetRecentAsync();
}
Result

On the interactive page OrderSummary shows the current customer, loaded into the circuit's session, and the currency from the root-level value; a customer cascaded or stored by the static MainLayout would be gone there once the page turns interactive.

Setup
  1. A Blazor Web App project (dotnet new blazor -o Shop --interactivity Server)
  2. The registrations go in Program.cs (and in the .Client project's Program.cs too when WebAssembly or Auto components use them); OrderSummary sits on an @rendermode InteractiveServer page
  3. CustomerService.GetCurrentAsync() looks the customer up for the signed-in user (for example from AuthenticationStateProvider); a CircuitHandler is the other place to fill the session

EditForm with DataAnnotations validation

`EditForm` with `DataAnnotationsValidator` checks the model's attributes, and in static SSR `FormName` with `[SupplyParameterFromForm]` binds the posted values.

@page "/checkout"
@inject IOrderService OrderService
@inject NavigationManager Navigation

<EditForm Model="Form" OnValidSubmit="PlaceOrderAsync" FormName="checkout">
    <DataAnnotationsValidator />
    <ValidationSummary />

    <label>Email <InputText @bind-Value="Form!.Email" /></label>
    <ValidationMessage For="() => Form!.Email" />

    <label>Quantity <InputNumber @bind-Value="Form!.Quantity" /></label>
    <ValidationMessage For="() => Form!.Quantity" />

    <button type="submit">Place order</button>
</EditForm>

@code {
    [SupplyParameterFromForm] private CheckoutForm? Form { get; set; }   // filled from the POST

    protected override void OnInitialized() => Form ??= new();

    private async Task PlaceOrderAsync()
    {
        var orderId = await OrderService.PlaceAsync(Form!);
        Navigation.NavigateTo($"orders/{orderId}");
    }
}
Result

In static SSR the form posts and, if the email is invalid or the quantity is outside 1–20, the server re-renders it with each message beside its field and in the summary; a valid post places the order and redirects to it, and EditForm adds the antiforgery token itself (with an interactive render mode, fields validate as you edit).

Setup
  1. A Blazor Web App project (dotnet new blazor -o Shop); CheckoutForm is the class in the next card
  2. Save as Components/Pages/Checkout.razor; with no @rendermode it works as a static SSR form post

The same validation, run without a browser

`DataAnnotationsValidator` runs the attributes from `System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations`, so calling `Validator` directly tests the form model or re-checks it on the server.

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

CheckoutForm[] drafts =
[
    new() { Email = "ada@example.com", Quantity = 2 },
    new() { Email = "not-an-email", Quantity = 0 },
    new() { Email = null, Quantity = 3 },
];

foreach (var form in drafts)
{
    var errors = new List<ValidationResult>();
    var context = new ValidationContext(form);
    var valid = Validator.TryValidateObject(form, context, errors, validateAllProperties: true);
    Console.WriteLine(valid ? "valid" : string.Join(" / ", errors.Select(e => e.ErrorMessage)));
}

public class CheckoutForm
{
    [Required(ErrorMessage = "Enter an email for the receipt.")]
    [EmailAddress(ErrorMessage = "That email doesn't look right.")]
    public string? Email { get; set; }

    [Range(1, 20, ErrorMessage = "Order between 1 and 20 items.")]
    public int Quantity { get; set; } = 1;
}
Result
valid
That email doesn't look right. / Order between 1 and 20 items.
Enter an email for the receipt.

JavaScript interop — when you need it

Use JS interop only for what .NET can't reach (browser APIs, DOM measurement, third-party JS), loading a collocated module after the first render and sending data in one call.

@implements IAsyncDisposable
@inject IJSRuntime JS

<div @ref="mapElement" class="route-map"></div>

@code {
    [Parameter, EditorRequired] public IReadOnlyList<Stop> Stops { get; set; } = default!;
    private ElementReference mapElement;
    private IJSObjectReference? module;

    protected override async Task OnAfterRenderAsync(bool firstRender)
    {
        // the element exists only after the first render; JS is unavailable while prerendering
        if (!firstRender) return;
        module = await JS.InvokeAsync<IJSObjectReference>("import", "./Components/OrderRouteMap.razor.js");
        await module.InvokeVoidAsync("drawRoute", mapElement, Stops);    // one call, every stop
    }

    async ValueTask IAsyncDisposable.DisposeAsync()
    {
        if (module is null) return;
        try { await module.DisposeAsync(); }
        catch (JSDisconnectedException) { }       // Server: the circuit is already gone
    }
}

// OrderRouteMap.razor.js
export function drawRoute(element, stops) { /* hand the stops to the map library */ }
Result

The delivery route is drawn once the map element exists, with a single interop call however many stops there are, and the module is released when the component goes away even if the tab has already disconnected.

Setup
  1. A Blazor Web App project (dotnet new blazor -o Shop)
  2. Save Components/OrderRouteMap.razor and, next to it, Components/OrderRouteMap.razor.js holding the exported function; the component needs an interactive render mode

Virtualize a long list

`Virtualize` renders only the rows in view and asks an items provider for each block as the user scrolls, so the DOM holds about a screenful of rows.

@page "/orders/history"
@rendermode InteractiveServer
@inject IOrderService OrderService

<div style="height: 600px; overflow-y: auto">
    <Virtualize ItemsProvider="LoadOrdersAsync" ItemSize="48" OverscanCount="4" Context="order">
        <ItemContent>
            <OrderRow @key="order.Id" Order="order" />
        </ItemContent>
        <Placeholder>
            <div class="row-skeleton"></div>
        </Placeholder>
    </Virtualize>
</div>

@code {
    private async ValueTask<ItemsProviderResult<Order>> LoadOrdersAsync(ItemsProviderRequest request)
    {
        var page = await OrderService.GetPageAsync(
            request.StartIndex, request.Count, request.CancellationToken);
        return new ItemsProviderResult<Order>(page.Items, page.TotalCount);
    }
}

Fifty thousand orders scroll with about a screenful of rows in the DOM, each block fetched as it comes into view, with skeleton rows until it arrives.

Skip a re-render with ShouldRender

`ShouldRender` lets a row ignore its parent's re-render when its own parameter did not change, which pays off when a parent re-renders often and holds many rows.

<li>#@Order.Id · @Order.Customer · @Order.Status</li>

@code {
    [Parameter, EditorRequired] public Order Order { get; set; } = default!;
    private Order? lastSeen;
    private bool orderChanged;

    protected override void OnParametersSet()
    {
        orderChanged = !Equals(lastSeen, Order);       // a record: equal values mean nothing to redraw
        lastSeen = Order;
    }

    // Not consulted for the first render; false also skips renders after this row's own events
    protected override bool ShouldRender() => orderChanged;
}
Result

When the parent list re-renders, only rows whose order record actually changed render again.

Setup
  1. A Blazor Web App project (dotnet new blazor -o Shop); Order is an immutable record
  2. Save as Components/OrderSummaryRow.razor

Sources: Blazor rendering performance best practices

Performance rules and pitfalls

Blazor's cost is the size of the render tree it diffs and, on Server, every message over the circuit.

  • Put @key on every looped element or component that has a stable id, so inserts and deletes move rows instead of rewriting them.
  • Use <Virtualize> (or QuickGrid with virtualization) for long lists: a few thousand component instances add measurable render time on WebAssembly.
  • Batch JS interop into one InvokeVoidAsync("saveAll", items) instead of a call per item: on Server, each call is a network round trip.
  • Override ShouldRender (or pass immutable, primitive parameters) where a parent re-renders often but a child's data rarely changes.
  • Wrap risky regions (third-party widgets, data-driven rows) in <ErrorBoundary> and call Recover() to retry; DispatchExceptionAsync reaches a boundary only from a component inside one, so a page under per-page interactivity must catch its own background failures or the circuit ends.
  • Calling StateHasChanged() at the end of every event handler: Blazor already re-renders after handlers and EventCallbacks, so call it only for timers, service events and other threads, through InvokeAsync.
  • Writing to a [Parameter] property inside the child: the parent's next render overwrites it, so raise ValueChanged and let the parent own the value.
  • Expensive work, timers or JS calls in OnInitializedAsync with prerendering on: it runs twice and JS is unavailable in the first pass, so check RendererInfo.IsInteractive or use OnAfterRenderAsync(firstRender).
  • Expecting a CascadingValue in a static layout to reach an interactive page: values don't cross render-mode boundaries, so register it with AddCascadingValue at the root or keep the state in a scoped service.
  • A scoped service on Server lives for the circuit (one per tab), not per request, and on WebAssembly it behaves like a singleton.

A list screen, imperative and declarative

Code-behind pulls values out of controls and pushes results back on every path, while XAML with bindings states what to show and leaves the data to the view model (full versions are on the C# UI and XAML sheets).

Imperative code-behind
public partial class OrdersPage : ContentPage
{
    private readonly IOrderService orders;
    private List<Order> all = [];

    public OrdersPage(IOrderService orders)
    {
        InitializeComponent();
        this.orders = orders;
        SearchBox.TextChanged += (_, e) => Show(e.NewTextValue);
    }

    protected override async void OnAppearing()
    {
        base.OnAppearing();
        all = await orders.GetAllAsync();
        Show(SearchBox.Text);
    }

    // every change must remember to call this
    private void Show(string? query)
    {
        var visible = all.Where(o => o.Customer.Contains(query ?? "",
            StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)).ToList();
        OrderList.ItemsSource = visible;      // a new list: every row is rebuilt
        CountLabel.Text = $"{visible.Count} orders";
    }
}
XAML with bindings
<!-- the filter, the count and navigation live in the view model -->
<Grid RowDefinitions="Auto,Auto,*" RowSpacing="8" Padding="16">
    <SearchBar Text="{Binding Query}" Placeholder="Search by customer" />

    <Label Grid.Row="1" Text="{Binding Orders.Count, StringFormat='{0} orders'}" />

    <CollectionView Grid.Row="2"
                    ItemsSource="{Binding Orders}"
                    SelectionMode="Single"
                    SelectedItem="{Binding SelectedOrder}"
                    SelectionChangedCommand="{Binding OpenSelectedCommand}">
        <CollectionView.ItemTemplate>
            <DataTemplate x:DataType="models:Order">
                <Label Text="{Binding Customer}" Padding="12" />
            </DataTemplate>
        </CollectionView.ItemTemplate>
    </CollectionView>
</Grid>

<!-- code-behind: InitializeComponent(); BindingContext = viewModel; -->
Result

Both show a searchable orders list with a count; on the right the filter and count are testable view-model code, the list updates in place, and selecting a row also navigates.

Setup
  1. A .NET MAUI app project (dotnet new maui -o Shop)
  2. Left: an OrdersPage.xaml that only names SearchBox, OrderList and CountLabel; right: the content of the XAML sheet's page, whose x:DataType is OrdersViewModel

Excerpt, not compiled or run here: it needs a .NET MAUI 9 app project; both columns compiled against Microsoft.Maui.Controls 9.0.120 (XamlC for the XAML).

The same screen as a Blazor component, on the same view model

Blazor re-renders after its own events, so changes the view model makes on its own (a load finishing, a push) arrive through `PropertyChanged` and become `InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged)`.

@page "/orders"
@rendermode InteractiveServer
@implements IDisposable
@inject OrdersViewModel ViewModel

<input placeholder="Search by customer" @bind="ViewModel.Query" @bind:event="oninput" />
<p>@ViewModel.Orders.Count orders</p>

<ul>
    @foreach (var order in ViewModel.Orders)
    {
        <li @key="order.Id" @onclick="() => OpenAsync(order)">@order.Customer</li>
    }
</ul>

@code {
    protected override async Task OnInitializedAsync()
    {
        ViewModel.PropertyChanged += OnViewModelChanged;
        ViewModel.Orders.CollectionChanged += OnViewModelChanged;
        await ViewModel.LoadAsync();
    }

    // the same members the XAML binds: SelectedItem, then SelectionChangedCommand
    private Task OpenAsync(Order order)
    {
        ViewModel.SelectedOrder = order;
        return ViewModel.OpenSelectedCommand.ExecuteAsync(null);
    }

    private void OnViewModelChanged(object? sender, EventArgs e) => _ = InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged);

    public void Dispose()
    {
        ViewModel.PropertyChanged -= OnViewModelChanged;
        ViewModel.Orders.CollectionChanged -= OnViewModelChanged;
    }
}
Result

The same searchable list and count rendered as HTML, where typing sets ViewModel.Query, the view model refilters Orders, and the component re-renders from the change events.

Setup
  1. A Blazor Web App (dotnet new blazor -o Shop --interactivity Server) or a Blazor Hybrid app, with OrdersViewModel registered with AddScoped
  2. The view model of the MAUI sheets, except that its Shell.Current.GoToAsync call goes through a small navigation interface each host implements (Shell in MAUI, NavigationManager here)

Excerpt, not compiled or run here: it needs a Blazor Web App project (dotnet new blazor) or a .NET MAUI Blazor Hybrid app; compiled with the .NET 9 SDK.

One state object, two kinds of listener

A XAML binding re-reads the one property named in `PropertyChanged`, a Blazor component re-renders its whole tree on a coarse `Changed` event, and in a hybrid app one singleton can serve both.

using System.ComponentModel;
using System.Globalization;

var cart = new CartState();
cart.PropertyChanged += (_, e) => Console.WriteLine($"binding: re-read {e.PropertyName}");
cart.Changed += () => Console.WriteLine("component: re-render");

cart.Add(new CartLine("USB-C cable", 2, 9.50m));
cart.Add(new CartLine("Charger", 1, 24.00m));
Console.WriteLine($"{cart.ItemCount} items, {cart.Total.ToString("C", CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("en-US"))}");

sealed class CartState : INotifyPropertyChanged
{
    private readonly List<CartLine> lines = [];

    public event PropertyChangedEventHandler? PropertyChanged;   // XAML bindings
    public event Action? Changed;                                 // Blazor components

    public int ItemCount => lines.Sum(l => l.Quantity);
    public decimal Total => lines.Sum(l => l.Quantity * l.UnitPrice);

    public void Add(CartLine line)
    {
        lines.Add(line);
        Raise(nameof(ItemCount));
        Raise(nameof(Total));
        Changed?.Invoke();
    }

    private void Raise(string name) => PropertyChanged?.Invoke(this, new PropertyChangedEventArgs(name));
}

record CartLine(string Product, int Quantity, decimal UnitPrice);
Result
binding: re-read ItemCount
binding: re-read Total
component: re-render
binding: re-read ItemCount
binding: re-read Total
component: re-render
3 items, $43.00

  1. .NET 8 SDK or later
  2. dotnet new console -o Demo, replace Demo/Program.cs with the example, then dotnet run --project Demo (in an app, the handlers are a binding and InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged))

Embedding Blazor in MAUI — BlazorWebView

Blazor Hybrid runs Razor components in-process inside a native web view, with no server and no WebAssembly, and XAML controls beside it share its DI services.

// MauiProgram.cs
builder.Services.AddMauiBlazorWebView();
#if DEBUG
builder.Services.AddBlazorWebViewDeveloperTools();
#endif
builder.Services.AddSingleton<CartState>();          // one instance for XAML pages and Razor components

<!-- MainPage.xaml -->
<ContentPage xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/dotnet/2021/maui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2009/xaml"
             xmlns:local="clr-namespace:ShopHybrid"
             x:Class="ShopHybrid.MainPage"
             x:DataType="local:CartState">
    <Grid RowDefinitions="*,Auto">
        <BlazorWebView x:Name="blazorWebView" HostPage="wwwroot/index.html">
            <BlazorWebView.RootComponents>
                <RootComponent Selector="#app" ComponentType="{x:Type local:Components.Routes}" />
            </BlazorWebView.RootComponents>
        </BlazorWebView>

        <!-- a native control under the web UI, bound to the same state -->
        <Label Grid.Row="1" Padding="12" Text="{Binding ItemCount, StringFormat='{0} items in cart'}" />
    </Grid>
</ContentPage>
Result

The app shows the Razor UI full screen with a native label under it, and adding to the cart in a Razor component updates the label through PropertyChanged because both use the one CartState.

Setup

  2. The registrations go in MauiProgram.cs and the markup in MainPage.xaml, whose code-behind sets BindingContext to the CartState singleton; Components/Routes.razor comes with the template

Embedding Blazor in WPF

WPF and Windows Forms have their own `BlazorWebView` (WinUI 3 has none), and native code can reach into the Blazor scope with `TryDispatchAsync`.

using System.Windows;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebView.Wpf;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;

public partial class MainWindow : Window
{
    private readonly BlazorWebView blazorWebView;

    public MainWindow()
    {
        InitializeComponent();

        var services = new ServiceCollection();
        services.AddWpfBlazorWebView();

        // the same as <blazor:BlazorWebView HostPage=… Services=…> in XAML
        blazorWebView = new BlazorWebView
        {
            HostPage = @"wwwroot\index.html",
            Services = services.BuildServiceProvider(),
        };
        blazorWebView.RootComponents.Add(
            new RootComponent { Selector = "#app", ComponentType = typeof(OrderHistory) });
        Content = blazorWebView;
    }

    // A native menu item opening a Razor page
    private async void OnShowOrdersClicked(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        var dispatched = await blazorWebView.TryDispatchAsync(sp =>
            sp.GetRequiredService<NavigationManager>().NavigateTo("/orders"));

        if (!dispatched)                              // Blazor hasn't started in the web view yet
            MessageBox.Show(this, "The order history is still loading. Try again in a moment.");
    }
}
Result

The WPF window hosts the Razor order history, and a native menu item can drive its router.

Setup
  1. A WPF app: dotnet add package Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebView.Wpf, set the project Sdk to Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Razor
  2. Add wwwroot/index.html with <div id="app"> and the _framework/blazor.webview.js script; this code goes in MainWindow.xaml.cs

MAUI views inside a native app

MAUI 9 can embed a MAUI view into an existing .NET for Android, iOS or WinUI app, from one shared `MauiApp` and a window context per native window.

// In the MAUI library: one MauiApp for the whole process
public static class EmbeddedShop
{
    private static readonly Lazy<MauiApp> app = new(() =>
        MauiApp.CreateBuilder().UseMauiEmbeddedApp<App>().Build());

    public static MauiApp Shared => app.Value;
}

// In the native Android app
[Activity(Label = "Order summary")]
public class OrderSummaryActivity : Activity
{
    protected override void OnCreate(Bundle? savedInstanceState)
    {
        base.OnCreate(savedInstanceState);

        var windowContext = EmbeddedShop.Shared.CreateEmbeddedWindowContext(this);   // per window
        Android.Views.View summary = new OrderSummaryView().ToPlatformEmbedded(windowContext);
        SetContentView(summary);
    }
}
Result

The Android activity shows a MAUI-built order summary as an ordinary Android view, while every activity shares one MAUI app and its services.

Setup
  1. A .NET for Android app referencing a MAUI library that holds App, OrderSummaryView and the EmbeddedShop class
  2. using Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Embedding; in the activity's file

What triggers a UI update

Most "the screen didn't update" bugs come from a change that never reached the mechanism in this table.

ModelAn update happens whenWhat gets redrawnThe trap
MAUI / WPF / WinUI {Binding}the source raises PropertyChanged or CollectionChangedonly the bound target property, or the affected rowsa property without INotifyPropertyChanged; a change raised off the UI thread (WinUI throws; WPF marshals properties but not collections; MAUI marshals binding updates itself)
WinUI {x:Bind}the same events, but only with Mode=OneWay or TwoWay; or Bindings.Update()the bound property, through generated codethe default OneTime keeps the first value forever
Imperative code-behindyour code assigns label.Text, ItemsSource, IsVisiblewhatever you toucheda code path that forgets to refresh leaves the screen stale
Blazoran event handler or EventCallback completes; new parameters arrive from a re-rendering parent; StateHasChanged()the component's render tree, diffed against the last one; children re-render when their parameters changetimers, service events and other threads need InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged)
Blazor Hybrid shared statethe native side raises the event; the component calls InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged)that componentforgetting to unsubscribe in Dispose leaks every component instance
Animations and visual statesan explicit call: FadeTo, VisualStateManager.GoToState, an AdaptiveTriggerthat elementdata changes don't animate on their own: start the animation from the change

Choosing a stack

Decide by target platform first and then by team skills and existing code, remembering that Blazor Hybrid can put Razor components inside MAUI or WPF.

If you need…ChooseBecause
Android and iOS (and Mac, Windows) from one C# codebase, with native controls.NET MAUI — XAML, or C# with Markupone project and native widgets, with device APIs built in
A Windows-only line-of-business app, existing WPF code, heavy third-party gridsWPFthe most mature desktop ecosystem; runs on .NET 9 as-is
A new Windows app with Fluent design and Windows 11 featuresWinUI 3 (Windows App SDK)the current native Windows UI stack
A web app, or a team of web developersBlazor Web Appany browser; choose static, Server or WebAssembly per page
The same UI on the web and in a store app with device accessBlazor Hybrid (BlazorWebView in MAUI, WPF or Windows Forms)shares Razor components between the web and native shells
An existing HTML/JS front end inside a MAUI appHybridWebView (MAUI 9)hosts any web content with JS ↔ C# messaging; no Blazor needed
A team that avoids XAML, or UI generated from dataC# code: plain MAUI APIs or CommunityToolkit.Maui.Markupthe same controls, refactorable, no XAML compiler
Linux desktop as wellnone of these officially: Blazor in a browser, or third-party Avalonia / Uno PlatformMAUI, WPF and WinUI don't target Linux

Interview talking points

Short answers to the questions that come up about .NET UI stacks.

  • XAML is declarative markup over a retained object tree: the controls live as long as the page, and bindings keep their properties in sync with the view model.
  • Blazor is declarative and diff-based, closer to SwiftUI or React: a component re-renders its tree, the renderer applies only the DOM differences, and @key is its identity.
  • Code-behind and C#-built UI are imperative: you create controls and mutate them, which is fine for structure and painful when you keep state in sync by hand.
  • XAML and C# markup are the same object model: anything in XAML can be written in C#, and MAUI 9's typed SetBinding lambdas close the compile-time-check gap (for members not written by another source generator).
  • Compiled bindings (x:DataType in MAUI, {x:Bind} in WinUI) move binding errors to build time, and MAUI requires them under full trimming and NativeAOT.
  • Every stack has one UI thread: MainThread, Dispatcher, DispatcherQueue, or Blazor's InvokeAsync; know each one's name.
  • Keep view models UI-free and test them in plain unit tests: the same INotifyPropertyChanged view model can back XAML pages and, through a small adapter, Razor components.
  • Migration is usually screen by screen: host Blazor in WPF or MAUI with BlazorWebView, or embed MAUI views in a native app with MAUI 9's native embedding.

One token idea, four UI stacks

The same decision lives in a different place on each stack; name tokens by role (`Surface`, `OnSurface`), never by value (`Gray100`).

Tokens as XAML resources: define once, merge once, StaticResource vs DynamicResource

StaticResource is looked up once when the page loads; DynamicResource keeps watching the key, so use it for anything a theme swap replaces.

<!-- Resources/Styles/Tokens.xaml -->
<?xaml-comp compile="true" ?>
<ResourceDictionary xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/dotnet/2021/maui"
                    xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2009/xaml">
    <Color x:Key="BrandPrimary">#512BD4</Color>
    <Color x:Key="Danger">#C62828</Color>
    <Color x:Key="CardBackground">#F7F7FA</Color>
    <Color x:Key="DisabledBackground">#E0E0E6</Color>
    <Color x:Key="DisabledText">#6E6E73</Color>
    <x:Double x:Key="SpaceM">16</x:Double>
    <Thickness x:Key="PagePadding">16,24</Thickness>
    <Thickness x:Key="ButtonPadding">20,12</Thickness>
    <x:Int32 x:Key="RadiusM">12</x:Int32>                <!-- Button.CornerRadius is an int -->
    <RoundRectangle x:Key="CardShape" CornerRadius="12" />  <!-- a Border's StrokeShape -->
    <x:Double x:Key="FontBody">16</x:Double>
    <x:Double x:Key="FontTitle">24</x:Double>
    <x:Double x:Key="FontCaption">13</x:Double>
</ResourceDictionary>

<!-- App.xaml: merged once, available to every page -->
<Application.Resources>
    <ResourceDictionary>
        <ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries>
            <ResourceDictionary Source="Resources/Styles/Tokens.xaml" />
            <ResourceDictionary Source="Resources/Styles/Styles.xaml" />
        </ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries>
    </ResourceDictionary>
</Application.Resources>

<!-- OrdersPage.xaml -->
<VerticalStackLayout Padding="{StaticResource PagePadding}" Spacing="{StaticResource SpaceM}">
    <Label Text="Order #1042" FontSize="{StaticResource FontTitle}" />
    <Border BackgroundColor="{DynamicResource CardBackground}" StrokeShape="{StaticResource CardShape}" />
</VerticalStackLayout>
Result

Every page reads spacing, type sizes and colours from one dictionary; replacing CardBackground at runtime repaints the card, while the StaticResource values stay as loaded.

  2. Add Resources/Styles/Tokens.xaml (build action MauiXaml), merge it in App.xaml, then use the keys from any page

Reusable styles: implicit, explicit with BasedOn, and style classes

An implicit style (no key) applies to every control of its type and an explicit one replaces it, so build both on a keyed base with BasedOn (WPF can base on `{StaticResource {x:Type Button}}`, WinUI on `DefaultButtonStyle`).

<!-- Resources/Styles/Styles.xaml (inside its ResourceDictionary) -->
<Style x:Key="BaseButton" TargetType="Button">
    <Setter Property="FontSize" Value="{StaticResource FontBody}" />
    <Setter Property="Padding" Value="{StaticResource ButtonPadding}" />
    <Setter Property="CornerRadius" Value="{StaticResource RadiusM}" />
    <Setter Property="BackgroundColor" Value="{StaticResource BrandPrimary}" />
    <Setter Property="TextColor" Value="White" />
</Style>

<!-- Implicit: every Button in scope -->
<Style TargetType="Button" BasedOn="{StaticResource BaseButton}" />

<!-- Explicit: opted into per element, inherits the base setters -->
<Style x:Key="DestructiveButton" TargetType="Button" BasedOn="{StaticResource BaseButton}">
    <Setter Property="BackgroundColor" Value="{StaticResource Danger}" />
</Style>

<!-- Style classes: combinable variants -->
<Style TargetType="Label" Class="Caption">
    <Setter Property="FontSize" Value="{StaticResource FontCaption}" />
    <Setter Property="Opacity" Value="0.8" />
</Style>

<!-- On a page -->
<Button Text="Place order" />
<Button Text="Cancel order" Style="{StaticResource DestructiveButton}" />
<Label Text="Ships in 2 days" StyleClass="Caption" />
Result

Both buttons share font, padding and radius; the destructive one is red; the caption is smaller and dimmer — with no value repeated on the page.

Light and dark: MAUI AppThemeBinding vs WinUI ThemeDictionaries

MAUI picks a value per property from the current theme; WinUI swaps whole keyed dictionaries and ThemeResource re-reads them.

.NET MAUI
<!-- Per property: the effective theme picks one value -->
<ContentPage BackgroundColor="{AppThemeBinding Light=#FFFFFF, Dark=#1B1B1F}">
    <Border BackgroundColor="{AppThemeBinding Light={StaticResource CardBackground}, Dark=#2C2C30}">
        <Label Text="Your orders" TextColor="{AppThemeBinding Light=#1B1B1F, Dark=#F2F2F7}" />
    </Border>
</ContentPage>

// Override the OS (AppTheme.Unspecified follows it again)
Application.Current!.UserAppTheme = AppTheme.Dark;

// Read and observe the effective theme
AppTheme effective = Application.Current!.RequestedTheme;
Application.Current!.RequestedThemeChanged += (_, e) =>
    Console.WriteLine($"now {e.RequestedTheme}");
WinUI 3
<!-- App.xaml resources: one dictionary per theme, the same keys in each -->
<ResourceDictionary.ThemeDictionaries>
    <ResourceDictionary x:Key="Light">
        <SolidColorBrush x:Key="CardBackgroundBrush" Color="#F7F7FA" />
    </ResourceDictionary>
    <ResourceDictionary x:Key="Dark">
        <SolidColorBrush x:Key="CardBackgroundBrush" Color="#2C2C30" />
    </ResourceDictionary>
</ResourceDictionary.ThemeDictionaries>

<!-- ThemeResource re-evaluates on a theme change; StaticResource would not -->
<Border Background="{ThemeResource CardBackgroundBrush}" CornerRadius="12" />

// Application.RequestedTheme is start-up only; at runtime theme a subtree
if (window.Content is FrameworkElement root)
    root.RequestedTheme = ElementTheme.Dark;
Result

The page and card switch between their light and dark values when the OS theme changes or the app overrides it, without reloading the page.

Swap a whole token set at runtime (MAUI and WPF)

For brand themes or a user's choice beyond light/dark: keep the same keys in each theme dictionary, replace the merged one, and consume them with DynamicResource.

// MAUI: LightTheme and DarkTheme are ResourceDictionary subclasses with the same keys
public static class ThemeSwitcher
{
    public static void Apply(ResourceDictionary theme)
    {
        var merged = Application.Current!.Resources.MergedDictionaries;
        if (merged.FirstOrDefault(d => d is LightTheme or DarkTheme) is { } current)
            merged.Remove(current);                // Tokens.xaml and Styles.xaml stay merged
        merged.Add(theme);                         // every DynamicResource consumer repaints
    }
}

ThemeSwitcher.Apply(new DarkTheme());

// WPF: the same move with a URI-loaded dictionary
var dictionaries = System.Windows.Application.Current.Resources.MergedDictionaries;
if (dictionaries.FirstOrDefault(d => d.Source?.OriginalString.StartsWith("Themes/") == true) is { } old)
    dictionaries.Remove(old);
var dark = new System.Windows.ResourceDictionary { Source = new Uri("Themes/Dark.xaml", UriKind.Relative) };
dictionaries.Add(dark);
Result

The running app repaints every element bound with DynamicResource to the new token set; StaticResource consumers keep the old values.

Theme choice in plain C#: system, light or dark

Keep the decision of which palette applies, and when it changes, in UI-free code you can run and test, so the UI side only swaps dictionaries on `Changed`.

var osIsDark = false;                                    // MAUI: RequestedTheme == AppTheme.Dark
var themes = new ThemeService(() => osIsDark);
themes.Changed += p => Console.WriteLine($"apply {p.Name}: surface {p.Surface}, text {p.OnSurface}");

themes.Choose(ThemePreference.Dark);                     // the user picks Dark in settings
themes.Choose(ThemePreference.System);                   // back to following the OS (light)
osIsDark = true;
themes.SystemThemeChanged();                             // MAUI: RequestedThemeChanged
themes.SystemThemeChanged();                             // nothing changed: no event, no repaint

enum ThemePreference { System, Light, Dark }

record Palette(string Name, string Surface, string OnSurface)
{
    public static readonly Palette Light = new("light", "#FFFFFF", "#1B1B1F");
    public static readonly Palette Dark = new("dark", "#1B1B1F", "#F2F2F7");
}

sealed class ThemeService(Func<bool> systemIsDark)
{
    private ThemePreference preference = ThemePreference.System;
    public Palette Current { get; private set; } = systemIsDark() ? Palette.Dark : Palette.Light;
    public event Action<Palette>? Changed;

    public void Choose(ThemePreference choice)
    {
        preference = choice;
        var next = choice switch
        {
            ThemePreference.Light => Palette.Light,
            ThemePreference.Dark => Palette.Dark,
            _ => systemIsDark() ? Palette.Dark : Palette.Light,
        };
        if (next == Current) return;
        Current = next;
        Changed?.Invoke(next);                           // the UI swaps its theme dictionary here
    }

    public void SystemThemeChanged() => Choose(preference);
}
Result
apply dark: surface #1B1B1F, text #F2F2F7
apply light: surface #FFFFFF, text #1B1B1F
apply dark: surface #1B1B1F, text #F2F2F7

Check token contrast in CI

Run every text/background token pair of both themes through the WCAG formula and exit non-zero when one fails AA, so CI stops the build (here the failing old grey is shown as data, since a ran example must exit 0).

using System.Globalization;

CultureInfo.CurrentCulture = CultureInfo.InvariantCulture;
var failures = CheckAA(
[
    ("light", "body text", "#1B1B1F", "#FFFFFF"),
    ("light", "primary button", "#FFFFFF", "#512BD4"),
    ("light", "muted caption", "#6E6E73", "#FFFFFF"),
    ("dark", "body text", "#F2F2F7", "#1B1B1F"),
    ("dark", "primary button", "#1B1B1F", "#AC99EA"),
    ("dark", "muted caption", "#98989F", "#1B1B1F"),
]);
Environment.ExitCode = failures == 0 ? 0 : 1;            // a non-zero exit stops the CI build
Console.WriteLine($"{failures} failure(s): exit code {Environment.ExitCode}");

// The muted grey the palette used to have, as data: it would stop the build
var before = CheckAA([("light", "muted caption", "#8E8E93", "#FFFFFF")]);
Console.WriteLine($"with #8E8E93: {before} failure(s), exit code would be {(before == 0 ? 0 : 1)}");

static int CheckAA((string Theme, string Role, string Text, string Background)[] pairs)
{
    var failures = 0;
    foreach (var (theme, role, text, background) in pairs)
    {
        var ratio = Ratio(text, background);
        Console.WriteLine($"{theme,-5} {role,-15} {ratio,5:0.00}:1 {(ratio >= 4.5 ? "AA" : "fails AA")}");
        if (ratio < 4.5) failures++;                     // xUnit: Assert.True(ratio >= 4.5, role)
    }
    return failures;
}

// WCAG 2.x: (lighter + 0.05) / (darker + 0.05); AA body text needs 4.5:1, large text 3:1
static double Ratio(string foreground, string background)
{
    var (a, b) = (Luminance(foreground), Luminance(background));
    return (Math.Max(a, b) + 0.05) / (Math.Min(a, b) + 0.05);
}

static double Luminance(string hex)
{
    var rgb = Convert.FromHexString(hex.TrimStart('#'));
    return 0.2126 * Linear(rgb[0] / 255.0) + 0.7152 * Linear(rgb[1] / 255.0)
        + 0.0722 * Linear(rgb[2] / 255.0);
}

static double Linear(double c) => c <= 0.04045 ? c / 12.92 : Math.Pow((c + 0.055) / 1.055, 2.4);
Result
light body text       17.17:1 AA
light primary button   7.94:1 AA
light muted caption    5.07:1 AA
dark  body text       15.39:1 AA
dark  primary button   6.95:1 AA
dark  muted caption    5.99:1 AA
0 failure(s): exit code 0
light muted caption    3.26:1 fails AA
with #8E8E93: 1 failure(s), exit code would be 1

Pressed, hover and disabled with VisualStateManager

States live in the style so every button gets the same feedback, and a group must include `Normal` (WPF uses `Style.Triggers`; WinUI overrides lightweight-styling keys such as `ButtonBackgroundPressed`).

<!-- Added to the BaseButton style in Styles.xaml -->
<Style x:Key="BaseButton" TargetType="Button">
    <!-- …the setters from the styles card… -->
    <Setter Property="VisualStateManager.VisualStateGroups">
        <VisualStateGroupList>
            <VisualStateGroup x:Name="CommonStates">
                <VisualState x:Name="Normal" />
                <VisualState x:Name="Pressed">
                    <VisualState.Setters>
                        <Setter Property="Scale" Value="0.97" />
                        <Setter Property="Opacity" Value="0.85" />
                    </VisualState.Setters>
                </VisualState>
                <VisualState x:Name="PointerOver">
                    <VisualState.Setters>
                        <Setter Property="Opacity" Value="0.92" />
                    </VisualState.Setters>
                </VisualState>
                <VisualState x:Name="Disabled">
                    <VisualState.Setters>
                        <Setter Property="BackgroundColor" Value="{StaticResource DisabledBackground}" />
                        <Setter Property="TextColor" Value="{StaticResource DisabledText}" />
                    </VisualState.Setters>
                </VisualState>
            </VisualStateGroup>
        </VisualStateGroupList>
    </Setter>
</Style>

<!-- IsEnabled drives the Disabled state; a command's CanExecute does the same -->
<Button Text="Place order" Command="{Binding PlaceOrderCommand}" />
Result

Responsive and adaptive: OnIdiom, OnPlatform, AdaptiveTrigger, font scaling

OnIdiom and OnPlatform are resolved once at load; AdaptiveTrigger follows the window as it resizes; text scales with the user's OS setting unless you opt out.

<!-- Per device and platform, resolved when the page loads -->
<Label Text="Your orders"
       FontSize="{OnIdiom Phone=22, Tablet=28, Desktop=28}"
       Margin="{OnPlatform iOS='0,8,0,0', Default='0'}" />

<!-- Follows the OS text size by default; opt out only for fixed-size chrome -->
<Label Text="{Binding UnreadCount}" FontSize="12" FontAutoScalingEnabled="False" />

<!-- Breakpoints: list above details when narrow, side by side from 800 wide -->
<FlexLayout Direction="Column">
    <VisualStateManager.VisualStateGroups>
        <VisualStateGroup x:Name="WidthStates">
            <VisualState x:Name="Narrow">
                <VisualState.StateTriggers>
                    <AdaptiveTrigger MinWindowWidth="0" />
                </VisualState.StateTriggers>
                <VisualState.Setters>
                    <Setter Property="Direction" Value="Column" />
                </VisualState.Setters>
            </VisualState>
            <VisualState x:Name="Wide">
                <VisualState.StateTriggers>
                    <AdaptiveTrigger MinWindowWidth="800" />
                </VisualState.StateTriggers>
                <VisualState.Setters>
                    <Setter Property="Direction" Value="Row" />
                </VisualState.Setters>
            </VisualState>
        </VisualStateGroup>
    </VisualStateManager.VisualStateGroups>
    <views:OrderList FlexLayout.Basis="40%" />
    <views:OrderDetails FlexLayout.Grow="1" />
</FlexLayout>
Result

On a phone the title is 22 and on a tablet or desktop 28; whenever the window is at least 800 wide (most tablets in landscape, desktop windows) the list and details sit side by side, otherwise stacked.

Blazor: tokens as CSS custom properties, styles scoped per component

Global tokens go in `app.css`; a `.razor.css` file next to a component is rewritten to apply only to that component, and `::deep` reaches its children.

/* wwwroot/app.css: the tokens, once */
:root {
  --color-surface: #ffffff;
  --color-on-surface: #1b1b1f;
  --space-m: 1rem;
  --radius-m: 12px;
}
[data-theme="dark"] {                 /* set from C# through JS interop, or follow the OS: */
  --color-surface: #1b1b1f;
  --color-on-surface: #f2f2f7;
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { --color-surface: #1b1b1f; --color-on-surface: #f2f2f7; }
}

/* Components/OrderCard.razor.css: scoped to OrderCard by a generated b-xxxxxxxxxx attribute */
.card {
  background: var(--color-surface);
  color: var(--color-on-surface);
  padding: var(--space-m);
  border-radius: var(--radius-m);
}
.card ::deep .badge { font-size: 0.8rem; }   /* StatusBadge is a child component */
@media (min-width: 800px) {
  .card { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr auto; }
}

@* Components/OrderCard.razor *@
<article class="card">
    <h3>Order @Order.Number</h3>
    <StatusBadge Status="@Order.Status" />
</article>
@code { [Parameter, EditorRequired] public Order Order { get; set; } = default!; }

<!-- Components/App.razor, in <head> (.NET 9; earlier: href="Shop.styles.css") -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="@Assets["Shop.styles.css"]" />
Result

Each order card picks up the global tokens, flips with the theme, and its .card rule cannot leak into other components.

Rules and pitfalls

Most styling bugs are a static lookup, a missing BasedOn, or a hard-coded value.

  • {StaticResource …} for a themed key: it is read once, so a theme swap leaves it stale. Use DynamicResource (MAUI, WPF), ThemeResource (WinUI) or AppThemeBinding.
  • An explicit Style without BasedOn: it replaces the implicit style, and the button silently loses its padding and radius.
  • Hex values and magic numbers in pages: name a token by role (Surface, SpaceM) so dark mode and rebrands are one-file changes.
  • FontAutoScalingEnabled="False" on body text, or fixed-height rows around text: users who enlarge text get clipped content.
  • A VisualStateGroup without a Normal state: setters from the previous state are never undone.
  • Check every text/background token pair for 4.5:1 contrast (3:1 for large text) in a unit test, in both themes.
  • Order merged dictionaries tokens-first: a style that reads {StaticResource BrandPrimary} must come after the dictionary that defines it.
  • MAUI implicit styles do not apply to subclasses unless the style sets ApplyToDerivedTypes="True".
  • Blazor scoped CSS only matches elements in the component's own markup; reach child components with ::deep under an element you own.

Unidirectional State — Reducers, MVU & Fluxor

State → action → pure reducer → new state → the view; async work lives in effects that dispatch actions back. A small store written by hand, then the same feature in Fluxor.

The nouns, and their TCA and Redux twins

The loop is the same everywhere: a view sends an action, a pure reducer computes the next state, effects do the async work and send actions back.

NounIn C#TCARedux / Redux Toolkit
Statean immutable record with ImmutableList<T> / ImmutableArray<T> inside@ObservableState struct Statea plain object, frozen by Immer in RTK
Actionan abstract record and one sealed record per eventenum Action{ type, payload }, createSlice action creators

Effecta Task that receives dispatch and a CancellationToken.run { send in … }thunks, listener middleware, sagas
cancel in flightcancel the previous effect's CancellationTokenSource.cancellable(id:cancelInFlight: true)AbortController, takeLatest
Storeholds State, runs the reducer, raises StateChangedStore / StoreOf<F>createStore / configureStore

A minimal feature, end to end

The skeleton to type from memory: immutable state, actions as records, a pure reducer, and a store that only notifies when the state really changed.

using System.Collections.Immutable;

var store = new Store<CartState, CartAction>(new CartState([]), CartFeature.Reduce);
store.StateChanged += cart =>
    Console.WriteLine($"{cart.Lines.Count} line(s), {cart.Lines.Sum(l => l.Quantity)} item(s)");

store.Dispatch(new ItemAdded("SKU-1", "USB-C cable"));
store.Dispatch(new ItemAdded("SKU-1", "USB-C cable"));        // the same item: quantity 2
store.Dispatch(new ItemAdded("SKU-7", "Laptop stand"));
store.Dispatch(new ItemRemoved("SKU-404"));                    // nothing to remove: no render
store.Dispatch(new ItemRemoved("SKU-1"));

record CartLine(string Sku, string Name, int Quantity);
record CartState(ImmutableList<CartLine> Lines);
abstract record CartAction;
sealed record ItemAdded(string Sku, string Name) : CartAction;
sealed record ItemRemoved(string Sku) : CartAction;

static class CartFeature
{
    public static CartState Reduce(CartState state, CartAction action) => action switch
    {
        ItemAdded added when state.Lines.Find(l => l.Sku == added.Sku) is { } line =>
            state with { Lines = state.Lines.Replace(line, line with { Quantity = line.Quantity + 1 }) },
        ItemAdded added => state with { Lines = state.Lines.Add(new CartLine(added.Sku, added.Name, 1)) },
        ItemRemoved removed => state with { Lines = state.Lines.RemoveAll(l => l.Sku == removed.Sku) },
        _ => state,
    };
}

sealed class Store<TState, TAction>(TState initial, Func<TState, TAction, TState> reducer)
{
    public TState State { get; private set; } = initial;
    public event Action<TState>? StateChanged;

    public void Dispatch(TAction action)
    {
        var next = reducer(State, action);
        if (EqualityComparer<TState>.Default.Equals(next, State)) return;   // record equality: no change
        State = next;
        StateChanged?.Invoke(next);
    }
}
Result
1 line(s), 1 item(s)
1 line(s), 2 item(s)
2 line(s), 3 item(s)
1 line(s), 1 item(s)

Actions are events, not setters

Name what happened, not what to set, so the reducer owns every rule (here, ignoring a stale answer) in one place — and both columns provably reach the same state.

Setters — the view decides how state changes
using System.Collections.Immutable;

SearchAction[] dispatched =
[
    new SetQuery("desk"), new SetLoading(true),               // four actions for one search
    new SetResults(["Oak desk", "Standing desk"]), new SetLoading(false),
];
Console.WriteLine(dispatched.Aggregate(new SearchState("", false, []), Reduce));

static SearchState Reduce(SearchState state, SearchAction action) => action switch
{
    SetQuery a => state with { Query = a.Query },
    SetLoading a => state with { IsLoading = a.IsLoading },
    SetResults a => state with { Results = a.Results },          // a stale answer overwrites
    _ => state,
};

record SearchState(string Query, bool IsLoading, ImmutableArray<string> Results)
{
    public override string ToString() => $"'{Query}': {Results.Length} results, loading {IsLoading}";
}
abstract record SearchAction;
sealed record SetQuery(string Query) : SearchAction;
sealed record SetLoading(bool IsLoading) : SearchAction;
sealed record SetResults(ImmutableArray<string> Results) : SearchAction;
Events — the reducer decides
using System.Collections.Immutable;

SearchAction[] dispatched =
[
    new SearchSubmitted("desk"),                              // what the user did
    new ResultsLoaded("desk", ["Oak desk", "Standing desk"]),  // what the server answered
];
Console.WriteLine(dispatched.Aggregate(new SearchState("", false, []), Reduce));

static SearchState Reduce(SearchState state, SearchAction action) => action switch
{
    SearchSubmitted a => state with { Query = a.Query, IsLoading = true },
    ResultsLoaded a when a.Query == state.Query => state with { IsLoading = false, Results = a.Results },
    ResultsLoaded => state,                                    // an answer to an old query
    _ => state,
};

record SearchState(string Query, bool IsLoading, ImmutableArray<string> Results)
{
    public override string ToString() => $"'{Query}': {Results.Length} results, loading {IsLoading}";
}
abstract record SearchAction;
sealed record SearchSubmitted(string Query) : SearchAction;
sealed record ResultsLoaded(string Query, ImmutableArray<string> Results) : SearchAction;
Result
'desk': 2 results, loading False

Immutable updates: with, immutable collections, and record equality

`with` copies one level, so copy every level you change; unchanged parts are shared, and records compare collections by reference.

using System.Collections.Immutable;

var checkout = new Checkout("ana@shop.example", new Address("Rua Augusta 1", "Lisbon"), ["WELCOME10"]);

var moved = checkout with { Shipping = checkout.Shipping with { City = "Porto" } };   // nested: two copies
Console.WriteLine($"{checkout.Shipping.City} -> {moved.Shipping.City}");
Console.WriteLine($"coupons shared, not copied: {ReferenceEquals(checkout.Coupons, moved.Coupons)}");

var withFreeShipping = moved with { Coupons = moved.Coupons.Add("FREESHIP") };       // a new list
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", withFreeShipping.Coupons));

// Equal contents, different list instance: the records are NOT equal
var rebuilt = checkout with { Coupons = ["WELCOME10"] };
var sameContents = checkout.Coupons.SequenceEqual(rebuilt.Coupons);
Console.WriteLine($"records equal: {checkout == rebuilt}, contents equal: {sameContents}");

// Many edits at once: a builder, then one new immutable list
var builder = withFreeShipping.Coupons.ToBuilder();
builder.Remove("WELCOME10");
builder.Add("VIP");
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", builder.ToImmutable()));

record Address(string Street, string City);
record Checkout(string Email, Address Shipping, ImmutableList<string> Coupons);
Result
Lisbon -> Porto
coupons shared, not copied: True
WELCOME10, FREESHIP
records equal: False, contents equal: True
FREESHIP, VIP

Effects that end in an action — superseded ones cancelled, late answers dropped, failures reported

The reducer stays pure and returns the next state plus a description of async work, and the store runs it, cancels the one in flight, drops what a cancelled effect returns, and turns a failure into an action.

var answers = new Dictionary<string, TaskCompletionSource<string>>();   // a server that ignores tokens

var store = new Store<SearchState, SearchAction>(new("", ""), Reduce,
    error => new Shown($"unavailable ({error.Message})"));    // a failed effect still ends in an action
store.StateChanged += s => Console.WriteLine($"'{s.Query}': {s.Text}");
store.Dispatch(new QueryChanged("d"));
store.Dispatch(new QueryChanged("desk"));                   // supersedes 'd' while it is in flight
answers["d"].SetResult("Desk lamp");                        // the late answer is dropped: nothing printed
answers["desk"].SetException(new HttpRequestException("503"));

(SearchState, Effect<SearchAction>?) Reduce(SearchState state, SearchAction action) => action switch
{
    QueryChanged q => (state with { Query = q.Query, Text = "searching…" },
        async token => new Shown(await (answers[q.Query] = new()).Task)),    // the search, as an effect
    Shown r => (state with { Text = r.Text }, null),
    _ => (state, null),
};

delegate Task<TAction> Effect<TAction>(CancellationToken token);    // async work that ends in one action

sealed class Store<TState, TAction>(TState state, Func<TState, TAction, (TState, Effect<TAction>?)> reducer,
    Func<Exception, TAction> failed)
{
    private CancellationTokenSource? inFlight;               // one effect at a time; key them to have more
    public event Action<TState>? StateChanged;

    public void Dispatch(TAction action) => _ = DispatchAsync(action);   // call it on the UI thread

    private async Task DispatchAsync(TAction action)
    {
        (state, var effect) = reducer(state, action);
        StateChanged?.Invoke(state);
        if (effect is null) return;
        inFlight?.Cancel();                                   // a new effect supersedes the one in flight
        var cancel = inFlight = new CancellationTokenSource();   // no timer inside: nothing to Dispose
        var attempt = effect(cancel.Token);
        await Task.WhenAny(attempt);                          // wait without throwing, back on the UI thread
        if (cancel.IsCancellationRequested) return;           // superseded: drop its answer, or its failure
        var error = attempt.Exception?.GetBaseException() ?? new OperationCanceledException();
        await DispatchAsync(attempt.IsCompletedSuccessfully ? attempt.Result : failed(error));   // never lost
    }
}

record SearchState(string Query, string Text);
abstract record SearchAction;
sealed record QueryChanged(string Query) : SearchAction;
sealed record Shown(string Text) : SearchAction;
Result
'd': searching…
'desk': searching…
'desk': unavailable (503)

Selectors — derived state, recomputed only when its input changes

A memoised selector recomputes when its input reference changes, which with immutable state is a cheap `ReferenceEquals`, but an equal new list still recomputes, so the view model compares the selected value before raising.

using System.Collections.Immutable;

var computations = 0;
var selectTotal = Cart.CreateTotalSelector(() => computations++);

var state = new CartState([], null);
CartAction[] actions =
    [new ItemAdded(25m), new ItemAdded(15m), new CouponApplied("WELCOME10"), new PricesReloaded()];
foreach (var action in actions)
{
    state = Cart.Reduce(state, action);
    var total = selectTotal(state);
    Console.WriteLine($"{action.GetType().Name,-14} total {total}, computed {computations} time(s)");
}

static class Cart
{
    public static CartState Reduce(CartState state, CartAction action) => action switch
    {
        ItemAdded a => state with { Prices = state.Prices.Add(a.Price) },
        CouponApplied c => state with { Coupon = c.Code },             // Prices untouched: the same list
        PricesReloaded => state with { Prices = [.. state.Prices] },    // equal contents, a new list
        _ => state,
    };

    // Recomputes only when the input reference changes: a cheap check, because state is immutable
    public static Func<CartState, string> CreateTotalSelector(Action onCompute)
    {
        ImmutableList<decimal>? lastInput = null;
        var lastOutput = "";
        return state =>
        {
            if (ReferenceEquals(state.Prices, lastInput)) return lastOutput;
            onCompute();
            (lastInput, lastOutput) = (state.Prices, $"{state.Prices.Sum()}");
            return lastOutput;
        };
    }
}

record CartState(ImmutableList<decimal> Prices, string? Coupon);
abstract record CartAction;
sealed record ItemAdded(decimal Price) : CartAction;
sealed record CouponApplied(string Code) : CartAction;
sealed record PricesReloaded : CartAction;
Result
ItemAdded      total 25, computed 1 time(s)
ItemAdded      total 40, computed 2 time(s)
CouponApplied  total 40, computed 2 time(s)
PricesReloaded total 40, computed 3 time(s)
