DRM: which key system applies where

Package once as CMAF with `cbcs` encryption and the same segments serve all three systems (older PlayReady clients and Android before 7.1 need `cenc`), with only the licence request differing per platform and none of it reachable through `MediaElement`'s own API.

Key systemWhere it appliesFrom .NET
FairPlay StreamingiOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, SafariAVPlayer with AVContentKeySession in a MAUI handler for iOS / Mac Catalyst; EME in Safari for Blazor
WidevineAndroid, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Android TV, ChromecastMedia3 DrmSessionManager in a MAUI handler for Android (cbcs from Android 7.1, API 25); EME through hls.js or dash.js for Blazor
PlayReadyWindows apps, Edge on Windows, Xbox, many smart TVsMediaProtectionManager with MediaPlayer in WinUI or MAUI on Windows; EME in Edge
AES-128 HLS encryptionevery HLS playerno DRM: the key is fetched over HTTPS (with your auth); it stops casual copying, not a determined user
SAMPLE-AES HLS encryptionAVPlayer, hls.js — not Media3 / ExoPlayer, so not MAUI on Androidno DRM either; prefer AES-128 or a real key system
LibVLCSharp, WPF MediaElement—no commercial DRM: choose a platform player for protected content

Background playback and the app lifecycle in MAUI

Decide per screen: a product video pauses when the app leaves the foreground, while a talk keeps playing, which needs the Android foreground service and the iOS audio background mode.

// MauiProgram.cs — MediaElement 6.x declares the Android foreground service and its permissions itself;
// from 8.0 (MAUI 10) it is opt-in: UseMauiCommunityToolkitMediaElement(true).
builder.UseMauiApp<App>().UseMauiCommunityToolkitMediaElement();

// TalkPage.xaml.cs — a long talk that may keep playing with the screen off.
// The page holds <toolkit:MediaElement x:Name="player" MetadataTitle="…" MetadataArtworkUrl="…"/>.
using CommunityToolkit.Maui.Core;

namespace Shop;

public partial class TalkPage : ContentPage
{
    public TalkPage() => InitializeComponent();

    static bool KeepPlayingInBackground => Preferences.Default.Get("background_playback", false);

    protected override void OnAppearing()
    {
        base.OnAppearing();
        if (Window is { } window) window.Stopped += OnAppBackgrounded;
    }

    protected override void OnDisappearing()
    {
        if (Window is { } window) window.Stopped -= OnAppBackgrounded;
        player.Stop();
        base.OnDisappearing();
    }

    void OnAppBackgrounded(object? sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        // The user comes back to a paused video, not to one that played on without them.
        if (!KeepPlayingInBackground && player.CurrentState == MediaElementState.Playing)
            player.Pause();
    }
}
Result

When the app is sent to the background the talk pauses, unless the user enabled background playback; then it continues with lock-screen controls and metadata on Android (foreground service) and iOS (audio background mode).

Pitfalls worth saying out loud

Most playback bugs reported from the field are one of these.

  • Expecting WPF's MediaElement to play .m3u8 or .mpd: it plays progressive files only. Use WinUI, LibVLCSharp or a WebView2 page.
  • Serving DASH to iOS or Mac Catalyst: AVPlayer plays HLS only. Publish both manifests, or HLS with CMAF segments for everyone.
  • Updating UI from player events without dispatching: StateChanged, PlaybackStateChanged and bitrate events can arrive off the UI thread.
  • Treating Buffering as an error: show a spinner, and only intervene on Failed or MediaFailed.
  • A plain http:// stream on Android or iOS: cleartext is blocked by default. Serve HTTPS rather than weakening the platform policy.
  • Stop (and on WinUI dispose) the player when the page goes away: decoders, the network and the screen-on lock are held until you do. MediaElement is IDisposable too.
  • For live, start three target durations behind the edge and reload on the target duration; for VOD, remember the position so a reload resumes there.
  • Set MetadataTitle and artwork for lock-screen controls, and keep the DRM licence request behind your own authentication.
  • Test on real devices and with throttled networks: emulators often lack hardware decoders and DRM (Widevine L1, FairPlay).

Where does this secret go?

Anything compiled into an app or shipped to a browser is public: a client app holds only the user's own tokens, never the API's keys.

SecretPut it inNever in
an API key or connection string, in developmentdotnet user-secrets set "Payments:ApiKey" "…" (a file in your profile) or an environment variableappsettings.json committed to source control
the same, in productiona vault (Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) read with a managed identity, or the host's secret storethe container image, a config file in the repo, the build log
the user's refresh token on a phone (MAUI)SecureStorage.Default.SetAsync — iOS Keychain, Android Keystore-encrypted preferencesPreferences, a file, a SQLite table in clear
a token or credential in a Windows desktop app (WPF, WinUI unpackaged)ProtectedData.Protect(…, DataProtectionScope.CurrentUser) (DPAPI; the System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData package), or the Credential Lockerthe registry or a settings file in clear

OAuth 2.0 authorization code with PKCE

A public client (MAUI, WPF, WinUI, Blazor WebAssembly) redirects to a reverse-DNS scheme it owns, checks `state` and `error` on the way back, and proves with a one-time verifier that it started the sign-in, so a stolen code is useless.

using System.Buffers.Text;
using System.Security.Cryptography;
using System.Text;
using System.Web;

// RFC 7636, appendix B: this verifier must give this challenge.
var rfcChallenge = Challenge("dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk");
Console.WriteLine(rfcChallenge == "E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM");

const string Redirect = "com.shop.app:/callback";              // RFC 8252: a reverse-DNS scheme you own
var verifier = NewSecret();                                      // kept in memory until the callback
var state = NewSecret();
var authorize = "https://login.shop.example/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=shop-app"
    + $"&redirect_uri={Uri.EscapeDataString(Redirect)}&scope=openid%20orders%20offline_access"
    + $"&state={state}&code_challenge={Challenge(verifier)}&code_challenge_method=S256";
var seenByServer = HttpUtility.ParseQueryString(new Uri(authorize).Query)["code_challenge"]!;

// The browser returns to the redirect URI; WebAuthenticator or MSAL hands its query back.
string[] callbacks =
    [$"error=access_denied&state={state}", "code=c-1&state=forged", $"code=c-1&state={state}"];
foreach (var query in callbacks)
{
    var callback = HttpUtility.ParseQueryString(query);
    if (callback["state"] != state) Console.WriteLine("rejected: state mismatch, not our sign-in");
    else if (callback["error"] is { } error) Console.WriteLine($"sign-in failed: {error}");
    else
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"stolen code, no verifier: {Redeem(callback["code"]!, NewSecret())}");
        Console.WriteLine($"our code and verifier: {Redeem(callback["code"]!, verifier)}");
    }
}

// The app POSTs grant_type=authorization_code, code, redirect_uri, client_id and code_verifier to /token;
// the server answers only if SHA-256(code_verifier) equals the code_challenge it saw at /authorize.
// Later it POSTs grant_type=refresh_token: for a public client the server must rotate that token.
string Redeem(string code, string codeVerifier) =>
    code == "c-1" && Challenge(codeVerifier) == seenByServer ? "200 tokens" : "400 invalid_grant";

static string NewSecret() => Base64Url.EncodeToString(RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(32));   // 43 characters

static string Challenge(string verifier) =>
    Base64Url.EncodeToString(SHA256.HashData(Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes(verifier)));
Result
True
sign-in failed: access_denied
rejected: state mismatch, not our sign-in
stolen code, no verifier: 400 invalid_grant
our code and verifier: 200 tokens
Setup
  1. .NET 9 SDK or later (Base64Url is new in .NET 9)
  2. dotnet new console -o Demo, replace Demo/Program.cs with the example, then dotnet run --project Demo

Ran with .NET SDK 9.0.304 (net9.0, C# 13) on 2026-11-16: the output matched the result shown.

Sign-in against Microsoft Entra ID with MSAL

MSAL runs the authorization-code flow with PKCE, caches the tokens and refreshes them, so try the silent call first and show the interactive sign-in only when MSAL says it must.

using Microsoft.Identity.Client;

// Silent first (the cache, or a refresh), interactive only when it must.
public sealed class EntraSignIn
{
    private static readonly string[] Scopes = ["api://orders-api/Orders.Read"];
    private readonly IPublicClientApplication app = PublicClientApplicationBuilder
        .Create("11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555")
        .WithAuthority(AzureCloudInstance.AzurePublic, "contoso.onmicrosoft.com")
        .WithRedirectUri("msal11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555://auth")   // Android and iOS
        .WithIosKeychainSecurityGroup("com.microsoft.adalcache")              // the iOS token cache
        .Build();

    public async Task<string> GetAccessTokenAsync(object parentWindow, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var account = (await app.GetAccountsAsync()).FirstOrDefault();
        try { return (await app.AcquireTokenSilent(Scopes, account).ExecuteAsync(ct)).AccessToken; }
        catch (MsalUiRequiredException)
        {
            var interactive = app.AcquireTokenInteractive(Scopes).WithParentActivityOrWindow(parentWindow);
            return (await interactive.ExecuteAsync(ct)).AccessToken;
        }
    }
}
Result

MSAL returns an access token silently while its cached refresh token is valid, and shows the Entra sign-in only when it throws MsalUiRequiredException.

Setup
  1. MSAL: dotnet add package Microsoft.Identity.Client; a public-client registration with the redirect URI msal{client-id}://auth. Android: a BrowserTabActivity intent filter for that scheme and AuthenticationContinuationHelper.SetAuthenticationContinuationEventArgs in MainActivity.OnActivityResult; iOS: the com.microsoft.adalcache keychain access group in Entitlements.plist. On Windows use MSAL's WAM broker or an http://localhost redirect instead

Sign-in against your own backend: WebAuthenticator, bound by PKCE

The backend runs the provider's flow and redirects back with a one-time code, and the PKCE verifier that never left the app is what makes an intercepted code useless to another app that claimed the scheme.

using System.Net.Http.Json;
using Microsoft.Maui.Authentication;

// Your backend runs the provider's flow and redirects back to the app with a short-lived one-time code.
public sealed class BackendSignIn(HttpClient api)
{
    public async Task<string> SignInAsync()
    {
        var verifier = Pkce.NewSecret();                        // the PKCE card's helpers; it stays in memory
        // No state parameter: PKCE, enforced by the backend, already gives the CSRF protection (RFC 9700).
        var start = "https://shop.example/mobileauth/start"
            + $"?code_challenge={Pkce.Challenge(verifier)}&code_challenge_method=S256";
        var result = await WebAuthenticator.Default.AuthenticateAsync(new WebAuthenticatorOptions
        {
            Url = new Uri(start),
            CallbackUrl = new Uri("com.shop.app://callback"),       // RFC 8252: a reverse-DNS scheme you own
            PrefersEphemeralWebBrowserSession = true,               // iOS: no cookies shared between sign-ins
        });

        // An app that intercepts the scheme gets the code but not the verifier, so it cannot redeem it:
        // the backend answers only if SHA-256(code_verifier) equals the challenge sent to /start.
        var redeem = new { code = result.Properties["code"], code_verifier = verifier };
        using var redeemed = await api.PostAsJsonAsync("mobileauth/redeem", redeem);
        redeemed.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
        return await redeemed.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();       // keep the refresh token in SecureStorage
    }
}
Result

The system browser runs the sign-in and returns a one-time code; the app redeems it with its verifier for tokens over HTTPS (a TaskCanceledException if the user closes the browser), and an app that intercepted the callback holds a code it cannot redeem.

Setup
  1. WebAuthenticator (.NET MAUI, Android and iOS only — it does not work on Windows today): a WebAuthenticatorCallbackActivity with an intent filter for com.shop.app on Android, the scheme in CFBundleURLSchemes on iOS; an App Link or Universal Link (https) is better still
  2. The PKCE card's NewSecret and Challenge helpers, kept in a static class Pkce; the backend's /mobileauth/redeem answers only when SHA-256 of code_verifier matches the challenge it saw at /start

What validating a JWT means, 1: the signature, by hand

To see what the vetted handler (the third card from here) checks, never to replace it: pin the algorithm, verify ECDsa over `header.payload`, and trust nothing in the payload until that passes.

using System.Buffers.Text;
using System.Security.Cryptography;
using System.Text;
using System.Text.Json;

using var idp = ECDsa.Create(ECCurve.NamedCurves.nistP256);              // the identity provider's key
const string Claims = """{"iss":"https://id.example","sub":"u-42","aud":"orders-api","exp":1800000300}""";

var good = Sign(Claims).Split('.');
foreach (var (label, jwt) in new[]
{
    ("valid", string.Join('.', good)),
    ("payload edited", $"{good[0]}.{B64(Claims.Replace("u-42", "admin"))}.{good[2]}"),
    ("alg none", $"{B64("""{"alg":"none"}""")}.{good[1]}."),
    ("alg as a number", $"{B64("""{"alg":256}""")}.{good[1]}.{good[2]}"),
    ("header is an array", $"{B64("""["ES256"]""")}.{good[1]}.{good[2]}"),
    ("garbage", "a.b!.c"),
})
    Console.WriteLine($"{label}: {VerifySignature(jwt, idp) ?? "rejected"}");

string Sign(string claims)
{
    var input = $"{B64("""{"alg":"ES256","typ":"JWT"}""")}.{B64(claims)}";
    var signature = idp.SignData(Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes(input), HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);   // r||s
    return $"{input}.{Base64Url.EncodeToString(signature)}";
}

static string B64(string json) => Base64Url.EncodeToString(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(json));

// The payload's JSON once the signature over "head.body" verifies, else null; until then it is all hostile.
static string? VerifySignature(string jwt, ECDsa key)
{
    if (jwt.Split('.') is not [var head, var body, var sig]) return null;
    try
    {
        using var header = JsonDocument.Parse(Base64Url.DecodeFromChars(head));
        var h = header.RootElement;
        if (h.ValueKind != JsonValueKind.Object || !h.TryGetProperty("alg", out var alg)) return null;
        if (alg.ValueKind != JsonValueKind.String || alg.GetString() != "ES256") return null;   // pinned
        var signed = Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes($"{head}.{body}");
        if (!key.VerifyData(signed, Base64Url.DecodeFromChars(sig), HashAlgorithmName.SHA256)) return null;
        return Encoding.UTF8.GetString(Base64Url.DecodeFromChars(body));
    }
    catch (Exception e) when (e is FormatException or JsonException) { return null; }   // bad base64 or JSON
}
Result
valid: {"iss":"https://id.example","sub":"u-42","aud":"orders-api","exp":1800000300}
payload edited: rejected
alg none: rejected
alg as a number: rejected
header is an array: rejected
garbage: rejected
Setup

What validating a JWT means, 2: the claims

After the signature, the issuer must match, the audience (a string or an array) must name this API, `exp` must be present and in the future and `nbf` in the past, each within a small clock skew, and a payload of the wrong shape (not JSON, an array, a missing `sub`, an unreadable `exp` or `nbf`) is a rejection, not a crash, while a fractional NumericDate is accepted.

using System.Text.Json;

const long Now = 1_800_000_000;                                           // an injected clock, Unix seconds
foreach (var claims in new[]
{
    """{"iss":"https://id.example","sub":"u-42","aud":"orders-api","exp":1800000300}""",
    """{"iss":"https://id.example","sub":"u-42","aud":["web","orders-api"],"exp":1800000300}""",
    """{"iss":"https://id.example","sub":"u-42","aud":"orders-api","exp":1800000300.5}""",
    """{"iss":"https://id.example","sub":"u-42","aud":"billing","exp":1800000300}""",
    """{"iss":"https://id.example","sub":"u-42","aud":"orders-api","exp":1799999000}""",
    """{"iss":"https://id.example","sub":"u-42","aud":"orders-api"}""",
    """{"iss":"https://id.example","sub":"u-42","aud":"orders-api","exp":1800000300,"nbf":1830000000}""",
    """{"iss":"https://id.example","sub":"u-42","aud":"orders-api","exp":1800000300,"nbf":"soon"}""",
    """{"iss":"https://id.example","aud":"orders-api","exp":1800000300}""",
    """["https://id.example","u-42"]""", "{",
})
    Console.WriteLine(CheckClaims(claims, Now));

// Run only on a payload whose signature verified (previous card); its shapes are still not trusted.
static string CheckClaims(string json, long now)
{
    const long Skew = 30;                                                 // seconds of clock drift allowed
    JsonElement c;
    try { c = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<JsonElement>(json); }            // no document to dispose
    catch (JsonException) { return "rejected: not JSON"; }
    if (c.ValueKind != JsonValueKind.Object) return "rejected: not a claims object";
    if (Text(c, "iss") != "https://id.example") return "rejected: issuer";
    if (!c.TryGetProperty("aud", out var aud)) return "rejected: no audience";
    JsonElement[] audiences = aud.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array ? [.. aud.EnumerateArray()] : [aud];
    if (!audiences.Any(a => a.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.String && a.GetString() == "orders-api"))
        return "rejected: audience";
    if (Seconds(c, "exp") is not { } exp) return "rejected: no usable exp";   // required, a NumericDate
    if (exp + Skew < now) return "rejected: expired";
    var nbf = c.TryGetProperty("nbf", out _) ? Seconds(c, "nbf") ?? long.MaxValue : long.MinValue;
    if (nbf > now + Skew) return "rejected: not valid yet";          // an unreadable nbf fails closed
    return Text(c, "sub") is { } sub ? $"valid: sub={sub}" : "rejected: no subject";
}

static string? Text(JsonElement claims, string name) =>
    claims.TryGetProperty(name, out var v) && v.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.String ? v.GetString() : null;

static long? Seconds(JsonElement claims, string name) =>
    claims.TryGetProperty(name, out var v) && v.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Number && v.TryGetDouble(out var s)
        && Math.Abs(s) < 1e12 ? (long)Math.Floor(s) : null;
Result
valid: sub=u-42
valid: sub=u-42
valid: sub=u-42
rejected: audience
rejected: expired
rejected: no usable exp
rejected: not valid yet
rejected: not valid yet
rejected: no subject
rejected: not a claims object
rejected: not JSON

The real thing: JwtBearer and TokenValidationParameters

In the ASP.NET Core API behind a MAUI or Blazor app, `Authority` fetches and rotates the signing keys, and the handler makes every check of the previous two cards plus the algorithm list (and `typ`, once you set `ValidTypes` for an issuer that types its tokens), so leave each `Validate…` switch on.

using System.Security.Claims;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer;
using Microsoft.IdentityModel.Tokens;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer(options =>
    {
        options.Authority = "https://login.shop.example/";        // discovery document + signing keys (JWKS)
        options.Audience = "orders-api";
        options.MapInboundClaims = false;                         // keep "sub", not a long XML claim type
        options.TokenValidationParameters = new TokenValidationParameters
        {
            ValidateIssuer = true,                                // off: tokens from any tenant are accepted
            ValidIssuer = "https://login.shop.example/",
            ValidateAudience = true,                              // off: another API's token works here
            ValidateLifetime = true,                              // off: a leaked token works forever
            ClockSkew = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30),                 // the default is 5 minutes
            ValidateIssuerSigningKey = true,
            RequireSignedTokens = true,                           // never accept alg "none"
            RequireExpirationTime = true,
            ValidAlgorithms = [SecurityAlgorithms.EcdsaSha256, SecurityAlgorithms.RsaSha256],
            // ValidTypes = ["at+jwt"]: only if your issuer types access tokens per RFC 9068.
            // Microsoft Entra ID sends typ "JWT", so with Entra leave it unset (null: any typ).
        };
        // Never: options.RequireHttpsMetadata = false outside local development,
        // or a SignatureValidator that returns the token unchecked.
    });
builder.Services.AddAuthorization();

var app = builder.Build();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapGet("/orders", (ClaimsPrincipal user) => $"orders of {user.FindFirst("sub")?.Value}")
    .RequireAuthorization();
app.Run();
Result

Requests to /orders without a valid bearer token get 401; a token with the wrong issuer, audience, type or algorithm, an expired one, or one whose signature does not match the issuer's published keys is rejected.

Setup

AES-GCM encryption, bound to its owner

AES-GCM gives secrecy and tamper detection in one call with a fresh 12-byte nonce every time, and a record that was changed, belongs to someone else or is too short is rejected (not in Blazor WebAssembly, where `AesGcm.IsSupported` is false).

using System.Security.Cryptography;
using System.Text;

var key = RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(32);                    // from a vault or SecureStorage, never code
const string Address = "221B Baker Street, London";
var first = Seal(key, Address, userId: "u-42");
Console.WriteLine($"same text, same ciphertext? {first.SequenceEqual(Seal(key, Address, "u-42"))}");
Console.WriteLine(Open(key, first, userId: "u-42"));

try { Open(key, first, userId: "u-7"); }                              // bound to its owner by associated data
catch (AuthenticationTagMismatchException) { Console.WriteLine("another user's record: rejected"); }

var flipped = first.ToArray();
flipped[^1] ^= 1;
try { Open(key, flipped, userId: "u-42"); }
catch (AuthenticationTagMismatchException) { Console.WriteLine("one flipped bit: rejected"); }

try { Open(key, first[..20], userId: "u-42"); }                       // shorter than nonce + tag
catch (AuthenticationTagMismatchException) { Console.WriteLine("a truncated record: rejected"); }

static byte[] Seal(byte[] key, string plaintext, string userId)
{
    var nonce = RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(AesGcm.NonceByteSizes.MaxSize);       // 12 bytes, never reused
    var data = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(plaintext);
    var (cipher, tag) = (new byte[data.Length], new byte[AesGcm.TagByteSizes.MaxSize]);
    using var aes = new AesGcm(key, tag.Length);
    aes.Encrypt(nonce, data, cipher, tag, Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(userId));
    return [.. nonce, .. tag, .. cipher];                                            // stored together
}

static string Open(byte[] key, byte[] box, string userId)
{
    if (box.Length < 28) throw new AuthenticationTagMismatchException();             // 12 nonce + 16 tag
    var plain = new byte[box.Length - 28];
    using var aes = new AesGcm(key, tagSizeInBytes: 16);
    aes.Decrypt(box[..12], box[28..], box[12..28], plain, Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(userId));
    return Encoding.UTF8.GetString(plain);                                           // never tampered data
}
Result
same text, same ciphertext? False
221B Baker Street, London
another user's record: rejected
one flipped bit: rejected
a truncated record: rejected

An HMAC-signed webhook, verified without throwing

An HMAC over `timestamp.body` proves a webhook came from whoever holds the secret, and a malformed signature header is a `false`, never an exception.

using System.Buffers;
using System.Security.Cryptography;

var secret = "whsec-test-only"u8.ToArray();
var signed = """1800000000.{"order":"o-1","status":"paid"}"""u8.ToArray();   // "timestamp.body"
var header = Convert.ToHexStringLower(HMACSHA256.HashData(secret, signed));        // the sender's X-Signature

Console.WriteLine($"genuine: {VerifyWebhook(secret, signed, header)}");
Console.WriteLine($"body altered: {VerifyWebhook(secret, [.. signed, (byte)' '], header)}");
Console.WriteLine($"header not hex: {VerifyWebhook(secret, signed, "zz")}");
Console.WriteLine($"header too short: {VerifyWebhook(secret, signed, header[..62])}");

// Also reject a timestamp older than a few minutes, or a captured request can be replayed.
static bool VerifyWebhook(byte[] secret, byte[] body, string signatureHex)
{
    var claimed = new byte[32];
    var status = Convert.FromHexString(signatureHex, claimed, out _, out var written);   // never throws
    return status == OperationStatus.Done && written == 32
        && CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals(HMACSHA256.HashData(secret, body), claimed);
}
Result
genuine: True
body altered: False
header not hex: False
header too short: False

Passwords: PBKDF2 with a salt, parsed defensively, compared in constant time

On the server only, store the algorithm, iteration count, salt and hash together, fail closed on any record that does not parse, and rehash on sign-in when the count goes up (OWASP prefers Argon2id, which .NET lacks, so use PBKDF2 where FIPS matters or ASP.NET Core Identity's `PasswordHasher<TUser>`).

using System.Security.Cryptography;

const string Secret = "correct horse battery staple";
var stored = Passwords.Hash(Secret);
Console.WriteLine($"right password: {Passwords.Verify(Secret, stored, out var rehash)}");
Console.WriteLine($"wrong password: {Passwords.Verify("Correct horse battery staple", stored, out _)}");
Console.WriteLine($"same password, same record: {Passwords.Hash(Secret) == stored}");

var older = Passwords.Hash("hunter2!", iterations: 210_000);             // written by an older release
Console.WriteLine($"older record: {Passwords.Verify("hunter2!", older, out rehash)}, rehash: {rehash}");

// A damaged or forged record never verifies, and never throws.
string[] broken = ["pbkdf2-sha256$600000$AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA==$", "", "pbkdf2-sha1$600000$AA$AA", "x$1$y"];
foreach (var record in broken)
    Console.WriteLine($"[{record}] -> {Passwords.Verify("anything", record, out _)}");

static class Passwords
{
    public const int CurrentIterations = 600_000;                       // OWASP's PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 figure

    public static string Hash(string password, int iterations = CurrentIterations)
    {
        var salt = RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(16);
        var hash = Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2(password, salt, iterations, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, 32);
        return $"pbkdf2-sha256${iterations}${Convert.ToBase64String(salt)}${Convert.ToBase64String(hash)}";
    }

    public static bool Verify(string password, string stored, out bool needsRehash)
    {
        needsRehash = false;
        var parts = stored.Split('$');
        if (parts.Length != 4 || parts[0] != "pbkdf2-sha256") return false;          // the algorithm, checked
        if (!int.TryParse(parts[1], out var rounds) || rounds is < 100_000 or > 10_000_000) return false;
        Span<byte> salt = stackalloc byte[64];
        Span<byte> expected = stackalloc byte[64];
        if (!Convert.TryFromBase64String(parts[2], salt, out var saltLength) || saltLength < 16) return false;
        if (!Convert.TryFromBase64String(parts[3], expected, out var hashLength) || hashLength != 32)
            return false;                                                     // an empty hash lands here
        Span<byte> actual = stackalloc byte[32];
        Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2(password, salt[..saltLength], actual, rounds, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
        var ok = CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals(actual, expected[..hashLength]);   // constant time
        needsRehash = ok && rounds < CurrentIterations;
        return ok;
    }
}
Result
right password: True
wrong password: False
same password, same record: False
older record: True, rehash: True
[pbkdf2-sha256$600000$AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA==$] -> False
[] -> False
[pbkdf2-sha1$600000$AA$AA] -> False
[x$1$y] -> False
Setup
  1. .NET 9 SDK or later (Base64Url is new in .NET 9)
  2. dotnet new console -o Demo, replace Demo/Program.cs with the example, then dotnet run --project Demo

Ran with .NET SDK 9.0.304 (net9.0, C# 13) on 2026-11-16: the output matched the result shown.

SQL: concatenated versus parameterised

Input becomes code when it is pasted into SQL, so send it as a parameter, which EF Core's `FromSql` and LINQ do for you (its analyzer, EF1002, flags `FromSqlRaw` with interpolation).

The input runs as SQL
// email = "x' OR '1'='1" returns every order; "x'; DROP TABLE Orders;--" is worse.
var sql = $"SELECT Id, Total FROM Orders WHERE Email = '{email}'";
using var command = new SqlCommand(sql, connection);
using var reader = await command.ExecuteReaderAsync(ct);

// EF Core: FromSqlRaw takes a plain string, so the value is pasted in first.
var orders = await db.Orders.FromSqlRaw($"SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Email = '{email}'").ToListAsync(ct);
The input stays a value
// A parameter travels beside the statement, never inside it.
using var command = new SqlCommand("SELECT Id, Total FROM Orders WHERE Email = @email", connection);
command.Parameters.Add("@email", SqlDbType.NVarChar, 256).Value = email;
using var reader = await command.ExecuteReaderAsync(ct);

// EF Core: FromSql turns each interpolated value into a DbParameter (LINQ queries do the same).
var orders = await db.Orders.FromSql($"SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Email = {email}").ToListAsync(ct);
Result

The parameterised query and FromSql return only the orders for that exact email; the concatenated ones run whatever the input contains.

Razor: encoded text versus MarkupString and javascript: links

`@value` HTML-encodes everything in Blazor and Razor, so XSS comes back only through `MarkupString` (raw HTML) or an attribute that takes a URL, which needs an `http`/`https` allow-list.

The input runs as script
@* A review body of <img src=x onerror="…"> runs script in every reader's browser. *@
<p>@((MarkupString)review.Body)</p>

@* Encoded, yet a website of javascript:… still runs when clicked. *@
<a href="@review.Website">website</a>
The input stays text
@* @ HTML-encodes text; if markup is a feature, sanitize it with an allow-list library first. *@
<p>@review.Body</p>

<a href="@SafeLink(review.Website)">website</a>

@code {
    // Only http and https links; anything else (javascript:, data:) becomes a dead link.
    static string SafeLink(string url) =>
        Uri.TryCreate(url, UriKind.Absolute, out var uri) && uri.Scheme is "https" or "http"
            ? uri.ToString()
            : "#";
}
Result

The review renders as visible text, and a javascript: or data: website becomes a dead # link instead of running script.

Transport security and certificate pinning with SocketsHttpHandler

On desktop and server, run the normal chain checks first and then pin the public key, with a backup pin, never returning `true` blindly (Blazor WebAssembly cannot pin, and MAUI pins in Android's Network Security Config `<pin-set>` or iOS's `NSPinnedDomains`).

using System.Net.Security;
using System.Security.Cryptography;
using System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates;

using var ours = SelfSigned("api.shop.example");
using var impostor = SelfSigned("api.shop.example");                // valid for our name, someone else's key
string[] pins = [SpkiSha256(ours), "backup-pin-of-a-key-kept-offline="];

// Desktop and server apps (SocketsHttpHandler). On MAUI Android/iOS pin in the platform config instead.
var handler = new SocketsHttpHandler();
handler.SslOptions.RemoteCertificateValidationCallback = (_, certificate, _, errors) =>
    errors == SslPolicyErrors.None                                  // the normal checks first: chain, name
    && certificate is X509Certificate2 leaf && pins.Contains(SpkiSha256(leaf));
using var http = new HttpClient(handler);                           // every TLS handshake now checks the pin

// No TLS connection is made here: the callback is called directly with the errors a handshake would report.
// A real handshake would flag these self-signed certificates as RemoteCertificateChainErrors (so: false).
var check = handler.SslOptions.RemoteCertificateValidationCallback;
Console.WriteLine($"our key, valid chain: {check(http, ours, null, SslPolicyErrors.None)}");
Console.WriteLine($"another key, valid chain: {check(http, impostor, null, SslPolicyErrors.None)}");
var wrongName = SslPolicyErrors.RemoteCertificateNameMismatch;
Console.WriteLine($"our key, wrong host name: {check(http, ours, null, wrongName)}");

// Pin the key (SubjectPublicKeyInfo), not the certificate: a renewal with the same key keeps working.
static string SpkiSha256(X509Certificate2 cert) =>
    Convert.ToBase64String(SHA256.HashData(cert.PublicKey.ExportSubjectPublicKeyInfo()));

static X509Certificate2 SelfSigned(string host)
{
    using var key = ECDsa.Create(ECCurve.NamedCurves.nistP256);
    var request = new CertificateRequest($"CN={host}", key, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
    var now = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow;
    return request.CreateSelfSigned(now.AddMinutes(-5), now.AddDays(1));
}
Result
our key, valid chain: True
another key, valid chain: False
our key, wrong host name: False

Security and privacy rules

The ones reviewers and auditors ask about first.

  • A RemoteCertificateValidationCallback (or ServerCertificateCustomValidationCallback) that returns true: it turns HTTPS into plain text for anyone on the network. Fix the certificate instead.
  • Reusing an AES-GCM nonce with the same key: it leaks the XOR of both plaintexts and lets an attacker forge tags. Generate it with RandomNumberGenerator every time, and rotate the key long before 2^32 messages, the limit for random 96-bit nonces (NIST SP 800-38D).
  • System.Random, MD5, SHA-1 or a plain SHA-256 for anything secret: tokens and salts come from RandomNumberGenerator, passwords from a slow KDF. SHA256.HashData only fingerprints (a file, a cache key).
  • Comparing secrets, MACs or hashes with == or SequenceEqual: use CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals.
  • A client secret in a MAUI, WPF, WinUI or Blazor WebAssembly app: it can be extracted. Public clients use PKCE; secrets stay on a server.
  • Process.Start("convert", $"{input} out.png"): the string is split into arguments by the receiving program, so input can add flags. Use ProcessStartInfo.ArgumentList.Add(input) and never a shell.
  • Path.Combine(uploads, userFileName) alone: ../../appsettings.json or an absolute path escapes the folder. Take Path.GetFileName, or check that Path.GetFullPath(combined) still starts with the full root plus a separator.
  • Data minimisation: collect only what a feature needs, keep it only as long as it needs it, and delete it on account deletion — including backups and analytics.
  • Consent before analytics, crash reports with user data, location or contacts; the app works without it, and the choice can be changed in settings.
  • Never log passwords, tokens, keys, full card or ID numbers, or request bodies; log opaque ids through [LoggerMessage] templates and redact query strings and Authorization headers — a structured template still does not escape a newline inside a user's value.
  • Biometrics unlock a key on the device and never leave it. Passkeys replace passwords server-side: ASP.NET Core Identity supports them from .NET 10.
  • Validate every input at the boundary (type, length, range, allow-list) even when a client already did: the client is not yours once it ships.

Naming controls, images and headings

Give every control and meaningful image a name — icon-only buttons most of all — but never a `Description` on a `Label`, which would hide its own text.

<!-- .NET MAUI -->
<Label Text="Order A-1042" SemanticProperties.HeadingLevel="Level1" />
<ImageButton Source="trash.png" Command="{Binding DeleteCommand}"
             SemanticProperties.Description="Delete order"
             SemanticProperties.Hint="Removes the order from your history" />
<Label x:Name="EmailLabel" Text="Email for receipts" />
<!-- on Android a Description on an Entry breaks TalkBack editing: use Hint or Placeholder -->
<Entry Text="{Binding Email}" Keyboard="Email"
       SemanticProperties.Hint="{Binding x:DataType='Label', Source={x:Reference EmailLabel}, Path=Text}" />
<Image Source="confetti.png" AutomationProperties.ExcludedWithChildren="True" />   <!-- decoration -->

<!-- WPF / WinUI -->
<TextBlock Text="Order A-1042" AutomationProperties.HeadingLevel="Level1" />
<Button Command="{Binding DeleteCommand}" ToolTipService.ToolTip="Delete order"
        AutomationProperties.Name="Delete order"
        AutomationProperties.HelpText="Removes the order from your history">
    <Image Source="trash.png" />
</Button>
<TextBlock x:Name="EmailLabel" Text="Email for receipts" />
<TextBox Text="{Binding Email}" AutomationProperties.LabeledBy="{Binding ElementName=EmailLabel}" />

@* Blazor: native elements carry role and name; ARIA only where HTML has nothing *@
<h1>Order A-1042</h1>
<button type="button" @onclick="DeleteAsync" aria-label="Delete order">
    <img src="trash.svg" alt="" />
</button>
<label for="email">Email for receipts</label>
<input id="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" @bind="Email" />
<img src="confetti.svg" alt="" />
Result

TalkBack, VoiceOver and Narrator read "Order A-1042, heading", "Delete order, button" with its hint, and "Email for receipts, edit". The confetti image is skipped. Accessibility Insights reports no unnamed controls.

Setup

  2. Put each fragment in the page or component of its stack

Excerpt, not compiled or run here: it needs a .NET MAUI, WPF or WinUI app, or a Blazor component; checked against the MAUI semantic-properties and WPF AutomationProperties reference.

Sources: Semantic properties — .NET MAUI · AutomationProperties class — WPF · Basic accessibility information — Windows apps

What the screen reader says, built in the view model

When a row is drawn with symbols, colour and compact numbers, give its container one spoken summary from the view model, which on iOS also makes the row a single stop.

using System.Globalization;

var culture = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("en-US");
OrderRow[] rows =
[
    new("A-1042", Items: 3, Total: 25.50m, Status: OrderStatus.Shipped, Rating: 4.2, Reviews: 1203),
    new("A-1043", Items: 1, Total: 9.99m, Status: OrderStatus.PaymentFailed, Rating: 5, Reviews: 1),
];
foreach (var row in rows)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"shown:  {row.Visual(culture)}");
    Console.WriteLine($"spoken: {row.Spoken(culture)}");
}

enum OrderStatus { Shipped, PaymentFailed }

// a view model for one list row: the view binds the row container's
// SemanticProperties.Description (MAUI) or AutomationProperties.Name (WPF/WinUI) to Spoken
record OrderRow(string Number, int Items, decimal Total, OrderStatus Status, double Rating, int Reviews)
{
    // what sighted users see: symbols, a coloured dot, compact numbers
    public string Visual(CultureInfo c) => string.Create(c,
        $"#{Number} · {Items}× · {Total:C} · {Stars} ({Reviews:N0}) · {Dot}");

    // what a screen reader says: words instead of symbols, and the state the colour carries.
    // English only: a localized app picks plural forms per language (see the Localization sheet)
    public string Spoken(CultureInfo c) => string.Create(c,
        $"Order {Number}, {Items} {(Items == 1 ? "item" : "items")}, {Total:C}, "
        + $"rated {Rating:0.#} out of 5 from {Reviews:N0} {(Reviews == 1 ? "review" : "reviews")}, "
        + $"{StatusText}");

    private string Stars => new('★', (int)Math.Round(Rating));

    private string Dot => Status == OrderStatus.Shipped ? "✓" : "●";

    private string StatusText => Status switch
    {
        OrderStatus.Shipped => "shipped",
        OrderStatus.PaymentFailed => "payment failed, action needed",
        _ => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(Status)),
    };
}
Result
shown:  #A-1042 · 3× · $25.50 · ★★★★ (1,203) · ✓
spoken: Order A-1042, 3 items, $25.50, rated 4.2 out of 5 from 1,203 reviews, shipped
shown:  #A-1043 · 1× · $9.99 · ★★★★★ (1) · ●
spoken: Order A-1043, 1 item, $9.99, rated 5 out of 5 from 1 review, payment failed, action needed
Setup
  1. .NET 9 SDK or later
  2. dotnet new console -o Demo, replace Demo/Program.cs with the example, then dotnet run --project Demo (in the app, bind the row's SemanticProperties.Description to Spoken)

Focus order and moving focus

Write the markup in reading order so the default focus order follows it, and move focus only on purpose — after navigation, a dialog, an error or a user action.

<!-- .NET MAUI has no TabIndex: focus, Tab and reading order follow the XAML (and Grid) order -->
<Grid ColumnDefinitions="*,Auto">
    <SearchBar x:Name="SearchEntry" Placeholder="Search orders" />
    <Button x:Name="FiltersButton" Grid.Column="1" Text="Filters" />
</Grid>
<Label x:Name="ErrorLabel" IsVisible="{Binding HasError}" Text="{Binding Error}" />

<!-- only when the markup cannot follow the reading order (a reversed layout, a template you do not own):
     SemanticOrderView (CommunityToolkit.Maui) sets the TalkBack and VoiceOver order on Android, iOS and
     Mac Catalyst, and the Tab order on Windows -->
<toolkit:SemanticOrderView x:Name="PaymentRow">
    <FlexLayout Direction="RowReverse">
        <Button x:Name="PayButton" Text="Pay" />
        <Entry x:Name="CouponEntry" Placeholder="Coupon code" />
    </FlexLayout>
</toolkit:SemanticOrderView>

// code-behind: the coupon field before Pay, as on screen; after a failed search, read the error
PaymentRow.ViewOrder = [CouponEntry, PayButton];
ErrorLabel.SetSemanticFocus();

@* Blazor: Routes.razor moves focus to each new page's h1, so a component never focuses on first render *@
<FocusOnNavigate RouteData="routeData" Selector="h1" />

@* move focus only in response to the user: after "Clear filters", back to the search box *@
<input @ref="searchBox" type="search" aria-label="Search orders" @bind="query" />
<button type="button" @onclick="ClearAsync">Clear filters</button>
@code {
    private ElementReference searchBox;
    private string query = "";
    private async Task ClearAsync()
    {
        query = "";
        await searchBox.FocusAsync();
    }
}
Result

Tab and the screen reader go search box → Filters, as written. In the reversed payment row, TalkBack, VoiceOver and the Windows Tab key reach the coupon field before Pay, as on screen. A failed search moves the screen reader to the error. A Blazor navigation lands on the new page's heading, and Clear filters returns focus to the search box.

Keyboard operation in WPF and WinUI — access keys, default buttons, accelerators

Give every action a keyboard path: an access key for each labelled field and command, Enter and Esc for a dialog's buttons, and accelerators for frequent commands.

<!-- WPF: _ marks the access key (Alt+C focuses the box via Target); Enter and Esc map to the buttons;
     TabNavigation="Cycle" keeps Tab inside the dialog and wraps around -->
<StackPanel KeyboardNavigation.TabNavigation="Cycle">
    <Label Content="_Customer" Target="{Binding ElementName=CustomerBox}" />
    <TextBox x:Name="CustomerBox" />
    <Button Content="_Save" IsDefault="True" Command="{Binding SaveCommand}" />
    <Button Content="Cancel" IsCancel="True" />
</StackPanel>

<!-- WinUI: access keys show when Alt is pressed; accelerators work without showing anything -->
<StackPanel TabFocusNavigation="Cycle">
    <TextBox x:Name="CustomerBox" Header="Customer" AccessKey="C" />
    <Button Content="Save" AccessKey="S" Command="{x:Bind ViewModel.SaveCommand}">
        <Button.KeyboardAccelerators>
            <KeyboardAccelerator Modifiers="Control" Key="S" />
        </Button.KeyboardAccelerators>
    </Button>
</StackPanel>
Result

Without a mouse: Alt+C reaches the customer box, Alt+S or Ctrl+S saves, Enter and Esc press Save and Cancel in WPF, and Tab cycles inside the dialog instead of leaving it.

Announce changes that happen off focus

Announce changes the user is not focused on — a result count, a confirmation, a failed payment — politely, and interrupt only for errors.

// .NET MAUI (Microsoft.Maui.Accessibility): spoken only while a screen reader is on.
// Call it once the results arrive, not on every keystroke (debounce search-as-you-type)
ResultsLabel.Text = $"{orders.Count} orders";
SemanticScreenReader.Default.Announce($"{orders.Count} orders match \"{query}\"");

<!-- WPF / WinUI: mark the region live once -->
<TextBlock x:Name="StatusText" AutomationProperties.LiveSetting="Polite" />

// WPF (System.Windows.Automation.Peers): change the text, then raise the event
StatusText.Text = "Order A-1042 paid";
UIElementAutomationPeer.CreatePeerForElement(StatusText)
    .RaiseAutomationEvent(AutomationEvents.LiveRegionChanged);

// WinUI (Microsoft.UI.Xaml.Automation.Peers): the same event
FrameworkElementAutomationPeer.FromElement(StatusText)?
    .RaiseAutomationEvent(AutomationEvents.LiveRegionChanged);

@* Blazor: the live region is in the page from the start; only its text changes *@
<div role="status" aria-live="polite" class="visually-hidden">@statusMessage</div>
<div role="alert">@paymentError</div>
@code {
    private string statusMessage = "";
    private string? paymentError;
    private async Task PayAsync()
    {
        (statusMessage, paymentError) = ("", null);
        StateHasChanged();                    // empty the region first, so paying twice is announced twice
        await Task.Yield();
        try
        {
            await Payments.ChargeAsync(order);
            statusMessage = $"Order {order.Number} paid";
        }
        catch (PaymentDeclinedException declined) { paymentError = declined.Message; }
    }
}
Result

Once the results arrive the screen reader says: 12 orders match "cocoa". Paying says "Order A-1042 paid" without moving focus, and says it again when paying twice. A payment error is read at once because role="alert" is assertive.

Text scaling and reduced motion

Let text grow and layouts follow it, and read the reduce-motion setting before animating — MAUI has no cross-platform API for it, so ask each platform.

<!-- .NET MAUI: FontAutoScalingEnabled is true by default; rows size to their text -->
<Grid RowDefinitions="Auto,Auto" ColumnDefinitions="*,Auto">
    <Label Text="{Binding Customer}" LineBreakMode="WordWrap" />
    <Label Grid.Column="1" Text="{Binding Total, StringFormat='{0:C}'}" />
</Grid>

// .NET MAUI has no cross-platform reduce-motion setting: ask each platform
public static bool PrefersReducedMotion()
{
#if IOS || MACCATALYST
    return UIKit.UIAccessibility.IsReduceMotionEnabled;
#elif ANDROID
    var resolver = Android.App.Application.Context.ContentResolver;
    var scale = Android.Provider.Settings.Global.GetFloat(
        resolver, Android.Provider.Settings.Global.AnimatorDurationScale, 1f);
    return scale == 0f;                                       // "Remove animations" is on
#elif WINDOWS
    return !new Windows.UI.ViewManagement.UISettings().AnimationsEnabled;
#else
    return false;
#endif
}

// WPF: SystemParameters.ClientAreaAnimation is false when Windows animations are turned off

/* Blazor CSS: rem units follow the browser's text size; animate only when the user allows it */
.order-total { font-size: 1.125rem; }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
    * { animation: none !important; transition: none !important; }
}
Result

At the largest text size the customer name wraps instead of being cut off, and with reduce motion (or Remove animations) on, the app and the page skip their transitions.

High contrast — Windows contrast themes and forced colours

In a Windows contrast theme, take every colour from the system palette in its documented foreground/background pair, never from your brand palette.

<!-- WinUI App.xaml: in HighContrast, use the system colours the user picked, in their documented pairs -->
<ResourceDictionary.ThemeDictionaries>
    <ResourceDictionary x:Key="Default">
        <SolidColorBrush x:Key="BadgeBrush" Color="#F59E0B" />
        <SolidColorBrush x:Key="BadgeTextBrush" Color="#111827" />
        <SolidColorBrush x:Key="BadgeBorderBrush" Color="Transparent" />
    </ResourceDictionary>
    <ResourceDictionary x:Key="HighContrast">
        <SolidColorBrush x:Key="BadgeBrush" Color="{ThemeResource SystemColorWindowColor}" />
        <SolidColorBrush x:Key="BadgeTextBrush" Color="{ThemeResource SystemColorWindowTextColor}" />
        <SolidColorBrush x:Key="BadgeBorderBrush" Color="{ThemeResource SystemColorWindowTextColor}" />
    </ResourceDictionary>
</ResourceDictionary.ThemeDictionaries>

<!-- WinUI: {ThemeResource} re-resolves when the user switches into or between contrast themes -->
<Border Background="{ThemeResource BadgeBrush}" BorderBrush="{ThemeResource BadgeBorderBrush}"
        BorderThickness="1" CornerRadius="4" Padding="6,2">
    <TextBlock Text="Overdue" Foreground="{ThemeResource BadgeTextBrush}" />
</Border>

<!-- WPF: SystemColors brushes follow the contrast theme (SystemParameters.HighContrast in code) -->
<Border BorderBrush="{DynamicResource {x:Static SystemColors.WindowTextBrushKey}}" BorderThickness="1"
        Background="{DynamicResource {x:Static SystemColors.WindowBrushKey}}">
    <TextBlock Text="Overdue" Foreground="{DynamicResource {x:Static SystemColors.WindowTextBrushKey}}" />
</Border>

/* Blazor CSS: under Windows contrast themes the browser forces system colours; keep the edge */
@media (forced-colors: active) {
    .badge { border: 1px solid CanvasText; }
}
Result

In every built-in contrast theme (Aquatic, Desert, Dusk, Night sky) the badge shows the user's window text on the window background with a visible border, instead of the brand's dark text on amber.

Setup
  1. A WinUI 3 or WPF app on Windows, or a Blazor app's stylesheet
  2. Turn a contrast theme on with Left Alt + Left Shift + Print Screen, or in Settings > Accessibility > Contrast themes

Check contrast in a test

Compute the WCAG contrast ratio for every foreground/background token pair of the theme, and in a test project assert that none fails, so a palette change cannot ship unreadable text.

using System.Globalization;

(string Use, string Foreground, string Background, bool LargeText)[] pairs =      // the theme's token pairs
[
    ("body text", "#1F2937", "#FFFFFF", false),
    ("secondary text", "#9CA3AF", "#FFFFFF", false),
    ("button label", "#FFFFFF", "#2563EB", false),
    ("price badge", "#FFFFFF", "#F59E0B", true),
    ("dark theme text", "#E5E7EB", "#111827", false),
];

var failures = 0;           // in a test project: Assert.True(passed, use), one [Theory] row per pair
foreach (var (use, foreground, background, largeText) in pairs)
{
    var ratio = Contrast.Ratio(Contrast.Parse(foreground), Contrast.Parse(background));
    var required = largeText ? 3.0 : 4.5;          // WCAG 2.2 AA: 4.5:1 text, 3:1 large text and UI parts
    var passed = ratio >= required;
    if (!passed) failures++;
    var line = FormattableString.Invariant($"{use,-16} {ratio,5:F2}:1  needs {required:F1}");
    Console.WriteLine($"{line}  {(passed ? "pass" : "FAIL")}");
}
Console.WriteLine($"{failures} of {pairs.Length} pairs fail");

static class Contrast
{
    public static (byte R, byte G, byte B) Parse(string hex) => (Hex(hex, 1), Hex(hex, 3), Hex(hex, 5));

    public static double Ratio((byte, byte, byte) a, (byte, byte, byte) b)
    {
        var (lighter, darker) = (Math.Max(Luminance(a), Luminance(b)), Math.Min(Luminance(a), Luminance(b)));
        return (lighter + 0.05) / (darker + 0.05);
    }

    // relative luminance from sRGB, as defined by WCAG
    private static double Luminance((byte R, byte G, byte B) c) =>
        0.2126 * Linear(c.R) + 0.7152 * Linear(c.G) + 0.0722 * Linear(c.B);

    private static double Linear(byte channel)
    {
        var c = channel / 255.0;
        return c <= 0.04045 ? c / 12.92 : Math.Pow((c + 0.055) / 1.055, 2.4);
    }

    private static byte Hex(string hex, int at) =>
        byte.Parse(hex.AsSpan(at, 2), NumberStyles.HexNumber, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
}
Result
body text        14.68:1  needs 4.5  pass
secondary text    2.54:1  needs 4.5  FAIL
button label      5.17:1  needs 4.5  pass
price badge       2.15:1  needs 3.0  FAIL
dark theme text  14.33:1  needs 4.5  pass
2 of 5 pairs fail
Setup
  1. .NET 9 SDK or later
  2. dotnet new console -o Demo, replace Demo/Program.cs with the example, then dotnet run --project Demo (in the app, bind the row's SemanticProperties.Description to Spoken)

Sources: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum) — WCAG · Relative luminance — WCAG 2.2 definition

A custom control made accessible — AutomationPeer in outline

A control drawn from scratch is invisible to UI Automation until a peer gives its role, name and value and lets assistive technology change it (WPF here; WinUI overrides `GetPatternCore`).

using System.Windows;
using System.Windows.Automation;
using System.Windows.Automation.Peers;
using System.Windows.Automation.Provider;
using System.Windows.Controls;

public class StarRating : Control                    // a 1–5 star picker drawn by its template
{
    public static readonly DependencyProperty ValueProperty = DependencyProperty.Register(
        nameof(Value), typeof(double), typeof(StarRating), new PropertyMetadata(1.0, OnValueChanged));
    public double Value { get => (double)GetValue(ValueProperty); set => SetValue(ValueProperty, value); }

    protected override AutomationPeer OnCreateAutomationPeer() => new StarRatingAutomationPeer(this);

    private static void OnValueChanged(DependencyObject d, DependencyPropertyChangedEventArgs e)
    {
        // tell a listening screen reader the value moved
        if (UIElementAutomationPeer.FromElement((StarRating)d) is StarRatingAutomationPeer peer)
            peer.RaisePropertyChangedEvent(
                RangeValuePatternIdentifiers.ValueProperty, e.OldValue, e.NewValue);
    }
}

public class StarRatingAutomationPeer(StarRating owner)
    : FrameworkElementAutomationPeer(owner), IRangeValueProvider
{
    protected override string GetClassNameCore() => nameof(StarRating);
    protected override AutomationControlType GetAutomationControlTypeCore() => AutomationControlType.Slider;
    // WinUI: override GetPatternCore instead
    public override object GetPattern(PatternInterface pattern) =>
        pattern == PatternInterface.RangeValue ? this : base.GetPattern(pattern);

    private StarRating Rating => (StarRating)Owner;
    public double Value => Rating.Value;
    public double Minimum => 1;
    public double Maximum => 5;
    public double SmallChange => 1;
    public double LargeChange => 1;
    public bool IsReadOnly => !Rating.IsEnabled;
    public void SetValue(double value) => Rating.Value = Math.Clamp(value, Minimum, Maximum);
}
Result

Narrator reads "Rating, slider, 4" (the name comes from AutomationProperties.Name on the instance). Accessibility Insights shows the RangeValue pattern, and changing the value from the pattern moves the stars.

Setup
  1. A WPF app on Windows (dotnet new wpf); the control also needs focus and arrow-key handling (Focusable, OnKeyDown)

Excerpt, not compiled or run here: it needs a WPF app on Windows (WindowsDesktop runtime).

An automated audit in the test suite — axe with Playwright for Blazor

Run axe on every page in end-to-end tests and Accessibility Insights FastPass on Windows and Android builds, then test by ear with the platform's screen reader, which no tool replaces.

using Deque.AxeCore.Commons;
using Deque.AxeCore.Playwright;
using Microsoft.Playwright;
using Microsoft.Playwright.NUnit;

public class AccessibilityTests : PageTest
{
    public override BrowserNewContextOptions ContextOptions() => new()
    {
        BaseURL = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("BASE_URL") ?? "https://localhost:7043",
        IgnoreHTTPSErrors = true,                          // the dev certificate is not trusted on CI runners
    };

    [TestCase("/orders")]
    [TestCase("/orders/A-1042")]
    [TestCase("/checkout")]
    public async Task PageHasNoWcagAaViolations(string path)
    {
        await Page.GotoAsync(path);
        await Expect(Page.GetByRole(AriaRole.Heading, new() { Level = 1 })).ToBeVisibleAsync();

        // each axe rule carries the tag of the one WCAG version and level that introduced it
        var options = new AxeRunOptions
        {
            RunOnly = new RunOnlyOptions
            {
                Type = "tag",
                Values = ["wcag2a", "wcag2aa", "wcag21a", "wcag21aa", "wcag22aa"],
            },
        };
        AxeResult result = await Page.RunAxe(options);

        Assert.That(result.Violations.Select(v => $"{v.Id}: {v.Help}"), Is.Empty);
    }
}
Result

dotnet test fails with the rule id and help text, for example color-contrast: Elements must meet minimum color contrast ratio thresholds, for each violation on a page. Clean pages pass.

Setup
  1. An NUnit test project (dotnet new nunit) with Microsoft.Playwright.NUnit and Deque.AxeCore.Playwright; install browsers with pwsh bin/Debug/net9.0/playwright.ps1 install
  2. The Blazor app running at the base URL (or started by the test's fixture)

Test it, and the pitfalls

Automated audits catch only part of the problems — the rest needs a person with a screen reader.

  • Test by ear on every platform you ship: TalkBack (Android), VoiceOver (iOS, macOS), Narrator (Windows, Win+Ctrl+Enter). Navigate the whole flow without looking.
  • Run Accessibility Insights for Windows FastPass on WPF, WinUI and MAUI Windows builds; it lists unnamed controls, missing patterns and contrast failures.
  • Prefer semantic properties in MAUI. AutomationProperties.Name, HelpText and LabeledBy are documented as deprecated there since .NET 8, but give no compiler warning.
  • Localize descriptions and hints like any other UI text, and keep AutomationId stable and untranslated for tests.
  • Colour as the only signal (a red dot for "failed"), fixed HeightRequest on text, and FontAutoScalingEnabled="False" on body text.
  • Positive tabindex in Blazor, or markup out of reading order in MAUI (which has no TabIndex). Fix the order of the markup; use SemanticOrderView only where the markup order cannot change.
  • A Description on a MAUI Label (it replaces the spoken text) or on a container whose children must stay reachable on iOS.
  • Target sizes: at least 44×44 points on iOS and 48×48 dp on Android for anything tappable. WCAG 2.2 sets a 24×24 CSS-pixel minimum.

Localization & Globalization

CurrentCulture, CurrentUICulture or invariant. Translated .resx resources with placeholders, plurals you select yourself, and dates, money, sorting and time zones per culture. Plus right-to-left, pseudo-localization and testing a culture in .NET MAUI, WPF, WinUI and Blazor.

CurrentCulture, CurrentUICulture, InvariantCulture

Each thread has two cultures that flow across `await` — one for formatting, one for translated text — and anything a machine reads back uses neither.

CultureDecidesUse it forNever for
CultureInfo.CurrentCulturenumber, date and currency formats; parsing; culture-sensitive compare and casingvalues shown to or typed by the userfiles, JSON, databases, logs, URLs
CultureInfo.CurrentUICulturewhich .resx satellite ResourceManager and IStringLocalizer loadthe language of the UI textformatting numbers (a Spanish UI can still use US dates)
CultureInfo.InvariantCulturea fixed, culture-independent format (English-like, never changes)persisted and exchanged data: ToString(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture), the "O" date formattext a person reads
StringComparison.Ordinalnot a culture: compares UTF-16 valueskeys, identifiers, file paths, protocol tokenssorting names for people
who sets themMAUI and WPF/WinUI: the OS settings at startup. ASP.NET Core and Blazor Server: UseRequestLocalization per request. Blazor WebAssembly: the browser, or CultureInfo.DefaultThreadCurrentCulture before the app runsset both early; DefaultThreadCurrent* for new threadschanging them mid-render (MAUI documents this as inconsistent across platforms)

.resx in a XAML app: resources, satellite assemblies, platform declarations

Keep one neutral `.resx` and one per language, which the build turns into satellite assemblies that lookups choose by `CurrentUICulture`.

<!-- AppResources.resx (AppResources.es.resx holds the same names, translated) -->
<data name="OrderShipped" xml:space="preserve">
  <value>Order {0} shipped to {1} on {2:d}.</value>
  <comment>{0} order number, {1} customer name, {2} ship date</comment>
</data>

// C#: the generated class and ResourceManager both read CurrentUICulture.
// Satellite assemblies are built to bin/<config>/<tfm>/es/Shop.resources.dll
var line = string.Format(CultureInfo.CurrentCulture, AppResources.OrderShipped,
    order.Number, order.Customer, order.ShippedOn);
var manager = new ResourceManager("Shop.Resources.Strings.AppResources", typeof(AppResources).Assembly);
var spanish = manager.GetString("OrderShipped", CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("es-MX")); // es-MX → es → neutral

<!-- .NET MAUI page (WPF: xmlns:props="clr-namespace:Shop.Properties" and the same x:Static) -->
<ContentPage xmlns:strings="clr-namespace:Shop.Resources.Strings" ...>
    <Label Text="{x:Static strings:AppResources.OrdersTitle}" />
</ContentPage>

<!-- Platforms/iOS/Info.plist (and MacCatalyst): without this the app stays in English -->
<key>CFBundleLocalizations</key>
<array>
    <string>en</string>
    <string>es</string>
</array>
<key>CFBundleDevelopmentRegion</key>
<string>en</string>

<!-- Platforms/Windows/Package.appxmanifest -->
<Resources>
    <Resource Language="en-US" />
    <Resource Language="es-ES" />
</Resources>

<!-- MAUI follows the device's layout direction; to override it set FlowDirection="RightToLeft"
     on the Window, page or root layout. WPF and WinUI: FlowDirection on the root element -->
Result

An es-MX device sees El pedido 1042 se envió a Ada el 08/03/2026. (es-ES formats the date 8/3/2026), a language without a translation falls back to the neutral English text, and an Arabic or Hebrew device lays the page out right to left.

Setup
  1. A .NET MAUI, WPF or WinUI app
  2. MAUI: add Resources/Strings/AppResources.resx (Access Modifier Public), translated copies with No code generation, and <NeutralLanguage>en-US</NeutralLanguage> in the project file
  3. MAUI on iOS and Mac Catalyst: list the languages under CFBundleLocalizations in each Info.plist; on Windows: replace <Resource Language="x-generate"/> with one <Resource Language="…"/> per language in Package.appxmanifest

Blazor: IStringLocalizer, request cultures, and lang/dir

Give formatting and UI cultures one list holding only the languages you translate, so a page's dates, `lang` and `dir` always match the text it shows.

// Program.cs: one list for both, holding only languages you translate. A neutral culture such as "es"
// formats like its default region (8/3/2026), so a bare Accept-Language: es never gets a US date
string[] cultures = ["en-US", "es", "es-MX", "es-ES"];
builder.Services.AddLocalization();
// …
app.UseRequestLocalization(new RequestLocalizationOptions()
    .SetDefaultCulture("en-US")
    .AddSupportedCultures(cultures)                     // formatting of dates, numbers, money
    .AddSupportedUICultures(cultures));                 // which .resx the text comes from

@* OrderSummary.razor *@
@using Microsoft.Extensions.Localization
@inject IStringLocalizer<OrderSummary> Loc
<h2>@Loc["OrdersTitle"]</h2>
<p>@Loc["OrderShipped", Order.Number, Order.Customer, Order.ShippedOn]</p>

@* App.razor: the document's language and direction follow the UI culture actually shown *@
@using System.Globalization
<html lang="@CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture.Name"
      dir="@(CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture.TextInfo.IsRightToLeft ? "rtl" : "ltr")">
Result

Accept-Language: es gets <html lang="es" dir="ltr"> and El pedido 1042 se envió a Ada el 8/3/2026.; es-MX gets lang="es-MX" and 08/03/2026. An ar-SA request, with no Arabic translation listed, gets <html lang="en-US" dir="ltr"> and English text formatted for en-US, as en-US does.

Placeholders, never concatenation, and the fallback walk

Keep the whole sentence in one resource with numbered placeholders so translators can reorder it, and format it with `string.Format(culture, template, args)`.

using System.Globalization;
using System.Resources;

// stands in for Strings.resx, Strings.es.resx and Strings.ja.resx: one key, a template per language
var resources = new Dictionary<string, Dictionary<string, string>>
{
    [""] = new()
    {
        ["OrderShipped"] = "Order {0} shipped to {1} on {2:d}.",
        ["ItemsInCart"] = "Items in cart: {0:N0}",
    },
    ["es"] = new() { ["OrderShipped"] = "El pedido {0} se envió a {1} el {2:d}." },
    ["ja"] = new()
    {
        ["OrderShipped"] = "注文 {0} は {2:d} に {1} 様へ発送されました。",
        ["ItemsInCart"] = "カート内の商品: {0:N0}",
    },
};

// the ResourceManager's fallback walk: es-MX → es → the neutral resources
string Lookup(string key, CultureInfo uiCulture)
{
    for (var culture = uiCulture; ; culture = culture.Parent)
    {
        if (resources.TryGetValue(culture.Name, out var texts) && texts.TryGetValue(key, out var template))
            return template;
        if (culture.Equals(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture))
            throw new MissingManifestResourceException($"no resource '{key}'");
    }
}

var shippedOn = new DateOnly(2026, 3, 8);
foreach (var name in new[] { "en-US", "es-MX", "ja-JP" })
{
    var culture = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo(name);
    // numbered placeholders let each language reorder the sentence; the culture formats the values
    Console.WriteLine(string.Format(culture, Lookup("OrderShipped", culture), 1042, "Ada", shippedOn));
    Console.WriteLine(string.Format(culture, Lookup("ItemsInCart", culture), 12500));
}
Result
Order 1042 shipped to Ada on 3/8/2026.
Items in cart: 12,500
El pedido 1042 se envió a Ada el 08/03/2026.
Items in cart: 12,500
注文 1042 は 2026/03/08 に Ada 様へ発送されました。
カート内の商品: 12,500

Plurals — select a CLDR category, then the message

.NET has no plural rule engine, so either write CLDR's rules for the languages you ship, as here, or use MessageFormat.NET, whose ICU MessageFormat `plural` and `select` (gender) ship with CLDR pluralizers for every locale.

using System.Globalization;
using static PluralCategory;

// what the translator writes: one message per plural category
var orders = new Dictionary<string, Dictionary<PluralCategory, string>>
{
    ["en"] = new() { [One] = "{0:N0} order", [Other] = "{0:N0} orders" },
    ["fr"] = new() { [One] = "{0:N0} commande", [Many] = "{0:N0} de commandes",
                     [Other] = "{0:N0} commandes" },
    ["ru"] = new() { [One] = "{0:N0} заказ", [Few] = "{0:N0} заказа", [Many] = "{0:N0} заказов" },
};

long[] counts = [0, 1, 2, 5, 21, 22, -21, 1_000_000];
foreach (var (language, messages) in orders)
{
    var phrases = counts.Select(n =>
        string.Format(CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo(language), messages[Plurals.Select(language, n)], n));
    // the no-break spaces French and Russian group digits with, shown as _
    var line = string.Join(" · ", phrases).Replace('\u202F', '_').Replace('\u00A0', '_');
    Console.WriteLine($"{language}: {line}");
}
Console.WriteLine($"pt, no rules written: {Plurals.Select("pt", 1)} {Plurals.Select("pt", 2)}");

enum PluralCategory { Zero, One, Two, Few, Many, Other }       // CLDR's six; Plurals holds its integer rules

static class Plurals
{
    public static PluralCategory Select(string language, long count)
    {
        var n = Math.Abs(count);                                    // CLDR rules use the absolute value
        return language switch
        {
            "en" or "de" => n == 1 ? One : Other,
            "fr" => n is 0 or 1 ? One : Millions(n),                  // "1 000 000 de commandes"
            "es" or "it" or "pt-PT" => n == 1 ? One : Millions(n),
            "ru" when n % 10 == 1 && n % 100 != 11 => One,
            "ru" when n % 10 is >= 2 and <= 4 && n % 100 is < 12 or > 14 => Few,
            "ru" => Many,
            "ja" or "zh" => Other,                                    // no grammatical plural
            _ => n == 1 ? One : Other,              // a fallback, not a rule: a UI formatter must not throw
        };
    }

    private static PluralCategory Millions(long n) => n != 0 && n % 1_000_000 == 0 ? Many : Other;
}
Result
en: 0 orders · 1 order · 2 orders · 5 orders · 21 orders · 22 orders · -21 orders · 1,000,000 orders
fr: 0 commande · 1 commande · 2 commandes · 5 commandes · 21 commandes · 22 commandes · -21 commandes · 1_000_000 de commandes
ru: 0 заказов · 1 заказ · 2 заказа · 5 заказов · 21 заказ · 22 заказа · -21 заказ · 1_000_000 заказов
pt, no rules written: One Other

Dates, numbers, currencies and percentages with a pinned culture

Format with an explicit `CultureInfo` (or `string.Create(culture, $"…")`), which supplies separators, grouping, symbol position and month names — but not units, which go into the translated template.

using System.Globalization;

decimal revenue = 1234567.891m;
var placed = new DateTime(2026, 3, 8, 14, 30, 0);

foreach (var name in new[] { "en-US", "en-GB", "de-DE", "fr-FR", "hi-IN", "it-IT", "pt-BR" })
{
    var culture = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo(name);
    var row = string.Create(culture,
        $"{name} | {revenue:N2} | {revenue:C} | {0.256:P1} | {placed:d} | {placed:MMMM}");
    Console.WriteLine(Visible(row));
}

// times and long dates: the pattern, the words and even the space characters come from the culture
var us = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("en-US");
var german = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("de-DE");
Console.WriteLine(Visible(string.Create(us, $"{placed:t} / {placed:D}")));
Console.WriteLine(Visible(string.Create(german, $"{placed:t} / {placed:D}")));

// a currency is not a culture: a price in euros for a US reader keeps US formatting with a € symbol
var euroForUs = (NumberFormatInfo)us.NumberFormat.Clone();
euroForUs.CurrencySymbol = "€";
Console.WriteLine($"{revenue.ToString("C", euroForUs)} {(-1234.5m).ToString("C", german)}");

// .NET has no unit formatter: put the unit in the translated template, convert with IsMetric
var parcelKg = 2.5;
Console.WriteLine(string.Format(german, "{0:N1} kg", parcelKg));
Console.WriteLine(string.Format(us, "{0:N1} lb", parcelKg * 2.20462));

// RegionInfo answers country questions: ISO currency code, metric or not
var japan = new RegionInfo("JP");
Console.WriteLine($"{japan.EnglishName} {japan.ISOCurrencySymbol} metric={japan.IsMetric}");
Console.WriteLine($"metric(US)={new RegionInfo("US").IsMetric}");

// no-break (U+00A0) and narrow no-break (U+202F) spaces shown as ·
static string Visible(string text) => text.Replace('\u00A0', '·').Replace('\u202F', '·');
Result
en-US | 1,234,567.89 | $1,234,567.89 | 25.6% | 3/8/2026 | March
en-GB | 1,234,567.89 | £1,234,567.89 | 25.6% | 08/03/2026 | March
de-DE | 1.234.567,89 | 1.234.567,89 € | 25,6 % | 08.03.2026 | März
fr-FR | 1·234·567,89 | 1·234·567,89 € | 25,6 % | 08/03/2026 | mars

Parse what users type in their culture; persist invariant

Read what users type with their culture and `TryParse` (fixed formats with `TryParseExact`), and write and read stored data with `InvariantCulture`, or the app breaks on the first German machine.

using System.Globalization;

var us = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("en-US");
var german = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("de-DE");
var british = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("en-GB");
var invariant = CultureInfo.InvariantCulture;

// what the user typed, read in the user's culture
foreach (var typed in new[] { "1.234,56", "1,234", "12,5 €" })
    Console.WriteLine($"{typed,-9} de-DE: {Read(typed, german),-8} en-US: {Read(typed, us)}");
var price = decimal.Parse("12,5 €", NumberStyles.Currency, german);   // Currency accepts the symbol
Console.WriteLine(price.ToString(invariant));

// the same digits are two different days
var usDate = DateOnly.Parse("03/08/2026", us);
var ukDate = DateOnly.Parse("03/08/2026", british);
Console.WriteLine($"{usDate.ToString("yyyy-MM-dd", invariant)} {ukDate.ToString("yyyy-MM-dd", invariant)}");
// a fixed format from a form field: exact parsing, no guessing
Console.WriteLine(DateOnly.TryParseExact("2026-02-30", "yyyy-MM-dd", invariant, DateTimeStyles.None, out _));

// persisted data — files, databases, JSON, logs — is written and read with the invariant culture
var total = 1234.5m;
var placed = new DateTimeOffset(2026, 3, 8, 14, 30, 0, TimeSpan.FromHours(1));
var line = string.Join(";", total.ToString(invariant), placed.ToString("O", invariant));
Console.WriteLine(line);

var fields = line.Split(';');
CultureInfo.CurrentCulture = german;                 // a German machine reads the same file back correctly
var totalBack = decimal.Parse(fields[0], invariant);
var placedBack = DateTimeOffset.Parse(fields[1], invariant);
Console.WriteLine($"{totalBack == total} {placedBack == placed}");
Console.WriteLine($"{decimal.Parse(fields[0])} — without a culture, \"1234.5\" is misread under de-DE");

static string Read(string typed, CultureInfo culture) =>
    decimal.TryParse(typed, NumberStyles.Number, culture, out var value)
        ? value.ToString(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)
        : "invalid";

Sorting, searching and the Turkish-i problem

Sort lists for people with `StringComparer.Create(culture, ignoreCase)` and search with `CompareInfo` options, but keep every machine-facing comparison ordinal, because the current culture can be Turkish.

using System.Globalization;

string[] cities = ["Zürich", "Ängelholm", "Århus", "Zaragoza", "Ørebro", "Istanbul", "Aachen", "Łódź"];
// Swedish sorts å, ä, ö after z; Danish also reads "aa" as å
foreach (var name in new[] { "en-US", "sv-SE", "da-DK" })
{
    var comparer = StringComparer.Create(CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo(name), ignoreCase: true);
    Console.WriteLine($"{name}: {string.Join(", ", cities.Order(comparer))}");
}

// search-as-you-type: culture-aware prefix match that ignores case and accents
var compare = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("pl-PL").CompareInfo;
var options = CompareOptions.IgnoreCase | CompareOptions.IgnoreNonSpace;
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", cities.Where(c => compare.IsPrefix(c, "a", options))));
Console.WriteLine(compare.IndexOf("Zürich", "UR", options));
Console.WriteLine(compare.IsPrefix("Łódź", "lodz", options));         // Ł is its own letter, not L + a mark

// the Turkish-i bug: code that upper-cases with the CURRENT culture breaks for Turkish users
CultureInfo.CurrentCulture = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("tr-TR");
var command = "quit";
Console.WriteLine($"{command.ToUpper()} {command.ToUpper() == "QUIT"}");
Console.WriteLine(command.ToUpperInvariant() == "QUIT");
Console.WriteLine(string.Equals(command, "QUIT", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase));

var cultureKeys = new HashSet<string>(StringComparer.CurrentCultureIgnoreCase) { "file-id" };
var ordinalKeys = new HashSet<string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase) { "file-id" };
Console.WriteLine($"{cultureKeys.Contains("FILE-ID")} {ordinalKeys.Contains("FILE-ID")}");

Time zones, DateTimeOffset, DateOnly and TimeOnly

Store instants as UTC or `DateTimeOffset`, future local events as local time plus a zone id, and dates without a time as `DateOnly`.

using System.Globalization;

// IANA ids work on Windows too (.NET 6+, with ICU)
var berlin = TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById("Europe/Berlin");
var bogota = TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById("America/Bogota");
var invariant = CultureInfo.InvariantCulture;

// store the instant (UTC or DateTimeOffset); convert to the reader's zone only to display it
var paidAt = new DateTimeOffset(2026, 3, 29, 0, 30, 0, TimeSpan.Zero);
foreach (var instant in new[] { paidAt, paidAt.AddHours(1) })
{
    var inBerlin = TimeZoneInfo.ConvertTime(instant, berlin).ToString("HH:mm zzz", invariant);
    var inBogota = TimeZoneInfo.ConvertTime(instant, bogota).ToString("HH:mm zzz", invariant);
    Console.WriteLine($"{instant.ToString("u", invariant)} → Berlin {inBerlin}, Bogotá {inBogota}");
}

// DST makes some local times impossible and others happen twice
Console.WriteLine(berlin.IsInvalidTime(new DateTime(2026, 3, 29, 2, 30, 0)));
Console.WriteLine(berlin.IsAmbiguousTime(new DateTime(2026, 10, 25, 2, 30, 0)));

// a future local event ("the shop opens at 09:00 on 30 March") is a date + time + zone id,
// resolved when needed, because the zone's rules may change before then
var opening = new DateOnly(2026, 3, 30).ToDateTime(new TimeOnly(9, 0));
var openingUtc = TimeZoneInfo.ConvertTimeToUtc(opening, berlin);
var utcText = openingUtc.ToString("HH:mm", invariant);              // ":" is the culture's time separator
Console.WriteLine($"{opening.ToString("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm", invariant)} Berlin = {utcText} UTC");

// a date of birth or a due date has no time and no zone
var due = DateOnly.ParseExact("2026-04-15", "yyyy-MM-dd", invariant);
var daysLeft = due.DayNumber - new DateOnly(2026, 3, 30).DayNumber;
Console.WriteLine($"{daysLeft} days, {due.ToString("D", CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("de-DE"))}");
var mapped = TimeZoneInfo.TryConvertIanaIdToWindowsId("Europe/Berlin", out var windowsId);
Console.WriteLine(mapped ? windowsId : "unknown");
Result

2026-03-29 01:30:00Z → Berlin 03:30 +02:00, Bogotá 20:30 -05:00
